Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: FIN7 has downloaded additional malware to execute on the victim's machine, including by using a PowerShell script to launch shellcode that retrieves an additional payload.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: FIN7 captured screenshots and desktop video recordings.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: FIN7 has used the PowerShell script 3CF9.ps1 to execute `net time`.
Uses T1125 Video Capture: FIN7 created a custom video recording capability that could be used to monitor operations in the victim's environment.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: FIN7 has decoded a malicious PowerShell script using `certutil -decode hex` and has decoded an XOR-obfuscated block of data with the key `qawsed1q2w3e`, which led to the installation of Lizar.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: FIN7 has compromised targeted organizations through exploitation of CVE-2021-31207 in Exchange.
Uses T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain: FIN7 has gained initial access by compromising a victim's software supply chain.

title: ATT&CK Group G0046: FIN7
text:
ATT&CK Group G0046: FIN7
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: FIN7 has used malicious links to lure victims into downloading malware.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: FIN7 lured victims to double-click on images in the attachments they sent which would then execute the hidden LNK file. Additionally, FIN7 has used malicious Microsoft Word and Excel files and Leo VBS to distribute an updated version of JSS …
Uses T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services: FIN7 has exploited ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472) against vulnerable domain controllers.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: FIN7 has used mshta.exe to execute VBScript to execute malicious code on victim systems.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: FIN7 has used `rundll32.exe` to execute malware on a compromised network.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: FIN7 has utilized the remote management tool Atera to download malware to a compromised system.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: FIN7 has encrypted virtual disk volumes on ESXi servers using a version of Darkside ransomware. Additionally, FIN7 has deployed ransomware as the end payload during big game hunting.
Uses T1497.002 User Activity Based Checks: FIN7 used images embedded into document lures that only activate the payload when a user double clicks to avoid sandboxes.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: FIN7 created new Windows services and added them to the startup directories for persistence.
Uses T1546.011 Application Shimming: FIN7 has used application shim databases for persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: FIN7 malware has created Registry Run and RunOnce keys to establish persistence, and has also added items to the Startup folder.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: FIN7 has signed Carbanak payloads with legally purchased code signing certificates. FIN7 has also digitally signed their phishing documents, backdoors and other staging tools to bypass security controls.

title: ATT&CK Group G0046: FIN7
text:
ATT&CK Group G0046: FIN7
Uses T1558.003 Kerberoasting: FIN7 has used Kerberoasting PowerShell commands such as, `Invoke-Kerberoast` for credential access and to enable lateral movement.
Uses T1559.002 Dynamic Data Exchange: FIN7 spear phishing campaigns have included malicious Word documents with DDE execution.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: FIN7 has added a firewall rule to allow TCP port 59999 inbound and a rule to allow sshd.exe on TCP port 9898.
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: FIN7 has used `attrib +h “C:\ProgramData\ssh”` to make the SSH folder hidden.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: FIN7 has used.txt files to conceal PowerShell commands.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: FIN7 sent spearphishing emails with either malicious Microsoft Documents or RTF files attached.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: FIN7 has conducted broad phishing campaigns using malicious links. Additionally, FIN7 has sent spearphishing emails containing a typosquatted link to “ip-sccanner[.]com.”
Uses T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage: FIN7 has exfiltrated stolen data to the MEGA file sharing site.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: FIN7 has started the SSH service by executing `sc start sshd`.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: FIN7 has used port-protocol mismatches on ports such as 53, 80, 443, and 8080 during C2. FIN7 has used TCP ports 59999 and 9898 for firewall rules.
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: FIN7 has tunneled C2 traffic via OpenSSH.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: FIN7 has registered look-alike domains for use in phishing campaigns. Additionally, FIN7 has registered a malicious domain as `advanced-ip-sccanner[.]com` that redirected to an adversary-controlled Dropbox which contained the malicious executable.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: FIN7 has set up Amazon S3 buckets to host trojanized digital products.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: FIN7 has developed malware for use in operations, including the creation of infected removable media.

title: ATT&CK Group G0046: FIN7
text:
ATT&CK Group G0046: FIN7
Uses T1588.002 Tool: FIN7 has utilized a variety of tools such as Cobalt Strike, PowerSploit, and the remote management tool, Atera for targeting efforts.
Uses T1591 Gather Victim Org Information: FIN7 has compiled a list of victims by filtering companies by revenue using Zoominfo, which is a service that provides business information.
Uses T1591.004 Identify Roles: FIN7 has identified IT staff and employees who had higher levels of administrative rights.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: FIN7 has staged legitimate software, that was trojanized to contain an Atera agent installer, on Amazon S3. FIN7 has also used an open directory web server as a staging server for payloads and other tools, such as OpenSSH and 7zip.
Uses T1608.004 Drive-by Target: FIN7 has compromised a digital product website and modified multiple download links to point to trojanized versions of offered digital products.
Uses T1608.005 Link Target: FIN7 has created a fake link that redirected to an adversary-controlled Dropbox that downloaded the malicious executable.
Uses T1620 Reflective Code Loading: FIN7 has loaded a.NET assembly into the currect execution context via `Reflection.Assembly::Load`.
Uses T1674 Input Injection: FIN7 has used malicious USBs to emulate keystrokes to launch PowerShell to download and execute malware from the adversary's server.

title: ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
text:
ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
UNC3886 is a China-nexus cyberespionage group that has been active since at least 2022, targeting defense, technology, and telecommunication organizations located in the United States and the Asia-Pacific-Japan (APJ) regions. UNC3886 has displayed a deep understanding of edge devices and virtualization technologies through the exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities and the use of novel malware families and utilities.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: UNC3886 has used MiniDump to dump process memory and search for cleartext credentials.
Uses T1008 Fallback Channels: UNC3886 has employed layers of redundancy to maintain access to compromised environments including network devices, hypervisors, and virtual machines.
Uses T1014 Rootkit: UNC3886 has used the publicly available rootkits REPTILE and MEDUSA on targeted VMs.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: UNC3886 has established remote SSH access to targeted ESXi hosts.
Uses T1027.005 Indicator Removal from Tools: UNC3886 has replaced atomic indicators mentioned in threat intelligence publications, sometimes as quickly as under a week after release.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: UNC3886 has named a file ‘fgfm’ in an attempt to disguise it as the legitimate service ‘fgfmd’ which facilitates communication between FortiManager and the FortiGate firewall.
Uses T1037 Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: UNC3886 has attempted to bypass digital signature verification checks at startup by adding a command to the startup config `/etc/init.d/localnet` within the rootfs.gz archive of both FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer devices.
Uses T1037.004 RC Scripts: UNC3886 has placed a bash installation script into `/etc/rc.local.d/` to establish persistence.
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: UNC3886 has used the LOOKOVER sniffer to sniff TACACS+ authentication packets.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: UNC3886 has run scripts to list all running processes on a guest VM from an ESXi host.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: UNC3886 has used a PowerShell script to search memory dumps for credentials.

title: ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
text:
ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: UNC3886 has executed Windows commands on guest virtual machines through `vmtoolsd.exe`.
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: UNC3886 has used a bash script to install malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs).
Uses T1059.006 Python: UNC3886 has used Python scripts to enumerate ESXi hosts and guest VMs.
Uses T1059.012 Hypervisor CLI: UNC3886 has used the esxcli command line utility to modify firewall rules, install malware, and for artifact removal.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: UNC3886 has exploited zero-day vulnerability CVE-2023-20867 to enable execution of privileged commands across Windows, Linux, and PhotonOS (vCenter) guest VMs.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: UNC3886 has used the the esxcli command line to remove files created by malicious vSphere Installation Bundles from disk.
Uses T1070.006 Timestomp: UNC3886 has used scripts to timestomp ESXi hosts prior to installing malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs).
Uses T1070.007 Clear Network Connection History and Configurations: UNC3886 has cleared specific events that contained the threat actor’s IP address from multiple log sources.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: UNC3886 has staged captured credentials in `var/log/ldapd<unique_keyword>.2.gz`.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: UNC3886 has used tools to hijack valid SSH accounts.
Uses T1078.001 Default Accounts: UNC3886 has harvested and used vCenter Server service accounts.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: UNC3886 has used `vmtoolsd.exe` to enumerate files on guest machines.
Uses T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol: UNC3886 has deployed backdoors that communicate over TCP to compromised network devices and over VMCI to ESXi hosts.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: UNC3886 has used installation scripts to collect the system time on targeted ESXi hosts.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: UNC3886 has exploited CVE-2022-42475 in FortiOS SSL VPNs to obtain access.

title: ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
text:
ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: UNC3886 has exoloited CVE-2023-34048 to enable command execution on vCenter servers and CVE-2023-20867 in VMware Tools to execute unauthenticated Guest Operations from ESXi hosts to guest VMs.
Uses T1205 Traffic Signaling: UNC3886 has used the TABLEFLIP traffic redirection utility to listen for specialized command packets on compromised FortiManager devices.
Uses T1205.001 Port Knocking: UNC3886 maintained persistence on FortiGate Firewalls through ICMP port knocking.
Uses T1212 Exploitation for Credential Access: UNC3886 exploited CVE-2022-22948 in VMware vCenter to obtain encrypted credentials from the vCenter postgresDB.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: UNC3886 has used rundll32.exe to execute MiniDump for dumping LSASS process memory.
Uses T1505.006 vSphere Installation Bundles: UNC3886 has used vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to install malware and establish persistence across ESXi hypervisors.
Uses T1548 Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: UNC3886 has used vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) that contained modified descriptor XML files with the `acceptance-level` set to `partner` which allowed for privilege escalation.
Uses T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary: UNC3886 has trojanized Fortinet firmware and replaced the legitimate `/usr/bin/tac_plus` TACACS+ daemon for Linux with a malicious version containing credential logging functionality.
Uses T1555.005 Password Managers: UNC3886 has targeted KeyPass password database files for credential access.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: UNC3886 has used Gzip and the Windows command `makecab` to compress files and stolen credentials from victim systems.
Uses T1560.003 Archive via Custom Method: UNC3886 has XOR encrypted and Gzip compressed captured credentials.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: UNC3886 has disabled OpenSSL digital signature verification of system files through corruption of boot files.
Uses T1562.003 Impair Command History Logging: UNC3886 has tampered with and disabled logging services on targeted systems.

title: ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
text:
ATT&CK Group G1048: UNC3886
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: UNC3886 has used the TABLEFLIP traffic redirection utility and the esxcli command line to modify firewall rules.
Uses T1564.011 Ignore Process Interrupts: UNC3886 modified the startup file `/etc/init.d/localnet` to execute the line `nohup /bin/support &` so the script would run when the system was rebooted.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: UNC3886 has utilzed Python scripts to transfer files between ESXi hosts and guest VMs.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: UNC3886 has deployed custom malware families on Fortinet and VMware systems.
Uses T1587.004 Exploits: UNC3886 has used zero-day vulnerabilities CVE-2022-41328 against FortiOS and CVE-2023-20867 and CVE-2023-34048 against VMware vCenter.
Uses T1588.001 Malware: UNC3886 has used the publicly available rootkits REPTILE and MEDUSA.
Uses T1588.004 Digital Certificates: UNC3886 has deployed malware using the victim's legitimate TLS certificate obtained from a compromised FortiGate device.
Uses T1673 Virtual Machine Discovery: UNC3886 has used scripts to enumerate ESXi hypervisors and their guest VMs.
Uses T1675 ESXi Administration Command: UNC3886 used `vmtoolsd.exe` to run commands on guest virtual machines from a compromised ESXi host.
Uses T1681 Search Threat Vendor Data: UNC3886 has replaced indicators mentioned in open-source threat intelligence publications at times under a week after their release.

title: ATT&CK Group G1047: Velvet Ant
text:
ATT&CK Group G1047: Velvet Ant
Velvet Ant is a threat actor operating since at least 2021. Velvet Ant is associated with complex persistence mechanisms, the targeting of network devices and appliances during operations, and the use of zero day exploits.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Velvet Ant has transferred tools within victim environments using SMB.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Velvet Ant used a malicious DLL, `iviewers.dll`, that mimics the legitimate "OLE/COM Object Viewer" within Windows.
Uses T1037.004 RC Scripts: Velvet Ant used a modified `/etc/rc.local` file on compromised F5 BIG-IP devices to maintain persistence.
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: Velvet Ant has used a custom tool, "VELVETTAP", to perform packet capture from compromised F5 BIG-IP devices.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Velvet Ant used the `wmiexec.py` tool within Impacket for remote process execution via WMI.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: Velvet Ant has enumerated existing network connections on victim devices.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: Velvet Ant initial execution included launching multiple `svchost` processes and injecting code into them.
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: Velvet Ant used a custom tool, VELVETSTING, to parse encoded inbound commands to compromised F5 BIG-IP devices and then execute them via the Unix shell.
Uses T1071 Application Layer Protocol: Velvet Ant has used reverse SSH tunnels to communicate to victim devices.
Uses T1078.003 Local Accounts: Velvet Ant accessed vulnerable Cisco switch devices using accounts with administrator privileges.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Velvet Ant has enumerated local files and folders on victim devices.
Uses T1090.001 Internal Proxy: Velvet Ant has tunneled traffic from victims through an internal, compromised host to proxy communications to command and control nodes.
Uses T1132 Data Encoding: Velvet Ant sent commands to compromised F5 BIG-IP devices in an encoded format requiring a passkey before interpretation and execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G1047: Velvet Ant
text:
ATT&CK Group G1047: Velvet Ant
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: Velvet Ant has leveraged access to internet-facing remote services to compromise and retain access to victim environments.
Uses T1211 Exploitation for Defense Evasion: Velvet Ant exploited CVE-2024-20399 in Cisco Switches to which the threat actor was already able to authenticate in order to escape the NX-OS command line interface and gain access to the underlying operating system for arbitrary command execution.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Velvet Ant attempted to disable local security tools and endpoint detection and response (EDR) software during operations.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: Velvet Ant modified system firewall settings during PlugX installation using `netsh.exe` to open a listening, random high number port on victim devices.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: Velvet Ant executed and installed PlugX as a Windows service.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: Velvet Ant transferred files laterally within victim networks through the Impacket toolkit.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: Velvet Ant has used random high number ports for PlugX listeners on victim devices.
Uses T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography: Velvet Ant has used a reverse SSH shell to securely communicate with victim devices.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Velvet Ant has used malicious DLLs executed via legitimate EXE files through DLL search order hijacking to launch follow-on payloads such as PlugX.

title: ATT&CK Group G0090: WIRTE
text:
ATT&CK Group G0090: WIRTE
WIRTE is a threat group that has been active since at least August 2018. WIRTE has targeted government, diplomatic, financial, military, legal, and technology organizations in the Middle East and Europe.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: WIRTE has named a first stage dropper `Kaspersky Update Agent` in order to appear legitimate.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: WIRTE has used PowerShell for script execution.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: WIRTE has used VBScript in its operations.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: WIRTE has used HTTP for network communication.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: WIRTE has downloaded PowerShell code from the C2 server to be executed.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: WIRTE has used Base64 to decode malicious VBS script.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: WIRTE has attempted to lure users into opening malicious MS Word and Excel files to execute malicious payloads.
Uses T1218.010 Regsvr32: WIRTE has used `regsvr32.exe` to trigger the execution of a malicious script.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: WIRTE has sent emails to intended victims with malicious MS Word and Excel attachments.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: WIRTE has used HTTPS over ports 2083 and 2087 for C2.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: WIRTE has obtained and used Empire for post-exploitation activities.

title: ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
Associated names: TEMP.Isotope, DYMALLOY, Berserk Bear, TG-4192, Crouching Yeti, IRON LIBERTY, Energetic Bear, Ghost Blizzard, BROMINE.
Dragonfly is a cyber espionage group that has been attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16. Active since at least 2010, Dragonfly has targeted defense and aviation companies, government entities, companies related to industrial control systems, and critical infrastructure sectors worldwide through supply chain, spearphishing, and drive-by compromise attacks.
Uses T1003.002 Security Account Manager: Dragonfly has dropped and executed SecretsDump to dump password hashes.
Uses T1003.003 NTDS: Dragonfly has dropped and executed SecretsDump to dump password hashes. They also obtained ntds.dit from domain controllers.
Uses T1003.004 LSA Secrets: Dragonfly has dropped and executed SecretsDump to dump password hashes.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Dragonfly has collected data from local victim systems.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Dragonfly has queried the Registry to identify victim information.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Dragonfly has used batch scripts to enumerate network information, including information about trusts, zones, and the domain.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Dragonfly has likely obtained a list of hosts in the victim environment.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Dragonfly has moved laterally via RDP.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: Dragonfly used the command query user on victim hosts.
Uses T1036.010 Masquerade Account Name: Dragonfly has created accounts disguised as legitimate backup and service accounts as well as an email administration account.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Dragonfly has used scheduled tasks to automatically log out of created accounts every 8 hours as well as to execute malicious files.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Dragonfly has used the command line for execution.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Dragonfly has used PowerShell scripts for execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Dragonfly has used various types of scripting to perform operations, including batch scripts.
Uses T1059.006 Python: Dragonfly has used various types of scripting to perform operations, including Python scripts. The group was observed installing Python 2.7 on a victim.
Uses T1069.002 Domain Groups: Dragonfly has used batch scripts to enumerate administrators and users in the domain.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: Dragonfly has cleared Windows event logs and other logs produced by tools they used, including system, security, terminal services, remote services, and audit logs. The actors also deleted specific Registry keys.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Dragonfly has deleted many of its files used during operations as part of cleanup, including removing applications and deleting screenshots.
Uses T1071.002 File Transfer Protocols: Dragonfly has used SMB for C2.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: Dragonfly has created a directory named "out" in the user's %AppData% folder and copied files to it.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Dragonfly has compromised user credentials and used valid accounts for operations.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Dragonfly has used a batch script to gather folder and file names from victim hosts.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: Dragonfly has used batch scripts to enumerate users on a victim domain controller.
Uses T1098.007 Additional Local or Domain Groups: Dragonfly has added newly created accounts to the administrators group to maintain elevated access.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Dragonfly has copied and installed tools for operations once in the victim environment.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: Dragonfly has attempted to brute force credentials to gain access.
Uses T1110.002 Password Cracking: Dragonfly has dropped and executed tools used for password cracking, including Hydra and CrackMapExec.

title: ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: Dragonfly has modified the Registry to perform multiple techniques through the use of Reg.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: Dragonfly has performed screen captures of victims, including by using a tool, scr.exe (which matched the hash of ScreenUtil).
Uses T1114.002 Remote Email Collection: Dragonfly has accessed email accounts using Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: Dragonfly has used VPNs and Outlook Web Access (OWA) to maintain access to victim networks.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: Dragonfly has identified and browsed file servers in the victim network, sometimes, viewing files pertaining to ICS or Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: Dragonfly has created accounts on victims, including administrator accounts, some of which appeared to be tailored to each individual staging target.
Uses T1187 Forced Authentication: Dragonfly has gathered hashed user credentials over SMB using spearphishing attachments with external resource links and by modifying.LNK file icon resources to collect credentials from virtualized systems.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Dragonfly has compromised targets via strategic web compromise (SWC) utilizing a custom exploit kit.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Dragonfly has conducted SQL injection attacks, exploited vulnerabilities CVE-2019-19781 and CVE-2020-0688 for Citrix and MS Exchange, and CVE-2018-13379 for Fortinet VPNs.
Uses T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain: Dragonfly has placed trojanized installers for control system software on legitimate vendor app stores.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Dragonfly has exploited CVE-2011-0611 in Adobe Flash Player to gain execution on a targeted system.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Dragonfly has used various forms of spearphishing in attempts to get users to open malicious attachments.
Uses T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services: Dragonfly has exploited a Windows Netlogon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472) to obtain access to Windows Active Directory servers.

title: ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G0035: Dragonfly
Uses T1221 Template Injection: Dragonfly has injected SMB URLs into malicious Word spearphishing attachments to initiate Forced Authentication.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: Dragonfly has commonly created Web shells on victims' publicly accessible email and web servers, which they used to maintain access to a victim network and download additional malicious files.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Dragonfly has added the registry value ntdll to the Registry Run key to establish persistence.
Uses T1560 Archive Collected Data: Dragonfly has compressed data into.zip files prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: Dragonfly has disabled host-based firewalls. The group has also globally opened port 3389.
Uses T1564.002 Hidden Users: Dragonfly has modified the Registry to hide created user accounts.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Dragonfly has sent emails with malicious attachments to gain initial access.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Dragonfly has registered domains for targeting intended victims.
Uses T1583.003 Virtual Private Server: Dragonfly has acquired VPS infrastructure for use in malicious campaigns.
Uses T1584.004 Server: Dragonfly has compromised legitimate websites to host C2 and malware modules.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Dragonfly has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz, CrackMapExec, and PsExec.
Uses T1591.002 Business Relationships: Dragonfly has collected open source information to identify relationships between organizations for targeting purposes.
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: Dragonfly has scanned targeted systems for vulnerable Citrix and Microsoft Exchange services.
Uses T1598.002 Spearphishing Attachment: Dragonfly has used spearphishing with Microsoft Office attachments to enable harvesting of user credentials.
Uses T1598.003 Spearphishing Link: Dragonfly has used spearphishing with PDF attachments containing malicious links that redirected to credential harvesting websites.
Uses T1608.004 Drive-by Target: Dragonfly has compromised websites to redirect traffic and to host exploit kits.

title: ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
text:
ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
Associated names: COBALT GYPSY, IRN2, APT34, Helix Kitten, Evasive Serpens, Hazel Sandstorm, EUROPIUM, ITG13, Earth Simnavaz, Crambus, TA452.
OilRig is a suspected Iranian threat group that has targeted Middle Eastern and international victims since at least 2014. The group has targeted a variety of sectors, including financial, government, energy, chemical, and telecommunications. It appears the group carries out supply chain attacks, leveraging the trust relationship between organizations to attack their primary targets. The group works on behalf of the Iranian government based on infrastructure details that contain references to Iran, use of Iranian infrastructure, and targeting that aligns with nation-state interests.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as Mimikatz to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1003.004 LSA Secrets: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as LaZagne to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1003.005 Cached Domain Credentials: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as LaZagne to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: OilRig has used PowerShell to upload files from compromised systems.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: OilRig has used sc query on a victim to gather information about services.
Uses T1008 Fallback Channels: OilRig malware ISMAgent falls back to its DNS tunneling mechanism if it is unable to reach the C2 server over HTTP.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: OilRig has used reg query “HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Default” on a victim to query the Registry.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: OilRig has run ipconfig /all on a victim.

title: ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
text:
ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: OilRig has used Remote Desktop Protocol for lateral movement. The group has also used tunneling tools to tunnel RDP into the environment.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: OilRig has used Putty to access compromised systems.
Uses T1025 Data from Removable Media: OilRig has used Wireshark’s usbcapcmd utility to capture USB traffic.
Uses T1027.005 Indicator Removal from Tools: OilRig has tested malware samples to determine AV detection and subsequently modified the samples to ensure AV evasion.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: OilRig has encrypted and encoded data in its malware, including by using base64.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: OilRig has run whoami on a victim.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: OilRig has used.doc file extensions to mask malicious executables.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: OilRig has named a downloaded copy of the Plink tunneling utility as \ProgramData\Adobe.exe.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: OilRig has used the publicly available tool SoftPerfect Network Scanner as well as a custom tool called GOLDIRONY to conduct network scanning.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: OilRig has used WMI for execution.
Uses T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol: OilRig has exfiltrated data via Microsoft Exchange and over FTP separately from its primary C2 channel over DNS.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: OilRig has used netstat -an on a victim to get a listing of network connections.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: OilRig has created scheduled tasks that run a VBScript to execute a payload on victim machines.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: OilRig has employed keyloggers including KEYPUNCH and LONGWATCH.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: OilRig has run tasklist on a victim's machine and used infostealers to capture processes.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: OilRig has used various types of scripting for execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
text:
ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: OilRig has used PowerShell scripts for execution, including use of a macro to run a PowerShell command to decode file contents.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: OilRig has used macros to deliver malware such as QUADAGENT and OopsIE. OilRig has used batch scripts.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: OilRig has used VBScript macros for execution on compromised hosts.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: OilRig has exploited the Windows Kernel Elevation of Privilege vulnerability, CVE-2024-30088.
Uses T1069.001 Local Groups: OilRig has used net localgroup administrators to find local administrators on compromised systems.
Uses T1069.002 Domain Groups: OilRig has used net group /domain, net group “domain admins” /domain, and net group “Exchange Trusted Subsystem” /domain to find domain group permission settings.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: OilRig has deleted files associated with their payload after execution.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: OilRig has used HTTP for C2.
Uses T1071.004 DNS: OilRig has used DNS for C2 including the publicly available requestbin.net tunneling service.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: OilRig has used compromised credentials to access other systems on a victim network.
Uses T1078.002 Domain Accounts: OilRig has used an exfiltration tool named STEALHOOK to retreive valid domain credentials.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: OilRig has run hostname and systeminfo on a victim.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: OilRig has run net user, net user /domain, net group “domain admins” /domain, and net group “Exchange Trusted Subsystem” /domain to get account listings on a victim.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: OilRig has run net user, net user /domain, net group “domain admins” /domain, and net group “Exchange Trusted Subsystem” /domain to get account listings on a victim.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: OilRig had downloaded remote files onto victim infrastructure.

title: ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
text:
ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
Uses T1110 Brute Force: OilRig has used brute force techniques to obtain credentials.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: OilRig has used reg.exe to modify system configuration.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: OilRig has a tool called CANDYKING to capture a screenshot of user's desktop.
Uses T1115 Clipboard Data: OilRig has used infostealer tools to copy clipboard data.
Uses T1119 Automated Collection: OilRig has used automated collection.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: OilRig has used tools to identify if a mouse is connected to a targeted system.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: OilRig uses remote services such as VPN, Citrix, or OWA to persist in an environment.
Uses T1137.004 Outlook Home Page: OilRig has abused the Outlook Home Page feature for persistence. OilRig has also used CVE-2017-11774 to roll back the initial patch designed to protect against Home Page abuse.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: A OilRig macro has run a PowerShell command to decode file contents. OilRig has also used certutil to decode base64-encoded files on victims.
Uses T1195 Supply Chain Compromise: OilRig has leveraged compromised organizations to conduct supply chain attacks on government entities.
Uses T1201 Password Policy Discovery: OilRig has used net.exe in a script with net accounts /domain to find the password policy of a domain.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: OilRig has exploited CVE-2024-30088 to run arbitrary code in the context of `SYSTEM`.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: OilRig has delivered malicious links to achieve execution on the target system.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: OilRig has delivered macro-enabled documents that required targets to click the "enable content" button to execute the payload on the system.
Uses T1218.001 Compiled HTML File: OilRig has used a CHM payload to load and execute another malicious file once delivered to a victim.

title: ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
text:
ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: OilRig has incorporated remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools into their operations including ngrok.
Uses T1497.001 System Checks: OilRig has used macros to verify if a mouse is connected to a compromised machine.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: OilRig has used web shells, often to maintain access to a victim network.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: OilRig has used a compromised Domain Controller to create a service on a remote host.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as LaZagne to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: OilRig has signed its malware with stolen certificates.
Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as LaZagne to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access.
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: OilRig has used credential dumping tools such as LaZagne to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system and to Outlook Web Access. OilRig has also used tool named PICKPOCKET to dump passwords from web browsers.
Uses T1555.004 Windows Credential Manager: OilRig has used credential dumping tool named VALUEVAULT to steal credentials from the Windows Credential Manager.
Uses T1556.002 Password Filter DLL: OilRig has registered a password filter DLL in order to drop malware.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: OilRig has modified Windows firewall rules to enable remote access.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: OilRig has sent spearphising emails with malicious attachments to potential victims using compromised and/or spoofed email accounts.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: OilRig has sent spearphising emails with malicious links to potential victims.
Uses T1566.003 Spearphishing via Service: OilRig has used LinkedIn to send spearphishing links.

title: ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
text:
ATT&CK Group G0049: OilRig
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: OilRig has used the Plink utility and other tools to create tunnels to C2 servers.
Uses T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography: OilRig used the PowerExchange utility and other tools to create tunnels to C2 servers.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: OilRig has set up fake VPN portals, conference sign ups, and job application websites to target victims.
Uses T1586.002 Email Accounts: OilRig has compromised email accounts to send phishing emails.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: OilRig actively developed and used a series of downloaders during 2022.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: OilRig has made use of the publicly available tools including Plink and Mimikatz.
Uses T1588.003 Code Signing Certificates: OilRig has obtained stolen code signing certificates to digitally sign malware.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: OilRig has hosted malware on fake websites designed to target specific audiences.

title: ATT&CK Group G0020: Equation
text:
ATT&CK Group G0020: Equation
Equation is a sophisticated threat group that employs multiple remote access tools. The group is known to use zero-day exploits and has developed the capability to overwrite the firmware of hard disk drives.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: Equation has used tools with the functionality to search for specific information about the attached hard drive that could be used to identify and overwrite the firmware.
Uses T1480.001 Environmental Keying: Equation has been observed utilizing environmental keying in payload delivery.
Uses T1542.002 Component Firmware: Equation is known to have the capability to overwrite the firmware on hard drives from some manufacturers.
Uses T1564.005 Hidden File System: Equation has used an encrypted virtual file system stored in the Windows Registry.

title: ATT&CK Group G0117: Fox Kitten
text:
ATT&CK Group G0117: Fox Kitten
Associated names: UNC757, Parisite, Pioneer Kitten, RUBIDIUM, Lemon Sandstorm.
Fox Kitten is threat actor with a suspected nexus to the Iranian government that has been active since at least 2017 against entities in the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, Australia, and North America. Fox Kitten has targeted multiple industrial verticals including oil and gas, technology, government, defense, healthcare, manufacturing, and engineering.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: Fox Kitten has used prodump to dump credentials from LSASS.
Uses T1003.003 NTDS: Fox Kitten has used Volume Shadow Copy to access credential information from NTDS.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Fox Kitten has searched local system resources to access sensitive documents.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Fox Kitten has accessed Registry hives ntuser.dat and UserClass.dat.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Fox Kitten has used Angry IP Scanner to detect remote systems.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Fox Kitten has used RDP to log in and move laterally in the target environment.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Fox Kitten has used valid accounts to access SMB shares.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Fox Kitten has used the PuTTY and Plink tools for lateral movement.
Uses T1021.005 VNC: Fox Kitten has installed TightVNC server and client on compromised servers and endpoints for lateral movement.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: Fox Kitten has base64 encoded scripts to avoid detection.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Fox Kitten has base64 encoded payloads to avoid detection.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Fox Kitten has named the task for a reverse proxy lpupdate to appear legitimate.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Fox Kitten has named binaries and configuration files svhost and dllhost respectively to appear legitimate.
Uses T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive: Fox Kitten has searched network shares to access sensitive documents.

title: ATT&CK Group G0117: Fox Kitten
text:
ATT&CK Group G0117: Fox Kitten
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: Fox Kitten has used tools including NMAP to conduct broad scanning to identify open ports.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Fox Kitten has used Scheduled Tasks for persistence and to load and execute a reverse proxy binary.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Fox Kitten has used a Perl reverse shell to communicate with C2.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Fox Kitten has used PowerShell scripts to access credential data.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Fox Kitten has used cmd.exe likely as a password changing mechanism.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Fox Kitten has used valid credentials with various services during lateral movement.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Fox Kitten has used WizTree to obtain network files and directory listings.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: Fox Kitten has accessed ntuser.dat and UserClass.dat on compromised hosts.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: Fox Kitten has used the Softerra LDAP browser to browse documentation on service accounts.
Uses T1090 Proxy: Fox Kitten has used the open source reverse proxy tools including FRPC and Go Proxy to establish connections from C2 to local servers.
Uses T1102 Web Service: Fox Kitten has used Amazon Web Services to host C2.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Fox Kitten has downloaded additional tools including PsExec directly to endpoints.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: Fox Kitten has brute forced RDP credentials.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: Fox Kitten has created a local user account with administrator privileges.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Fox Kitten has exploited known vulnerabilities in Fortinet, PulseSecure, and Palo Alto VPN appliances.
Uses T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services: Fox Kitten has exploited known vulnerabilities in remote services including RDP.
Uses T1213.005 Messaging Applications: Fox Kitten has accessed victim security and IT environments and Microsoft Teams to mine valuable information.

title: ATT&CK Group G0117: Fox Kitten
text:
ATT&CK Group G0117: Fox Kitten
Uses T1217 Browser Information Discovery: Fox Kitten has used Google Chrome bookmarks to identify internal resources and assets.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: Fox Kitten has installed web shells on compromised hosts to maintain access.
Uses T1530 Data from Cloud Storage: Fox Kitten has obtained files from the victim's cloud storage instances.
Uses T1546.008 Accessibility Features: Fox Kitten has used sticky keys to launch a command prompt.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: Fox Kitten has accessed files to gain valid credentials.
Uses T1555.005 Password Managers: Fox Kitten has used scripts to access credential information from the KeePass database.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: Fox Kitten has used 7-Zip to archive data.
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: Fox Kitten has used protocol tunneling for communication and RDP activity on compromised hosts through the use of open source tools such as ngrok and custom tool SSHMinion.
Uses T1585 Establish Accounts: Fox Kitten has created KeyBase accounts to communicate with ransomware victims.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: Fox Kitten has used a Twitter account to communicate with ransomware victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Associated names: Labyrinth Chollima, HIDDEN COBRA, Guardians of Peace, ZINC, NICKEL ACADEMY, Diamond Sleet.
Lazarus Group is a North Korean state-sponsored cyber threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB). Lazarus Group has been active since at least 2009 and is reportedly responsible for the November 2014 destructive wiper attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment, identified by Novetta as part of Operation Blockbuster. Malware used by Lazarus Group correlates to other reported campaigns, including Operation Flame, Operation 1Mission, Operation Troy, DarkSeoul, and Ten Days of Rain.

North Korea’s cyber operations have shown a consistent pattern of adaptation, forming and reorganizing units as national priorities shift. These units frequently share personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft, making it difficult to attribute specific operations with high confidence. Public reporting often uses “Lazarus Group” as an umbrella term for multiple North Korean cyber operators conducting espionage, destructive attacks, and financially motivated campaigns.
Uses T1001.003 Protocol or Service Impersonation: Lazarus Group malware also uses a unique form of communication encryption known as FakeTLS that mimics TLS but uses a different encryption method, potentially evading SSL traffic inspection/decryption.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Lazarus Group has collected data and files from compromised networks.
Uses T1008 Fallback Channels: Lazarus Group malware SierraAlfa sends data to one of the hard-coded C2 servers chosen at random, and if the transmission fails, chooses a new C2 server to attempt the transmission again.
Uses T1010 Application Window Discovery: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia obtains and sends to its C2 server the title of the window for each running process. The KilaAlfa keylogger also reports the title of the window in the foreground.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia checks Registry keys within HKCU and HKLM to determine if certain applications are present, including SecureCRT, Terminal Services, RealVNC, TightVNC, UltraVNC, Radmin, mRemote, TeamViewer, FileZilla, pcAnyware, and Remote Desktop. Another Lazarus Group malware sample checks for …
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia obtains and sends to its C2 server information about the first network interface card’s configuration, including IP address, gateways, subnet mask, DHCP information, and whether WINS is available.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Lazarus Group malware SierraCharlie uses RDP for propagation.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Lazarus Group malware SierraAlfa accesses the ADMIN$ share via SMB to conduct lateral movement.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Lazarus Group used SSH and the PuTTy PSCP utility to gain access to a restricted segment of a compromised network.
Uses T1027.007 Dynamic API Resolution: Lazarus Group has used a custom hashing method to resolve APIs used in shellcode.
Uses T1027.009 Embedded Payloads: Lazarus Group has distributed malicious payloads embedded in PNG files.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Lazarus Group has used multiple types of encryption and encoding for their payloads, including AES, Caracachs, RC4, XOR, Base64, and other tricks such as creating aliases in code for Native API function names.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: Various Lazarus Group malware enumerates logged-on users.
Uses T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities: Lazarus Group has renamed system utilities such as wscript.exe and mshta.exe.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Lazarus Group has used a scheduled task named `SRCheck` to mask the execution of a malicious.dll.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Lazarus Group has renamed malicious code to disguise it as Microsoft's narrator and other legitimate files.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: Lazarus Group has exfiltrated data and files over a C2 channel through its various tools and malware.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: Lazarus Group has used nmap from a router VM to scan ports on systems within the restricted segment of an enterprise network.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Lazarus Group has used WMIC for discovery as well as to execute payloads for persistence and lateral movement.
Uses T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol: Lazarus Group malware SierraBravo-Two generates an email message via SMTP containing information about newly infected victims.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: Lazarus Group has used net use to identify and establish a network connection with a remote host.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Lazarus Group has used schtasks for persistence including through the periodic execution of a remote XSL script or a dropped VBS payload.
Uses T1055.001 Dynamic-link Library Injection: A Lazarus Group malware sample performs reflective DLL injection.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: Lazarus Group malware KiloAlfa contains keylogging functionality.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Several Lazarus Group malware families gather a list of running processes on a victim system and send it to their C2 server. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group also gathers process times.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Lazarus Group has used PowerShell to execute commands and malicious code.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Lazarus Group malware uses cmd.exe to execute commands on a compromised host. A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group uses a batch file mechanism to delete its binaries from the system.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: Lazarus Group has used VBA and embedded macros in Word documents to execute malicious code.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1070 Indicator Removal: Lazarus Group has restored malicious KernelCallbackTable code to its original state after the process execution flow has been hijacked.
Uses T1070.003 Clear Command History: Lazarus Group has routinely deleted log files on a compromised router, including automatic log deletion through the use of the logrotate utility.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Lazarus Group malware has deleted files in various ways, including "suicide scripts" to delete malware binaries from the victim. Lazarus Group also uses secure file deletion to delete files from the victim.
Uses T1070.006 Timestomp: Several Lazarus Group malware families use timestomping, including modifying the last write timestamp of a specified Registry key to a random date, as well as copying the timestamp for legitimate.exe files (such as calc.exe or mspaint.exe) to its dropped files.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Lazarus Group has conducted C2 over HTTP and HTTPS.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia saves information gathered about the victim to a file that is saved in the %TEMP% directory, then compressed, encrypted, and uploaded to a C2 server.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Lazarus Group has used administrator credentials to gain access to restricted network segments.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Several Lazarus Group malware families collect information on the type and version of the victim OS, as well as the victim computer name and CPU information.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Lazarus Group malware can use a common function to identify target files by their extension, and some also enumerate files and directories, including a Destover-like variant that lists files and gathers information for all drives.
Uses T1090.001 Internal Proxy: Lazarus Group has used a compromised router to serve as a proxy between a victim network's corporate and restricted segments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1090.002 External Proxy: Lazarus Group has used multiple proxies to obfuscate network traffic from victims.
Uses T1098 Account Manipulation: Lazarus Group malware WhiskeyDelta-Two contains a function that attempts to rename the administrator’s account.
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: Lazarus Group has used GitHub as C2, pulling hosted image payloads then committing command execution output to files in specific directories.
Uses T1104 Multi-Stage Channels: Lazarus Group has used multi-stage malware components that inject later stages into separate processes.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Lazarus Group has downloaded files, malware, and tools from its C2 onto a compromised host.
Uses T1106 Native API: Lazarus Group has used the Windows API ObtainUserAgentString to obtain the User-Agent from a compromised host to connect to a C2 server. Lazarus Group has also used various, often lesser known, functions to perform various types of Discovery and Process …
Uses T1110.003 Password Spraying: Lazarus Group malware attempts to connect to Windows shares for lateral movement by using a generated list of usernames, which center around permutations of the username Administrator, and weak passwords.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: A Destover-like implant used by Lazarus Group can obtain the current system time and send it to the C2 server.
Uses T1132.001 Standard Encoding: A Lazarus Group malware sample encodes data with base64.
Uses T1134.002 Create Process with Token: Lazarus Group keylogger KiloAlfa obtains user tokens from interactive sessions to execute itself with API call CreateProcessAsUserA under that user's context.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: Lazarus Group has used shellcode within macros to decrypt and manually map DLLs and shellcode into memory at runtime.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Lazarus Group delivered RATANKBA and other malicious code to victims via a compromised legitimate website.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1202 Indirect Command Execution: Lazarus Group persistence mechanisms have used forfiles.exe to execute.htm files.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Lazarus Group has exploited Adobe Flash vulnerability CVE-2018-4878 for execution.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Lazarus Group has attempted to get users to launch a malicious Microsoft Word attachment delivered via a spearphishing email.
Uses T1218 System Binary Proxy Execution: Lazarus Group lnk files used for persistence have abused the Windows Update Client (wuauclt.exe) to execute a malicious DLL.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: Lazarus Group has used mshta.exe to execute HTML pages downloaded by initial access documents.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: Lazarus Group has used rundll32 to execute malicious payloads on a compromised host.
Uses T1485 Data Destruction: Lazarus Group has used a custom secure delete function to overwrite file contents with data from heap memory.
Uses T1489 Service Stop: Lazarus Group has stopped the MSExchangeIS service to render Exchange contents inaccessible to users.
Uses T1491.001 Internal Defacement: Lazarus Group replaced the background wallpaper of systems with a threatening image after rendering the system unbootable with a Disk Structure Wipe.
Uses T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: Lazarus Group has rebooted systems after destroying files and wiping the MBR on infected systems.
Uses T1542.003 Bootkit: Lazarus Group malware WhiskeyAlfa-Three modifies sector 0 of the Master Boot Record (MBR) to ensure that the malware will persist even if a victim machine shuts down.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: Several Lazarus Group malware families install themselves as new services.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Lazarus Group has maintained persistence by loading malicious code into a startup folder or by adding a Registry Run key.
Uses T1547.009 Shortcut Modification: Lazarus Group malware has maintained persistence on a system by creating a LNK shortcut in the user’s Startup folder.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: Lazarus Group has digitally signed malware and utilities to evade detection.
Uses T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay: Lazarus Group executed Responder using the command [Responder file path] -i [IP address] -rPv on a compromised host to harvest credentials and move laterally.
Uses T1560 Archive Collected Data: Lazarus Group has compressed exfiltrated data with RAR and used RomeoDelta malware to archive specified directories in.zip format, encrypt the.zip file, and upload it to C2.
Uses T1560.002 Archive via Library: Lazarus Group malware IndiaIndia saves information gathered about the victim to a file that is compressed with Zlib, encrypted, and uploaded to a C2 server.
Uses T1560.003 Archive via Custom Method: A Lazarus Group malware sample encrypts data using a simple byte based XOR operation prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1561.001 Disk Content Wipe: Lazarus Group has used malware like WhiskeyAlfa to overwrite the first 64MB of every drive with a mix of static and random buffers. A similar process is then used to wipe content in logical drives and, finally, attempt to wipe …
Uses T1561.002 Disk Structure Wipe: Lazarus Group malware SHARPKNOT overwrites and deletes the Master Boot Record (MBR) on the victim's machine and has possessed MBR wiper malware since at least 2009.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Lazarus Group malware TangoDelta attempts to terminate various processes associated with McAfee. Additionally, Lazarus Group malware SHARPKNOT disables the Microsoft Windows System Event Notification and Alerter services..
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: Various Lazarus Group malware modifies the Windows firewall to allow incoming connections or disable it entirely using netsh.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: Lazarus Group has used a VBA Macro to set its file attributes to System and Hidden and has named files with a dot prefix to hide them from the Finder application.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Lazarus Group has targeted victims with spearphishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Word documents.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Lazarus Group has sent malicious links to victims via email.
Uses T1566.003 Spearphishing via Service: Lazarus Group has used social media platforms, including LinkedIn and Twitter, to send spearphishing messages.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: Some Lazarus Group malware uses a list of ordered port numbers to choose a port for C2 traffic, creating port-protocol mismatches.
Uses T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography: Several Lazarus Group malware families encrypt C2 traffic using custom code that uses XOR with an ADD operation and XOR with a SUB operation. Another Lazarus Group malware sample XORs C2 traffic. Other Lazarus Group malware uses Caracachs encryption to …
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Lazarus Group has replaced `win_fw.dll`, an internal component that is executed during IDA Pro installation, with a malicious DLL to download and execute a payload. Lazarus Group utilized DLL side-loading to execute malicious payloads through abuse of the legitimate processes …
Uses T1574.013 KernelCallbackTable: Lazarus Group has abused the KernelCallbackTable to hijack process control flow and execute shellcode.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Lazarus Group has acquired domains related to their campaigns to act as distribution points and C2 channels.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: Lazarus Group has hosted malicious downloads on Github.
Uses T1584.004 Server: Lazarus Group has compromised servers to stage malicious tools.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: Lazarus Group has created new Twitter accounts to conduct social engineering against potential victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0032: Lazarus Group
Uses T1585.002 Email Accounts: Lazarus Group has created new email accounts for spearphishing operations.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: Lazarus Group has developed custom malware for use in their operations.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Lazarus Group has obtained a variety of tools for their operations, including Responder and PuTTy PSCP.
Uses T1588.004 Digital Certificates: Lazarus Group has obtained SSL certificates for their C2 domains.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: Lazarus Group collected email addresses belonging to various departments of a targeted organization which were used in follow-on phishing campaigns.
Uses T1591 Gather Victim Org Information: Lazarus Group has studied publicly available information about a targeted organization to tailor spearphishing efforts against specific departments and/or individuals.
Uses T1620 Reflective Code Loading: Lazarus Group has changed memory protection permissions then overwritten in memory DLL function code with shellcode, which was later executed via KernelCallbackTable hijacking. Lazarus Group has also used shellcode within macros to decrypt and manually map DLLs into memory at …
Uses T1680 Local Storage Discovery: A Destover-like variant used by Lazarus Group collects disk space information and sends it to its C2 server.

title: ATT&CK Group G0143: Aquatic Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0143: Aquatic Panda
Aquatic Panda is a suspected China-based threat group with a dual mission of intelligence collection and industrial espionage. Active since at least May 2020, Aquatic Panda has primarily targeted entities in the telecommunications, technology, and government sectors.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: Aquatic Panda has attempted to harvest credentials through LSASS memory dumping.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Aquatic Panda captured local Windows security event log data from victim machines using the wevtutil utility to extract contents to an evtx output file.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: Aquatic Panda has attempted to discover services for third party EDR products.
Uses T1021 Remote Services: Aquatic Panda used remote scheduled tasks to install malicious software on victim systems during lateral movement actions.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Aquatic Panda leveraged stolen credentials to move laterally via RDP in victim environments.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Aquatic Panda used remote shares to enable lateral movement in victim environments.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Aquatic Panda used SSH with captured user credentials to move laterally in victim environments.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: Aquatic Panda has encoded PowerShell commands in Base64.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: Aquatic Panda gathers information on recently logged-in users on victim devices.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Aquatic Panda created new, malicious services using names such as Windows User Service to attempt to blend in with legitimate items on victim systems.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Aquatic Panda renamed or moved malicious binaries to legitimate locations to evade defenses and blend into victim environments.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Aquatic Panda used WMI for lateral movement in victim environments.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Aquatic Panda has downloaded additional scripts and executed Base64 encoded commands in PowerShell.

title: ATT&CK Group G0143: Aquatic Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0143: Aquatic Panda
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Aquatic Panda has attempted and failed to run Bash commands on a Windows host by passing them to cmd /C.
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: Aquatic Panda used malicious shell scripts in Linux environments following access via SSH to install Linux versions of Winnti malware.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: Aquatic Panda clears Windows Event Logs following activity to evade defenses.
Uses T1070.003 Clear Command History: Aquatic Panda cleared command history in Linux environments to remove traces of activity after operations.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Aquatic Panda has deleted malicious executables from compromised machines.
Uses T1078.002 Domain Accounts: Aquatic Panda used multiple mechanisms to capture valid user accounts for victim domains to enable lateral movement and access to additional hosts in victim environments.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Aquatic Panda has used native OS commands to understand privilege levels and system details.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: Aquatic Panda used the last command in Linux environments to identify recently logged-in users on victim machines.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Aquatic Panda has downloaded additional malware onto compromised hosts.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: Aquatic Panda modified the victim registry to enable the `RestrictedAdmin` mode feature, allowing for pass the hash behaviors to function via RDP.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: Aquatic Panda used rundll32.exe to proxy execution of a malicious DLL file identified as a keylogging binary.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: Aquatic Panda has attempted to discover third party endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools on compromised systems.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: Aquatic Panda created new Windows services for persistence that masqueraded as legitimate Windows services via name change.

title: ATT&CK Group G0143: Aquatic Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0143: Aquatic Panda
Uses T1550.002 Pass the Hash: Aquatic Panda used a registry edit to enable a Windows feature called RestrictedAdmin in victim environments. This change allowed Aquatic Panda to leverage "pass the hash" mechanisms as the alteration allows for RDP connections with a valid account name and …
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: Aquatic Panda has used several publicly available tools, including WinRAR and 7zip, to compress collected files and memory dumps prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Aquatic Panda has attempted to stop endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools on compromised systems.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Aquatic Panda has used DLL search-order hijacking to load `exe`, `dll`, and `dat` files into memory. Aquatic Panda loaded a malicious DLL into the legitimate Windows Security Health Service executable (SecurityHealthService.exe) to execute malicious code on victim systems.
Uses T1574.006 Dynamic Linker Hijacking: Aquatic Panda modified the ld.so preload file in Linux environments to enable persistence for Winnti malware.
Uses T1588.001 Malware: Aquatic Panda has acquired and used njRAT in its operations.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Aquatic Panda has acquired and used Cobalt Strike in its operations.
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: Aquatic Panda has used publicly accessible DNS logging services to identify servers vulnerable to Log4j (CVE 2021-44228).
Uses T1654 Log Enumeration: Aquatic Panda enumerated logs related to authentication in Linux environments prior to deleting selective entries for defense evasion purposes.

title: ATT&CK Group G1034: Daggerfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G1034: Daggerfly
Associated names: Evasive Panda, BRONZE HIGHLAND.
Daggerfly is a People's Republic of China-linked APT entity active since at least 2012. Daggerfly has targeted individuals, government and NGO entities, and telecommunication companies in Asia and Africa. Daggerfly is associated with exclusive use of MgBot malware and is noted for several potential supply chain infection campaigns.
Uses T1003.002 Security Account Manager: Daggerfly used Reg to dump the Security Account Manager (SAM) hive from victim machines for follow-on credential extraction.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Daggerfly used Reg to dump the Security Account Manager (SAM), System, and Security Windows registry hives from victim machines.
Uses T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities: Daggerfly used a renamed version of rundll32.exe, such as "dbengin.exe" located in the `ProgramData\Microsoft\PlayReady` directory, to proxy malicious DLL execution.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Daggerfly has attempted to use scheduled tasks for persistence in victim environments.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Daggerfly used PowerShell to download and execute remote-hosted files on victim systems.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Daggerfly uses HTTP for command and control communication.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Daggerfly utilizes victim machine operating system information to create custom User Agent strings for subsequent command and control communication.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Daggerfly has used PowerShell and BITSAdmin to retrieve follow-on payloads from external locations for execution on victim machines.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: Daggerfly created a local account on victim machines to maintain access.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Daggerfly has used strategic website compromise for initial access against victims.
Uses T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain: Daggerfly is associated with several supply chain compromises using malicious updates to compromise victims.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Daggerfly has used strategic website compromise to deliver a malicious link requiring user interaction.

title: ATT&CK Group G1034: Daggerfly
text:
ATT&CK Group G1034: Daggerfly
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: Daggerfly proxied execution of malicious DLLs through a renamed rundll32.exe binary.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: Daggerfly has used signed, but not notarized, malicious files for execution in macOS environments.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Daggerfly has used legitimate software to side-load PlugX loaders onto victim systems. Daggerfly is also linked to multiple other instances of side-loading for initial loading activity.
Uses T1584.004 Server: Daggerfly compromised web servers hosting updates for software as part of a supply chain intrusion.
Uses T1587.002 Code Signing Certificates: Daggerfly created code signing certificates to sign malicious macOS files.

title: ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
text:
ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
TeamTNT is a threat group that has primarily targeted cloud and containerized environments. The group as been active since at least October 2019 and has mainly focused its efforts on leveraging cloud and container resources to deploy cryptocurrency miners in victim environments.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: TeamTNT has searched for services such as Alibaba Cloud Security's aliyun service and BMC Helix Cloud Security's bmc-agent service in order to disable them.
Uses T1014 Rootkit: TeamTNT has used rootkits such as the open-source Diamorphine rootkit and their custom bots to hide cryptocurrency mining activities on the machine.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: TeamTNT has enumerated the host machine’s IP address.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: TeamTNT has used SSH to connect back to victim machines. TeamTNT has also used SSH to transfer tools and payloads onto victim hosts and execute them.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: TeamTNT has used UPX and Ezuri packer to pack its binaries.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: TeamTNT has encrypted its binaries via AES and encoded files using Base64.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: TeamTNT has disguised their scripts with docker-related file names.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: TeamTNT has replaced.dockerd and.dockerenv with their own scripts and cryptocurrency mining software.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: TeamTNT has used masscan to search for open Docker API ports and Kubernetes clusters. TeamTNT has also used malware that utilizes zmap and zgrab to search for vulnerable services in cloud environments.
Uses T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: TeamTNT has sent locally staged files with collected credentials to C2 servers using cURL.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: TeamTNT has run netstat -anp to search for rival malware connections. TeamTNT has also used `libprocesshider` to modify /etc/ld.so.preload.

title: ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
text:
ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: TeamTNT has searched for rival malware and removes it if found. TeamTNT has also searched for running processes containing the strings aliyun or liyun to identify machines running Alibaba Cloud Security tools.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: TeamTNT has executed PowerShell commands in batch scripts.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: TeamTNT has used batch scripts to download tools and executing cryptocurrency miners.
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: TeamTNT has used shell scripts for execution.
Uses T1059.009 Cloud API: TeamTNT has leveraged AWS CLI to enumerate cloud environments with compromised credentials.
Uses T1059.013 Container CLI/API: TeamTNT targeted misconfigured containers and used container CLI tools.
Uses T1070.002 Clear Linux or Mac System Logs: TeamTNT has removed system logs from /var/log/syslog.
Uses T1070.003 Clear Command History: TeamTNT has cleared command history with history -c.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: TeamTNT has used a payload that removes itself after running. TeamTNT also has deleted locally staged files for collecting credentials or scan results for local IP addresses after exfiltrating them.
Uses T1071 Application Layer Protocol: TeamTNT has used an IRC bot for C2 communications.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: TeamTNT has the `curl` command to send credentials over HTTP and the `curl` and `wget` commands to download new software. TeamTNT has also used a custom user agent HTTP header in shell scripts.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: TeamTNT has aggregated collected credentials in text files before exfiltrating.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: TeamTNT has searched for system version, architecture, and hostname information.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: TeamTNT has used a script that checks `/proc/*/environ` for environment variables related to AWS.
Uses T1098.004 SSH Authorized Keys: TeamTNT has added RSA keys in authorized_keys.
Uses T1102 Web Service: TeamTNT has leveraged iplogger.org to send collected data back to C2.

title: ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
text:
ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: TeamTNT has the curl and wget commands as well as batch scripts to download new tools.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: TeamTNT has searched for attached VGA devices using lspci.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: TeamTNT has used open-source tools such as Weave Scope to target exposed Docker API ports and gain initial access to victim environments. TeamTNT has also targeted exposed kubelets for Kubernetes environments.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: TeamTNT has created local privileged users on victim machines.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: TeamTNT has used a script that decodes a Base64-encoded version of WeaveWorks Scope.
Uses T1204.003 Malicious Image: TeamTNT has relied on users to download and execute malicious Docker images.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: TeamTNT has established tmate sessions for C2 communications.
Uses T1222.002 Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification: TeamTNT has modified the permissions on binaries with chattr.
Uses T1496.001 Compute Hijacking: TeamTNT has deployed XMRig Docker images to mine cryptocurrency. TeamTNT has also infected Docker containers and Kubernetes clusters with XMRig, and used RainbowMiner and lolMiner for mining cryptocurrency.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: TeamTNT has searched for security products on infected machines.
Uses T1543.002 Systemd Service: TeamTNT has established persistence through the creation of a cryptocurrency mining system service using systemctl.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: TeamTNT has used malware that adds cryptocurrency miners as a service.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: TeamTNT has added batch scripts to the startup folder.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: TeamTNT has searched for unsecured AWS credentials and Docker API credentials.
Uses T1552.004 Private Keys: TeamTNT has searched for unsecured SSH keys.
Uses T1552.005 Cloud Instance Metadata API: TeamTNT has queried the AWS instance metadata service for credentials.

title: ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
text:
ATT&CK Group G0139: TeamTNT
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: TeamTNT has disabled and uninstalled security tools such as Alibaba, Tencent, and BMC cloud monitoring agents on cloud-based infrastructure.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: TeamTNT has disabled iptables.
Uses T1569.003 Systemctl: TeamTNT has created system services to execute cryptocurrency mining software.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: TeamTNT has obtained domains to host their payloads.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: TeamTNT has developed custom malware such as Hildegard.
Uses T1595.001 Scanning IP Blocks: TeamTNT has scanned specific lists of target IP addresses.
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: TeamTNT has scanned for vulnerabilities in IoT devices and other related resources such as the Docker API.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: TeamTNT has uploaded backdoored Docker images to Docker Hub.
Uses T1609 Container Administration Command: TeamTNT executed Hildegard through the kubelet API run command and by executing commands on running containers.
Uses T1610 Deploy Container: TeamTNT has deployed different types of containers into victim environments to facilitate execution. TeamTNT has also transferred cryptocurrency mining software to Kubernetes clusters discovered within local IP address ranges.
Uses T1611 Escape to Host: TeamTNT has deployed privileged containers that mount the filesystem of victim machine.
Uses T1613 Container and Resource Discovery: TeamTNT has checked for running containers with docker ps and for specific container names with docker inspect. TeamTNT has also searched for Kubernetes pods running in a local network.
Uses T1680 Local Storage Discovery: TeamTNT has searched for disk partition and logical volume information.

title: ATT&CK Group G0092: TA505
text:
ATT&CK Group G0092: TA505
Associated names: Hive0065, Spandex Tempest, CHIMBORAZO.
TA505 is a cyber criminal group that has been active since at least 2014. TA505 is known for frequently changing malware, driving global trends in criminal malware distribution, and ransomware campaigns involving Clop.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: TA505 has used UPX to obscure malicious code.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: TA505 has used base64 encoded PowerShell commands.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: TA505 has password-protected malicious Word documents.
Uses T1055.001 Dynamic-link Library Injection: TA505 has been seen injecting a DLL into winword.exe.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: TA505 has used PowerShell to download and execute malware and reconnaissance scripts.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: TA505 has executed commands using cmd.exe.
