Uses T1566.003 Spearphishing via Service: EXOTIC LILY has used the e-mail notification features of legitimate file sharing services for spearphishing.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: EXOTIC LILY has registered domains to spoof targeted organizations by changing the top-level domain (TLD) to “.us”, “.co” or “.biz”.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: EXOTIC LILY has established social media profiles to mimic employees of targeted companies.
Uses T1585.002 Email Accounts: EXOTIC LILY has created e-mail accounts to spoof targeted organizations.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: EXOTIC LILY has gathered targeted individuals' e-mail addresses through open source research and website contact forms.
Uses T1593.001 Social Media: EXOTIC LILY has copied data from social media sites to impersonate targeted individuals.

title: ATT&CK Group G1011: EXOTIC LILY
text:
ATT&CK Group G1011: EXOTIC LILY
Uses T1594 Search Victim-Owned Websites: EXOTIC LILY has used contact forms on victim websites to generate phishing e-mails.

Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: EXOTIC LILY has uploaded malicious payloads to file-sharing services including TransferNow, TransferXL, WeTransfer, and OneDrive.

title: ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
Associated names: GOLD KINGSWOOD, Cobalt Gang, Cobalt Spider.
Cobalt Group is a financially motivated threat group that has primarily targeted financial institutions since at least 2016. The group has conducted intrusions to steal money via targeting ATM systems, card processing, payment systems and SWIFT systems. Cobalt Group has mainly targeted banks in Eastern Europe, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia. One of the alleged leaders was arrested in Spain in early 2018, but the group still appears to be active. The group has been known to target organizations in order to use their access to then compromise additional victims. Reporting indicates there may be links between Cobalt Group and both the malware Carbanak and the group Carbanak.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Cobalt Group has used Remote Desktop Protocol to conduct lateral movement.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: Cobalt Group obfuscated several scriptlets and code used on the victim’s machine, including through use of XOR and RC4.
Uses T1037.001 Logon Script (Windows): Cobalt Group has added persistence by registering the file name for the next stage malware under HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: Cobalt Group leveraged an open-source tool called SoftPerfect Network Scanner to perform network scanning.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Cobalt Group has created Windows tasks to establish persistence.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: Cobalt Group has injected code into trusted processes.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Cobalt Group has used powershell.exe to download and execute scripts.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Cobalt Group has used a JavaScript backdoor that is capable of launching cmd.exe to execute shell commands. The group has used an exploit toolkit known as Threadkit that launches.bat files.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: Cobalt Group has sent Word OLE compound documents with malicious obfuscated VBA macros that will run upon user execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: Cobalt Group has executed JavaScript scriptlets on the victim's machine.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: Cobalt Group has used exploits to increase their levels of rights and privileges.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Cobalt Group deleted the DLL dropper from the victim’s machine to cover their tracks.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Cobalt Group has used HTTPS for C2.
Uses T1071.004 DNS: Cobalt Group has used DNS tunneling for C2.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Cobalt Group has used public sites such as github.com and sendspace.com to upload files and then download them to victim computers. The group's JavaScript backdoor is also capable of downloading files.
Uses T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain: Cobalt Group has compromised legitimate web browser updates to deliver a backdoor.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Cobalt Group had exploited multiple vulnerabilities for execution, including Microsoft’s Equation Editor (CVE-2017-11882), an Internet Explorer vulnerability (CVE-2018-8174), CVE-2017-8570, CVE-2017-0199, and CVE-2017-8759.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Cobalt Group has sent emails containing malicious links that require users to execute a file or macro to infect the victim machine.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Cobalt Group has sent emails containing malicious attachments that require users to execute a file or macro to infect the victim machine.
Uses T1218.003 CMSTP: Cobalt Group has used the command cmstp.exe /s /ns C:\Users\ADMINI~W\AppData\Local\Temp\XKNqbpzl.txt to bypass AppLocker and launch a malicious script.
Uses T1218.008 Odbcconf: Cobalt Group has used odbcconf to proxy the execution of malicious DLL files.
Uses T1218.010 Regsvr32: Cobalt Group has used regsvr32.exe to execute scripts.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: Cobalt Group used the Ammyy Admin tool as well as TeamViewer for remote access, including to preserve remote access if a Cobalt Strike module was lost.

title: ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0080: Cobalt Group
Uses T1220 XSL Script Processing: Cobalt Group used msxsl.exe to bypass AppLocker and to invoke Jscript code from an XSL file.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: Cobalt Group used a JavaScript backdoor that is capable of collecting a list of the security solutions installed on the victim's machine.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: Cobalt Group has created new services to establish persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Cobalt Group has used Registry Run keys for persistence. The group has also set a Startup path to launch the PowerShell shell command and download Cobalt Strike.
Uses T1548.002 Bypass User Account Control: Cobalt Group has bypassed UAC.
Uses T1559.002 Dynamic Data Exchange: Cobalt Group has sent malicious Word OLE compound documents to victims.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Cobalt Group has sent spearphishing emails with various attachment types to corporate and personal email accounts of victim organizations. Attachment types have included.rtf,.doc,.xls, archives containing LNK files, and password protected archives containing.exe and.scr executables.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Cobalt Group has sent emails with URLs pointing to malicious documents.
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: Cobalt Group has used the Plink utility to create SSH tunnels.
Uses T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography: Cobalt Group has used the Plink utility to create SSH tunnels.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Cobalt Group has obtained and used a variety of tools including Mimikatz, PsExec, Cobalt Strike, and SDelete.

title: ATT&CK Group G0138: Andariel
text:
ATT&CK Group G0138: Andariel
Associated names: Silent Chollima, PLUTONIUM, Onyx Sleet.
Andariel is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that has been active since at least 2009. Andariel has primarily focused its operations--which have included destructive attacks--against South Korean government agencies, military organizations, and a variety of domestic companies; they have also conducted cyber financial operations against ATMs, banks, and cryptocurrency exchanges. Andariel's notable activity includes Operation Black Mine, Operation GoldenAxe, and Campaign Rifle.

Andariel is considered a sub-set of Lazarus Group, and has been attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Andariel has collected large numbers of files from compromised network systems for later extraction.
Uses T1027.003 Steganography: Andariel has hidden malicious executables within PNG files.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: Andariel has used the netstat -naop tcp command to display TCP connections on a victim's machine.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Andariel has used tasklist to enumerate processes and find a specific string.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Andariel has downloaded additional tools and malware onto compromised hosts.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Andariel has used watering hole attacks, often with zero-day exploits, to gain initial access to victims within a specific IP range.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Andariel has exploited numerous ActiveX vulnerabilities, including zero-days.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Andariel has attempted to lure victims into enabling malicious macros within email attachments.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Andariel has conducted spearphishing campaigns that included malicious Word or Excel attachments.
Uses T1588.001 Malware: Andariel has used a variety of publicly-available remote access Trojans (RATs) for its operations.

title: ATT&CK Group G0138: Andariel
text:
ATT&CK Group G0138: Andariel
Uses T1590.005 IP Addresses: Andariel has limited its watering hole attacks to specific IP address ranges.
Uses T1592.002 Software: Andariel has inserted a malicious script within compromised websites to collect potential victim information such as browser type, system language, Flash Player version, and other data.

title: ATT&CK Group G0125: HAFNIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0125: HAFNIUM
Associated names: Operation Exchange Marauder, Silk Typhoon.
HAFNIUM is a likely state-sponsored cyber espionage group operating out of China that has been active since at least January 2021. HAFNIUM primarily targets entities in the US across a number of industry sectors, including infectious disease researchers, law firms, higher education institutions, defense contractors, policy think tanks, and NGOs. HAFNIUM has targeted remote management tools and cloud software for intial access and has demonstrated an ability to quickly operationalize exploits for identified vulnerabilities in edge devices.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: HAFNIUM has used procdump to dump the LSASS process memory.
Uses T1003.003 NTDS: HAFNIUM has stolen copies of the Active Directory database (NTDS.DIT).
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: HAFNIUM has collected data and files from a compromised machine.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: HAFNIUM has collected IP information via IPInfo.
Uses T1016.001 Internet Connection Discovery: HAFNIUM has checked for network connectivity from a compromised host using `ping`, including attempts to contact `google[.]com`.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: HAFNIUM has enumerated domain controllers using `net group "Domain computers"` and `nltest /dclist`.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: HAFNIUM has used `whoami` to gather user information.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: HAFNIUM has used `tasklist` to enumerate processes.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: HAFNIUM has used the Exchange Power Shell module Set-OabVirtualDirectoryPowerShell to export mailbox data.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: HAFNIUM has used `cmd.exe` to execute commands on the victim's machine.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: HAFNIUM has targeted unpatched applications to elevate access in targeted organizations.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: HAFNIUM has cleared actor-performed actions from logs.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: HAFNIUM has used open-source C2 frameworks, including Covenant.
Uses T1078.003 Local Accounts: HAFNIUM has used the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account to create files on Exchange servers.

title: ATT&CK Group G0125: HAFNIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0125: HAFNIUM
Uses T1078.004 Cloud Accounts: HAFNIUM has abused service principals in compromised environments to enable data exfiltration.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: HAFNIUM has searched file contents on a compromised host.
Uses T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol: HAFNIUM has used TCP for C2.
Uses T1098 Account Manipulation: HAFNIUM has granted privileges to domain accounts and reset the password for default admin accounts.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: HAFNIUM has downloaded malware and tools--including Nishang and PowerCat--onto a compromised host.
Uses T1110.003 Password Spraying: HAFNIUM has gained initial access through password spray attacks.
Uses T1114.002 Remote Email Collection: HAFNIUM has used web shells and MSGraph to export mailbox data.
Uses T1119 Automated Collection: HAFNIUM has used MSGraph to exfiltrate data from email, OneDrive, and SharePoint.
Uses T1132.001 Standard Encoding: HAFNIUM has used ASCII encoding for C2 traffic.
Uses T1136.002 Domain Account: HAFNIUM has created domain accounts.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: HAFNIUM has exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise edge devices and on-premises versions of Microsoft Exchange Server.
Uses T1199 Trusted Relationship: HAFNIUM has used stolen API keys and credentials associated with privilege access management (PAM), cloud app providers, and cloud data management companies to access downstream customer environments.
Uses T1213.002 Sharepoint: HAFNIUM has abused compromised credentials to exfiltrate data from SharePoint.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: HAFNIUM has used rundll32 to load malicious DLLs.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: HAFNIUM has deployed multiple web shells on compromised servers including SIMPLESEESHARP, SPORTSBALL, China Chopper, and ASPXSpy.
Uses T1530 Data from Cloud Storage: HAFNIUM has exfitrated data from OneDrive.
Uses T1550.001 Application Access Token: HAFNIUM has abused service principals with administrative permissions for data exfiltration.
Uses T1555.006 Cloud Secrets Management Stores: HAFNIUM has moved laterally from on-premises environments to steal passwords from Azure key vaults.

title: ATT&CK Group G0125: HAFNIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0125: HAFNIUM
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: HAFNIUM has used 7-Zip and WinRAR to compress stolen files for exfiltration.
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: HAFNIUM has hidden files on a compromised host.
Uses T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage: HAFNIUM has exfiltrated data to file sharing sites, including MEGA.
Uses T1583.003 Virtual Private Server: HAFNIUM has operated from leased virtual private servers (VPS) in the United States.
Uses T1583.005 Botnet: HAFNIUM has incorporated leased devices into covert networks to obfuscate communications.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: HAFNIUM has acquired web services for use in C2 and exfiltration.
Uses T1584.005 Botnet: HAFNIUM has used compromised devices in covert networks to obfuscate communications.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: HAFNIUM has collected e-mail addresses for users they intended to target.
Uses T1590 Gather Victim Network Information: HAFNIUM gathered the fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) for targeted Exchange servers in the victim's environment.
Uses T1590.005 IP Addresses: HAFNIUM has obtained IP addresses for publicly-accessible Exchange servers.
Uses T1592.004 Client Configurations: HAFNIUM has interacted with Office 365 tenants to gather details regarding target's environments.
Uses T1593.003 Code Repositories: HAFNIUM has discovered leaked corporate credentials on public repositories including GitHub.

title: ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
text:
ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
Associated names: ITG07, Chafer, Remix Kitten.
APT39 is one of several names for cyber espionage activity conducted by the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) through the front company Rana Intelligence Computing since at least 2014. APT39 has primarily targeted the travel, hospitality, academic, and telecommunications industries in Iran and across Asia, Africa, Europe, and North America to track individuals and entities considered to be a threat by the MOIS.
Uses T1003 OS Credential Dumping: APT39 has used different versions of Mimikatz to obtain credentials.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT39 has used Mimikatz, Windows Credential Editor and ProcDump to dump credentials.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT39 has used various tools to steal files from the compromised host.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: APT39 has used various strains of malware to query the Registry.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: APT39 has used NBTscan and custom tools to discover remote systems.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT39 has been seen using RDP for lateral movement and persistence, in some cases employing the rdpwinst tool for mangement of multiple sessions.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: APT39 has used SMB for lateral movement.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: APT39 used secure shell (SSH) to move laterally among their targets.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: APT39 has packed tools with UPX, and has repacked a modified version of Mimikatz to thwart anti-virus detection.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: APT39 has used malware to drop encrypted CAB files.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT39 used Remexi to collect usernames from the system.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: APT39 has used malware disguised as Mozilla Firefox and a tool named mfevtpse.exe to proxy C2 communications, closely mimicking a legitimate McAfee file mfevtps.exe.

title: ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
text:
ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: APT39 has exfiltrated stolen victim data through C2 communications.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: APT39 has used CrackMapExec and a custom port scanner known as BLUETORCH for network scanning.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT39 has created scheduled tasks for persistence.
Uses T1056 Input Capture: APT39 has utilized tools to capture mouse movements.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: APT39 has used tools for capturing keystrokes.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: APT39 has utilized custom scripts to perform internal reconnaissance.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT39 has used PowerShell to execute malicious code.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: APT39 has utilized malicious VBS scripts in malware.
Uses T1059.006 Python: APT39 has used a command line utility and a network scanner written in python.
Uses T1059.010 AutoHotKey & AutoIT: APT39 has utilized AutoIt malware scripts embedded in Microsoft Office documents or malicious links.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT39 has used malware to delete files after they are deployed on a compromised host.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT39 has used HTTP in communications with C2.
Uses T1071.004 DNS: APT39 has used remote access tools that leverage DNS in communications with C2.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: APT39 has utilized tools to aggregate data prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT39 has used stolen credentials to compromise Outlook Web Access (OWA).
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT39 has used tools with the ability to search for files on a compromised host.
Uses T1090.001 Internal Proxy: APT39 used custom tools to create SOCK5 and custom protocol proxies between infected hosts.
Uses T1090.002 External Proxy: APT39 has used various tools to proxy C2 communications.
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: APT39 has communicated with C2 through files uploaded to and downloaded from DropBox.

title: ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
text:
ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT39 has downloaded tools to compromised hosts.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: APT39 has used Ncrack to reveal credentials.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: APT39 has used a screen capture utility to take screenshots on a compromised host.
Uses T1115 Clipboard Data: APT39 has used tools capable of stealing contents of the clipboard.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: APT39 has used the post exploitation tool CrackMapExec to enumerate network shares.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: APT39 has created accounts on multiple compromised hosts to perform actions within the network.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: APT39 has used malware to decrypt encrypted CAB files.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: APT39 has used SQL injection for initial compromise.
Uses T1197 BITS Jobs: APT39 has used the BITS protocol to exfiltrate stolen data from a compromised host.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: APT39 has sent spearphishing emails in an attempt to lure users to click on a malicious link.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT39 has sent spearphishing emails in an attempt to lure users to click on a malicious attachment.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: APT39 has installed ANTAK and ASPXSPY web shells.
Uses T1546.010 AppInit DLLs: APT39 has used malware to set LoadAppInit_DLLs in the Registry key SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows in order to establish persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT39 has maintained persistence using the startup folder.
Uses T1547.009 Shortcut Modification: APT39 has modified LNK shortcuts.
Uses T1553.006 Code Signing Policy Modification: APT39 has used malware to turn off the RequireSigned feature which ensures only signed DLLs can be run on Windows.
Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: APT39 has used the Smartftp Password Decryptor tool to decrypt FTP passwords.

title: ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
text:
ATT&CK Group G0087: APT39
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: APT39 has used WinRAR and 7-Zip to compress an archive stolen data.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT39 leveraged spearphishing emails with malicious attachments to initially compromise victims.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: APT39 leveraged spearphishing emails with malicious links to initially compromise victims.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: APT39 has used post-exploitation tools including RemCom and the Non-sucking Service Manager (NSSM) to execute processes.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT39 has modified and used customized versions of publicly-available tools like PLINK and Mimikatz.

title: ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
text:
ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
Associated names: Earth Vetala, MERCURY, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros, Mango Sandstorm, TA450.
MuddyWater is a cyber espionage group assessed to be a subordinate element within Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Since at least 2017, MuddyWater has targeted a range of government and private organizations across sectors, including telecommunications, local government, defense, and oil and natural gas organizations, in the Middle East, Asia, Africa, Europe, and North America.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with Mimikatz and procdump64.exe.
Uses T1003.004 LSA Secrets: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne.
Uses T1003.005 Cached Domain Credentials: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: MuddyWater has used malware to collect the victim’s IP address and domain name.
Uses T1027.003 Steganography: MuddyWater has stored obfuscated JavaScript code in an image file named temp.jpg.
Uses T1027.004 Compile After Delivery: MuddyWater has used the.NET csc.exe tool to compile executables from downloaded C# code.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: MuddyWater has used Daniel Bohannon’s Invoke-Obfuscation framework and obfuscated PowerShell scripts. The group has also used other obfuscation methods, including Base64 obfuscation of VBScripts and PowerShell commands.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: MuddyWater has used malware that can collect the victim’s username.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: MuddyWater has disguised malicious executables and used filenames and Registry key names associated with Windows Defender.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: MuddyWater has used C2 infrastructure to receive exfiltrated data.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: MuddyWater has used malware that leveraged WMI for execution and querying host information.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: MuddyWater has used a PowerShell backdoor to check for Skype connections on the target machine.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: MuddyWater has used scheduled tasks to establish persistence.

title: ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
text:
ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: MuddyWater has used malware to obtain a list of running processes on the system.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: MuddyWater has used PowerShell for execution.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: MuddyWater has used a custom tool for creating reverse shells.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: MuddyWater has used VBScript files to execute its POWERSTATS payload, as well as macros.
Uses T1059.006 Python: MuddyWater has developed tools in Python including Out1.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: MuddyWater has used JavaScript files to execute its POWERSTATS payload.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: MuddyWater has used HTTP for C2 communications.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: MuddyWater has stored a decoy PDF file within a victim's `%temp%` folder.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: MuddyWater has used malware that can collect the victim’s OS version and machine name.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: MuddyWater has used malware that checked if the ProgramData folder had folders or files with the keywords "Kasper," "Panda," or "ESET."
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: MuddyWater has used cmd.exe net user /domain to enumerate domain users.
Uses T1090.002 External Proxy: MuddyWater has controlled POWERSTATS from behind a proxy network to obfuscate the C2 location. MuddyWater has used a series of compromised websites that victims connected to randomly to relay information to command and control (C2).
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: MuddyWater has used web services including OneHub to distribute remote access tools.
Uses T1104 Multi-Stage Channels: MuddyWater has used one C2 to obtain enumeration scripts and monitor web logs, but a different C2 to send data back.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: MuddyWater has used malware that can upload additional files to the victim’s machine.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: MuddyWater has used malware that can capture screenshots of the victim’s machine.

title: ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
text:
ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
Uses T1132.001 Standard Encoding: MuddyWater has used tools to encode C2 communications including Base64 encoding.
Uses T1137.001 Office Template Macros: MuddyWater has used a Word Template, Normal.dotm, for persistence.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: MuddyWater has decoded base64-encoded PowerShell, JavaScript, and VBScript.

Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: MuddyWater has distributed URLs in phishing e-mails that link to lure documents.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: MuddyWater has attempted to get users to open malicious PDF attachment and to enable macros and launch malicious Microsoft Word documents delivered via spearphishing emails.

Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: MuddyWater has added Registry Run key KCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\SystemTextEncoding to establish persistence.
Uses T1548.002 Bypass User Account Control: MuddyWater uses various techniques to bypass UAC.

title: ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
text:
ATT&CK Group G0069: MuddyWater
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: MuddyWater has run a tool that steals passwords saved in victim email.
Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: MuddyWater has performed credential dumping with LaZagne and other tools, including by dumping passwords saved in victim email.
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: MuddyWater has run tools including Browser64 to steal passwords saved in victim web browsers.
Uses T1559.001 Component Object Model: MuddyWater has used malware that has the capability to execute malicious code via COM, DCOM, and Outlook.
Uses T1559.002 Dynamic Data Exchange: MuddyWater has used malware that can execute PowerShell scripts via DDE.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: MuddyWater has used the native Windows cabinet creation tool, makecab.exe, likely to compress stolen data to be uploaded.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: MuddyWater can disable the system's local proxy settings.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: MuddyWater has compromised third parties and used compromised accounts to send spearphishing emails with targeted attachments to recipients.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: MuddyWater has sent targeted spearphishing e-mails with malicious links.
Uses T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography: MuddyWater has used AES to encrypt C2 responses.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: MuddyWater maintains persistence on victim networks through side-loading dlls to trick legitimate programs into running malware.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: MuddyWater has used file sharing services including OneHub, Sync, and TeraBox to distribute tools.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: MuddyWater has used legitimate tools ConnectWise, RemoteUtilities, and SimpleHelp to gain access to the target environment.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
Associated names: NICKEL GLADSTONE, BeagleBoyz, Bluenoroff, Stardust Chollima, Sapphire Sleet, COPERNICIUM.
APT38 is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that specializes in financial cyber operations; it has been attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Active since at least 2014, APT38 has targeted banks, financial institutions, casinos, cryptocurrency exchanges, SWIFT system endpoints, and ATMs in at least 38 countries worldwide. Significant operations include the 2016 Bank of Bangladesh heist, during which APT38 stole $81 million, as well as attacks against Bancomext and Banco de Chile; some of their attacks have been destructive.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT38 has collected data from a compromised host.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: APT38 has used several code packing methods such as Themida, Enigma, VMProtect, and Obsidium, to pack their implants.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT38 has identified primary users, currently logged in users, sets of users that commonly use a system, or inactive users.
Uses T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities: APT38 has renamed system utilities, such as `rundll32.exe` and `mshta.exe`, to avoid detection.
Uses T1036.006 Space after Filename: APT38 has put several spaces before a file extension to avoid detection and suspicion.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT38 installed a port monitoring tool, MAPMAKER, to print the active TCP connections on the local system.
Uses T1053.003 Cron: APT38 has used cron to create pre-scheduled and periodic background jobs on a Linux system.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT38 has used Task Scheduler to run programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. Additionally, APT38 has used living-off-the-land scripts to execute a malicious script via a scheduled task.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT38 has injected malicious payloads into the `explorer.exe` process.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to capture keystrokes from the victim’s machine.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT38 leveraged Sysmon to understand the processes, services in the organization.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT38 has used PowerShell to execute commands and other operational tasks.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: APT38 has used a command-line tunneler, NACHOCHEESE, to give them shell access to a victim’s machine. Additionally, APT38 has used batch scripts.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: APT38 has used VBScript to execute commands and other operational tasks.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: APT38 clears Window Event logs and Sysmon logs from the system.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT38 has used a utility called CLOSESHAVE that can securely delete a file from the system. They have also removed malware, tools, or other non-native files used during the intrusion to reduce their footprint or as part of the post-intrusion …
Uses T1070.006 Timestomp: APT38 has modified data timestamps to mimic files that are in the same folder on a compromised host.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT38 used a backdoor, QUICKRIDE, to communicate to the C2 server over HTTP and HTTPS.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT38 has attempted to get detailed information about a compromised host, including the operating system, version, patches, hotfixes, and service packs.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT38 have enumerated files and directories, or searched in specific locations within a compromised host.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT38 used a backdoor, NESTEGG, that has the capability to download and upload files to and from a victim’s machine. Additionally, APT38 has downloaded other payloads onto a victim’s machine.
Uses T1106 Native API: APT38 has used the Windows API to execute code within a victim's system.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: APT38 has used brute force techniques to attempt account access when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are unavailable.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: APT38 uses a tool called CLEANTOAD that has the capability to modify Registry keys.
Uses T1115 Clipboard Data: APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to collect data from the clipboard.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: APT38 has enumerated network shares on a compromised host.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: APT38 has used the RC4 algorithm to decrypt configuration data.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: APT38 has conducted watering holes schemes to gain initial access to victims.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: APT38 has used links to execute a malicious Visual Basic script.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT38 has attempted to lure victims into enabling malicious macros within email attachments. Additionally, APT38 has used malicious Word documents and shortcut files.
Uses T1217 Browser Information Discovery: APT38 has collected browser bookmark information to learn more about compromised hosts, obtain personal information about users, and acquire details about internal network resources.
Uses T1218.001 Compiled HTML File: APT38 has used CHM files to move concealed payloads.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: APT38 has used a renamed version of `mshta.exe` to execute malicious HTML files.
Uses T1218.007 Msiexec: APT38 has used `msiexec.exe` to execute malicious files.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: APT38 has used rundll32.exe to execute binaries, scripts, and Control Panel Item files and to execute code via proxy to avoid triggering security tools.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
Uses T1480.002 Mutual Exclusion: APT38 has created a mutex to avoid duplicate execution.
Uses T1485 Data Destruction: APT38 has used a custom secure delete function to make deleted files unrecoverable.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: APT38 has used Hermes ransomware to encrypt files with AES256.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: APT38 has used web shells for persistence or to ensure redundant access.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: APT38 has identified security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors installed on a compromised system.
Uses T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK, which will initiate a system reboot after wiping the victim's MBR.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: APT38 has installed a new Windows service to establish persistence.
Uses T1548.002 Bypass User Account Control: APT38 has used the legitimate application `ieinstal.exe` to bypass UAC.
Uses T1553.005 Mark-of-the-Web Bypass: APT38 has used ISO and VHD files to deploy malware and to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security measures.
Uses T1561.002 Disk Structure Wipe: APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK to render systems inoperable.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: APT38 has unhooked DLLs to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) or anti-virus (AV) tools.
Uses T1562.003 Impair Command History Logging: APT38 has prepended a space to all of their terminal commands to operate without leaving traces in the HISTCONTROL environment.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443.
Uses T1562.013 Disable or Modify Network Device Firewall: APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443.
Uses T1565.001 Stored Data Manipulation: APT38 has used DYEPACK to create, delete, and alter records in databases used for SWIFT transactions.

title: ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
text:
ATT&CK Group G0082: APT38
Uses T1565.002 Transmitted Data Manipulation: APT38 has used DYEPACK to manipulate SWIFT messages en route to a printer.
Uses T1565.003 Runtime Data Manipulation: APT38 has used DYEPACK.FOX to manipulate PDF data as it is accessed to remove traces of fraudulent SWIFT transactions from the data displayed to the end user.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT38 has conducted spearphishing campaigns using malicious email attachments.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: APT38 has created new services or modified existing ones to run executables, commands, or scripts.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: APT38 has created fake domains to imitate legitimate venture capital or bank domains.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT38 has obtained and used open-source tools such as Mimikatz.

title: ATT&CK Group G0134: Transparent Tribe
text:
ATT&CK Group G0134: Transparent Tribe
Associated names: COPPER FIELDSTONE, APT36, Mythic Leopard, ProjectM.
Transparent Tribe is a suspected Pakistan-based threat group that has been active since at least 2013, primarily targeting diplomatic, defense, and research organizations in India and Afghanistan.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Transparent Tribe has dropped encoded executables on compromised hosts.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Transparent Tribe can mimic legitimate Windows directories by using the same icons and names.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: Transparent Tribe has crafted VBS-based malicious documents.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Transparent Tribe has used websites with malicious hyperlinks and iframes to infect targeted victims with Crimson, njRAT, and other malicious tools.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Transparent Tribe has crafted malicious files to exploit CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333 for execution.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Transparent Tribe has directed users to open URLs hosting malicious content.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Transparent Tribe has used weaponized documents in e-mail to compromise targeted systems.
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: Transparent Tribe can hide legitimate directories and replace them with malicious copies of the same name.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Transparent Tribe has sent spearphishing e-mails with attachments to deliver malicious payloads.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Transparent Tribe has embedded links to malicious downloads in e-mails.
Uses T1568 Dynamic Resolution: Transparent Tribe has used dynamic DNS services to set up C2.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Transparent Tribe has registered domains to mimic file sharing, government, defense, and research websites for use in targeted campaigns.
Uses T1584.001 Domains: Transparent Tribe has compromised domains for use in targeted malicious campaigns.
Uses T1608.004 Drive-by Target: Transparent Tribe has set up websites with malicious hyperlinks and iframes to infect targeted victims with Crimson, njRAT, and other malicious tools.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Associated names: SeaLotus, OceanLotus, APT-C-00, Canvas Cyclone, BISMUTH.
APT32 is a suspected Vietnam-based threat group that has been active since at least 2014. The group has targeted multiple private sector industries as well as foreign governments, dissidents, and journalists with a strong focus on Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, the Philippines, Laos, and Cambodia. They have extensively used strategic web compromises to compromise victims.
Uses T1003 OS Credential Dumping: APT32 used GetPassword_x64 to harvest credentials.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT32 used Mimikatz and customized versions of Windows Credential Dumper to harvest credentials.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: APT32's backdoor can query the Windows Registry to gather system information.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: APT32 used the ipconfig /all command to gather the IP address from the system.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: APT32 has enumerated DC servers using the command net group "Domain Controllers" /domain. The group has also used the ping command.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: APT32 used Net to use Windows' hidden network shares to copy their tools to remote machines for execution.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: APT32 has used the `Invoke-Obfuscation` framework to obfuscate their PowerShell.
Uses T1027.011 Fileless Storage: APT32's backdoor has stored its configuration in a registry key.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: APT32 has performed code obfuscation, including encoding payloads using Base64 and using a framework called "Dont-Kill-My-Cat (DKMC). APT32 also encrypts the library used for network exfiltration with AES-256 in CBC mode in their macOS backdoor.
Uses T1027.016 Junk Code Insertion: APT32 includes garbage code to mislead anti-malware software and researchers.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT32 collected the victim's username and executed the whoami command on the victim's machine. APT32 executed shellcode to collect the username on the victim's machine.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1036 Masquerading: APT32 has disguised a Cobalt Strike beacon as a Flash Installer.
Uses T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities: APT32 has moved and renamed pubprn.vbs to a.txt file to avoid detection.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: APT32 has used hidden or non-printing characters to help masquerade service names, such as appending a Unicode no-break space character to a legitimate service name. APT32 has also impersonated the legitimate Flash installer file name "install_flashplayer.exe".
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: APT32 has renamed a NetCat binary to kb-10233.exe to masquerade as a Windows update. APT32 has also renamed a Cobalt Strike beacon payload to install_flashplayers.exe.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: APT32's backdoor has exfiltrated data using the already opened channel with its C&C server.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: APT32 performed network scanning on the network to search for open ports, services, OS finger-printing, and other vulnerabilities.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: APT32 used WMI to deploy their tools on remote machines and to gather information about the Outlook process.
Uses T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol: APT32's backdoor can exfiltrate data by encoding it in the subdomain field of DNS packets.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT32 used the netstat -anpo tcp command to display TCP connections on the victim's machine.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT32 has used scheduled tasks to persist on victim systems.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT32 malware has injected a Cobalt Strike beacon into Rundll32.exe.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: APT32 has abused the PasswordChangeNotify to monitor for and capture account password changes.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: APT32 has used COM scriptlets to download Cobalt Strike beacons.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT32 has used PowerShell-based tools, PowerShell one-liners, and shellcode loaders for execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: APT32 has used cmd.exe for execution.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: APT32 has used macros, COM scriptlets, and VBS scripts.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: APT32 has used JavaScript for drive-by downloads and C2 communications.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: APT32 has used CVE-2016-7255 to escalate privileges.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: APT32 has cleared select event log entries.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT32's macOS backdoor can receive a “delete” command.
Uses T1070.006 Timestomp: APT32 has used scheduled task raw XML with a backdated timestamp of June 2, 2016. The group has also set the creation time of the files dropped by the second stage of the exploit to match the creation time of …
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT32 has used JavaScript that communicates over HTTP or HTTPS to attacker controlled domains to download additional frameworks. The group has also used downloaded encrypted payloads over HTTP.
Uses T1071.003 Mail Protocols: APT32 has used email for C2 via an Office macro.
Uses T1072 Software Deployment Tools: APT32 compromised McAfee ePO to move laterally by distributing malware as a software deployment task.
Uses T1078.003 Local Accounts: APT32 has used legitimate local admin account credentials.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT32 has collected the OS version and computer name from victims. One of the group's backdoors can also query the Windows Registry to gather system information, and another macOS backdoor performs a fingerprint of the machine on its first connection …
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT32's backdoor possesses the capability to list files and directories on a machine.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: APT32 enumerated administrative users using the commands net localgroup administrators.
Uses T1102 Web Service: APT32 has used Dropbox, Amazon S3, and Google Drive to host malicious downloads.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT32 has added JavaScript to victim websites to download additional frameworks that profile and compromise website visitors.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: APT32's backdoor has modified the Windows Registry to store the backdoor's configuration.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: APT32 used the net view command to show all shares available, including the administrative shares such as C$ and ADMIN$.
Uses T1137 Office Application Startup: APT32 have replaced Microsoft Outlook's VbaProject.OTM file to install a backdoor macro for persistence.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: APT32 has infected victims by tricking them into visiting compromised watering hole websites.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT32 has used RTF document that includes an exploit to execute malicious code. (CVE-2017-11882)
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: APT32 has lured targets to download a Cobalt Strike beacon by including a malicious link within spearphishing emails.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT32 has attempted to lure users to execute a malicious dropper delivered via a spearphishing attachment.
Uses T1216.001 PubPrn: APT32 has used PubPrn.vbs within execution scripts to execute malware, possibly bypassing defenses.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: APT32 has used mshta.exe for code execution.
Uses T1218.010 Regsvr32: APT32 created a Scheduled Task/Job that used regsvr32.exe to execute a COM scriptlet that dynamically downloaded a backdoor and injected it into memory. The group has also used regsvr32 to run their backdoor.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: APT32 malware has used rundll32.exe to execute an initial infection process.
Uses T1222.002 Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification: APT32's macOS backdoor changes the permission of the file it wants to execute to 755.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: APT32 has used Web shells to maintain access to victim websites.

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: APT32 modified Windows Services to ensure PowerShell scripts were loaded on the system. APT32 also creates a Windows service to establish persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT32 established persistence using Registry Run keys, both to execute PowerShell and VBS scripts as well as to execute their backdoor directly.
Uses T1550.002 Pass the Hash: APT32 has used pass the hash for lateral movement.
Uses T1550.003 Pass the Ticket: APT32 successfully gained remote access by using pass the ticket.
Uses T1552.002 Credentials in Registry: APT32 used Outlook Credential Dumper to harvest credentials stored in Windows registry.
Uses T1560 Archive Collected Data: APT32's backdoor has used LZMA compression and RC4 encryption before exfiltration.
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: APT32's macOS backdoor hides the clientID file via a chflags function.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: APT32 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1564.004 NTFS File Attributes: APT32 used NTFS alternate data streams to hide their payloads.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT32 has sent spearphishing emails with a malicious executable disguised as a document or spreadsheet.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: APT32 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious links.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: APT32's backdoor has used Windows services as a way to execute its malicious payload.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: APT32 has deployed tools after moving laterally using administrative accounts.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: An APT32 backdoor can use HTTP over a non-standard TCP port (e.g 14146) which is specified in the backdoor configuration.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: APT32 ran legitimately-signed executables from Symantec and McAfee which load a malicious DLL. The group also side-loads its backdoor by dropping a library and a legitimate, signed executable (AcroTranscoder).

title: ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
text:
ATT&CK Group G0050: APT32
Uses T1583.001 Domains: APT32 has set up and operated websites to gather information and deliver malware.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: APT32 has set up Dropbox, Amazon S3, and Google Drive to host malicious downloads.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: APT32 has set up Facebook pages in tandem with fake websites.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT32 has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz and Cobalt Strike, and a variety of other open-source tools from GitHub.
Uses T1589 Gather Victim Identity Information: APT32 has conducted targeted surveillance against activists and bloggers.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: APT32 has collected e-mail addresses for activists and bloggers in order to target them with spyware.
Uses T1598.003 Spearphishing Link: APT32 has used malicious links to direct users to web pages designed to harvest credentials.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: APT32 has hosted malicious payloads in Dropbox, Amazon S3, and Google Drive for use during targeting.
Uses T1608.004 Drive-by Target: APT32 has stood up websites containing numerous articles and content scraped from the Internet to make them appear legitimate, but some of these pages include malicious JavaScript to profile the potential victim or infect them via a fake software update.

title: ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
text:
ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
Associated names: REDBALDKNIGHT, Tick.
BRONZE BUTLER is a cyber espionage group with likely Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2008. The group primarily targets Japanese organizations, particularly those in government, biotechnology, electronics manufacturing, and industrial chemistry.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: BRONZE BUTLER has used various tools (such as Mimikatz and WCE) to perform credential dumping.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: BRONZE BUTLER has exfiltrated files stolen from local systems.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has used TROJ_GETVERSION to discover system services.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER typically use ping and Net to enumerate systems.
Uses T1027.001 Binary Padding: BRONZE BUTLER downloader code has included "0" characters at the end of the file to inflate the file size in a likely attempt to evade anti-virus detection.
Uses T1027.003 Steganography: BRONZE BUTLER has used steganography in multiple operations to conceal malicious payloads.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: BRONZE BUTLER has masked executables with document file icons including Word and Adobe PDF.
Uses T1036.002 Right-to-Left Override: BRONZE BUTLER has used Right-to-Left Override to deceive victims into executing several strains of malware.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: BRONZE BUTLER has given malware the same name as an existing file on the file share server to cause users to unwittingly launch and install the malware on additional systems.
Uses T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive: BRONZE BUTLER has exfiltrated files stolen from file shares.
Uses T1053.002 At: BRONZE BUTLER has used at to register a scheduled task to execute malware during lateral movement.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: BRONZE BUTLER has used schtasks to register a scheduled task to execute malware during lateral movement.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: BRONZE BUTLER has used PowerShell for execution.

title: ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
text:
ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: BRONZE BUTLER has used batch scripts and the command-line interface for execution.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: BRONZE BUTLER has used VBS and VBE scripts for execution.
Uses T1059.006 Python: BRONZE BUTLER has made use of Python-based remote access tools.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: The BRONZE BUTLER uploader or malware the uploader uses command to delete the RAR archives after they have been exfiltrated.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: BRONZE BUTLER malware has used HTTP for C2.
Uses T1080 Taint Shared Content: BRONZE BUTLER has placed malware on file shares and given it the same name as legitimate documents on the share.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has collected a list of files from the victim and uploaded it to its C2 server, and then created a new list of specific files to steal.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: BRONZE BUTLER has used net user /domain to identify account information.
Uses T1102.001 Dead Drop Resolver: BRONZE BUTLER's MSGET downloader uses a dead drop resolver to access malicious payloads.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: BRONZE BUTLER has used various tools to download files, including DGet (a similar tool to wget).
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: BRONZE BUTLER has used a tool to capture screenshots.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has used net time to check the local time on a target system.
Uses T1132.001 Standard Encoding: Several BRONZE BUTLER tools encode data with base64 when posting it to a C2 server.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: BRONZE BUTLER downloads encoded payloads and decodes them on the victim.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: BRONZE BUTLER compromised three Japanese websites using a Flash exploit to perform watering hole attacks.

title: ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
text:
ATT&CK Group G0060: BRONZE BUTLER
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: BRONZE BUTLER has exploited Microsoft Office vulnerabilities CVE-2014-4114, CVE-2018-0802, and CVE-2018-0798 for execution.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: BRONZE BUTLER has attempted to get users to launch malicious Microsoft Word attachments delivered via spearphishing emails.
Uses T1518 Software Discovery: BRONZE BUTLER has used tools to enumerate software installed on an infected host.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: BRONZE BUTLER has used a batch script that adds a Registry Run key to establish malware persistence.
Uses T1548.002 Bypass User Account Control: BRONZE BUTLER has used a Windows 10 specific tool and xxmm to bypass UAC for privilege escalation.
Uses T1550.003 Pass the Ticket: BRONZE BUTLER has created forged Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) and Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets to maintain administrative access.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: BRONZE BUTLER has compressed data into password-protected RAR archives prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: BRONZE BUTLER has incorporated code into several tools that attempts to terminate anti-virus processes.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: BRONZE BUTLER used spearphishing emails with malicious Microsoft Word attachments to infect victims.
Uses T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography: BRONZE BUTLER has used RC4 encryption (for Datper malware) and AES (for xxmm malware) to obfuscate HTTP traffic. BRONZE BUTLER has also used a tool called RarStar that encodes data with a custom XOR algorithm when posting it to a …
Uses T1574.001 DLL: BRONZE BUTLER has used legitimate applications to side-load malicious DLLs.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: BRONZE BUTLER has obtained and used open-source tools such as Mimikatz, gsecdump, and Windows Credential Editor.

title: ATT&CK Group G1005: POLONIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G1005: POLONIUM
Associated names: Plaid Rain.
POLONIUM is a Lebanon-based group that has primarily targeted Israeli organizations, including critical manufacturing, information technology, and defense industry companies, since at least February 2022. Security researchers assess POLONIUM has coordinated their operations with multiple actors affiliated with Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), based on victim overlap as well as common techniques and tooling.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: POLONIUM has used valid compromised credentials to gain access to victim environments.
Uses T1090 Proxy: POLONIUM has used the AirVPN service for operational activity.

title: ATT&CK Group G1023: APT5
text:
ATT&CK Group G1023: APT5
Associated names: Mulberry Typhoon, MANGANESE, BRONZE FLEETWOOD, Keyhole Panda, UNC2630.
APT5 is a China-based espionage actor that has been active since at least 2007 primarily targeting the telecommunications, aerospace, and defense industries throughout the U.S., Europe, and Asia. APT5 has displayed advanced tradecraft and significant interest in compromising networking devices and their underlying software including through the use of zero-day exploits.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT5 has used the Task Manager process to target LSASS process memory in order to obtain NTLM password hashes. APT5 has also dumped clear text passwords and hashes from memory using Mimikatz hosted through an RDP mapped drive.
Uses T1003.002 Security Account Manager: APT5 has copied and exfiltrated the SAM Registry hive from targeted systems.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT5 has moved laterally throughout victim environments using RDP.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: APT5 has used SSH for lateral movement in compromised environments including for enabling access to ESXi host servers.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: APT5 has named exfiltration archives to mimic Windows Updates at times using filenames with a `KB<digits>.zip` pattern.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT5 has used the BLOODMINE utility to collect data on web requests from Pulse Secure Connect logs.
Uses T1053.003 Cron: APT5 has made modifications to the crontab file including in `/var/cron/tabs/`.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT5 has used the CLEANPULSE utility to insert command line strings into a targeted process to alter its functionality.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: APT5 has used malware with keylogging capabilities to monitor the communications of targeted entities.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT5 has used Windows-based utilities to carry out tasks including tasklist.exe.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT5 has used PowerShell to accomplish tasks within targeted environments.

text:
ATT&CK Group G1023: APT5

Uses T1070.003 Clear Command History: APT5 has cleared the command history on targeted ESXi servers.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT5 has deleted scripts and web shells to evade detection.

Uses T1078.004 Cloud Accounts: APT5 has accessed Microsoft M365 cloud environments using stolen credentials.

Uses T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary: APT5 has modified legitimate binaries and scripts for Pulse Secure VPNs including the legitimate DSUpgrade.pm file to install the ATRIUM webshell for persistence.

title: ATT&CK Group G1023: APT5
text:
ATT&CK Group G1023: APT5

title: ATT&CK Group G0135: BackdoorDiplomacy
text:
ATT&CK Group G0135: BackdoorDiplomacy
BackdoorDiplomacy is a cyber espionage threat group that has been active since at least 2017. BackdoorDiplomacy has targeted Ministries of Foreign Affairs and telecommunication companies in Africa, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: BackdoorDiplomacy has obfuscated tools and malware it uses with VMProtect.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: BackdoorDiplomacy has disguised their backdoor droppers with naming conventions designed to blend into normal operations.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: BackdoorDiplomacy has dropped implants in folders named for legitimate software.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: BackdoorDiplomacy has used SMBTouch, a vulnerability scanner, to determine whether a target is vulnerable to EternalBlue malware.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: BackdoorDiplomacy has used NetCat and PortQry to enumerate network connections and display the status of related TCP and UDP ports.
Uses T1055.001 Dynamic-link Library Injection: BackdoorDiplomacy has dropped legitimate software onto a compromised host and used it to execute malicious DLLs.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: BackdoorDiplomacy has copied files of interest to the main drive's recycle bin.
Uses T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol: BackdoorDiplomacy has used EarthWorm for network tunneling with a SOCKS5 server and port transfer functionalities.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: BackdoorDiplomacy has downloaded additional files and tools onto a compromised host.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: BackdoorDiplomacy has used an executable to detect removable media, such as USB flash drives.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: BackdoorDiplomacy has exploited CVE-2020-5902, an F5 BIP-IP vulnerability, to drop a Linux backdoor. BackdoorDiplomacy has also exploited mis-configured Plesk servers.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: BackdoorDiplomacy has used web shells to establish an initial foothold and for lateral movement within a victim's system.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: BackdoorDiplomacy has executed DLL search order hijacking.

title: ATT&CK Group G0135: BackdoorDiplomacy
text:
ATT&CK Group G0135: BackdoorDiplomacy
Uses T1588.001 Malware: BackdoorDiplomacy has obtained and used leaked malware, including DoublePulsar, EternalBlue, EternalRocks, and EternalSynergy, in its operations.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: BackdoorDiplomacy has obtained a variety of open-source reconnaissance and red team tools for discovery and lateral movement.

title: ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
Associated names: Black Banshee, Velvet Chollima, Emerald Sleet, THALLIUM, APT43, TA427, Springtail.
Kimsuky is a North Korea-based cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. The group initially targeted South Korean government agencies, think tanks, and subject-matter experts in various fields. Its operations expanded to include the United Nations and organizations in the government, education, business services, and manufacturing sectors across the United States, Japan, Russia, and Europe. Kimsuky has focused collection on foreign policy and national security issues tied to the Korean Peninsula, nuclear policy, and sanctions. Its operations have overlapped with other DPRK actors, likely due to ad hoc collaboration or limited resource sharing. Because of overlapping operations, some researchers group a wide range of North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the broader Lazarus Group umbrella rather than tracking separate subgroup or cluster distinctions.

Kimsuky was assessed to be responsible for the 2014 Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co. compromise; other notable campaigns include Operation STOLEN PENCIL (2018), Operation Kabar Cobra (2019), and Operation Smoke Screen (2019).

In 2023, Kimsuky was observed using commercial large language models to assist with vulnerability research, scripting, social engineering and reconnaissance.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: Kimsuky has gathered credentials using Mimikatz and ProcDump.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Kimsuky has collected Office, PDF, and HWP documents from its victims.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: Kimsuky has used an instrumentor script to gather the names of all services running on a victim's system.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Kimsuky has obtained specific Registry keys and values on a compromised host.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Kimsuky has used `ipconfig/all` and web beacons sent via email to gather network configuration information. Kimsuky has also identified Host IP addresses leveraging the WMI class `Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration`.

title: ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Kimsuky has used RDP for direct remote point-and-click access.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Kimsuky has obfuscated binary strings including the use of XOR encryption and Base64 encoding. Kimsuky has also modified the first byte of DLL implants targeting victims to prevent recognition of the executable file format.
Uses T1027.001 Binary Padding: Kimsuky has performed padding of PowerShell command line code with over 100 spaces.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: Kimsuky has packed malware with UPX.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: Kimsuky has encoded malicious PowerShell scripts using Base64.
Uses T1027.012 LNK Icon Smuggling: Kimsuky has used the LNK icon location to execute malicious scripts. Kimsuky has also padded the LNK target field properties with extra spaces to obscure the script.
Uses T1027.016 Junk Code Insertion: Kimsuky has obfuscated code by filling scripts with junk code and concatenating strings to hamper analysis and detection.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Kimsuky has disguised services to appear as benign software or related to operating system functions.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Kimsuky has renamed malware to legitimate names such as ESTCommon.dll or patch.dll. Kimsuky has also disguised payloads using legitimate file names including a PowerShell payload named chrome.ps1.
Uses T1036.007 Double File Extension: Kimsuky has used an additional filename extension to hide the true file type. Kimsuky has also masqueraded malicious LNK files as PDF objects using the double extension.pdf.lnk.
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: Kimsuky has used the Nirsoft SniffPass network sniffer to obtain passwords sent over non-secure protocols.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: Kimsuky has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.

title: ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Kimsuky has downloaded additional malware with scheduled tasks. Kimsuky has established persistence by creating a scheduled task named “ChromeUpdateTaskMachine” through the PowerShell cmdlet `Register-ScheduleTask` which was set to execute another PowerShell script once, then five minutes after its creation and …
Uses T1055 Process Injection: Kimsuky has used Win7Elevate to inject malicious code into explorer.exe.
Uses T1055.012 Process Hollowing: Kimsuky has used a file injector DLL to spawn a benign process on the victim's system and inject the malicious payload into it via process hollowing.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: Kimsuky has used a PowerShell-based keylogger as well as a tool called MECHANICAL to log keystrokes.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Kimsuky can gather a list of all processes running on a victim's machine. Kimsuky has also obtained running processes on the victim device utilizing PowerShell cmdlet `Get-Process`.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Kimsuky has executed a variety of PowerShell scripts including Invoke-Mimikatz. Kimsuky has also utilized PowerShell scripts for execution, persistence, and defense evasion.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Kimsuky has executed Windows commands by using `cmd` and running batch scripts.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: Kimsuky has used Visual Basic to download malicious payloads. Kimsuky has also used malicious VBA macros within maldocs disguised as forms that trigger when a victim types any content into the lure.
Uses T1059.006 Python: Kimsuky has used a macOS Python implant to gather data as well as MailFetcher.py code to automatically collect email data.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: Kimsuky has used JScript for logging and downloading additional tools. Kimsuky has used TRANSLATEXT, which contained four Javascript files for bypassing defenses, collecting sensitive information and screenshots, and exfiltrating data.

title: ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Kimsuky has deleted the exfiltrated data on disk after transmission. Kimsuky has also used an instrumentor script to terminate browser processes running on an infected system and then delete the cookie files on disk. Kimsuky has deleted files using the …

Kimsuky has also obtained system information such as OS type, OS version, and system type through querying various Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) classes …

text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky

Uses T1111 Multi-Factor Authentication Interception: Kimsuky has used a proprietary tool to intercept one time passwords required for two-factor authentication.

Uses T1136.001 Local Account: Kimsuky has created accounts with net user.

text:

text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky

text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky

text:
ATT&CK Group G0094: Kimsuky

title: ATT&CK Group G0065: Leviathan
text:
ATT&CK Group G0065: Leviathan
Associated names: MUDCARP, Kryptonite Panda, Gadolinium, BRONZE MOHAWK, TEMP.Jumper, APT40, TEMP.Periscope, Gingham Typhoon.
Leviathan is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group that has been attributed to the Ministry of State Security's (MSS) Hainan State Security Department and an affiliated front company. Active since at least 2009, Leviathan has targeted the following sectors: academia, aerospace/aviation, biomedical, defense industrial base, government, healthcare, manufacturing, maritime, and transportation across the US, Canada, Australia, Europe, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.
Uses T1003 OS Credential Dumping: Leviathan has used publicly available tools to dump password hashes, including HOMEFRY.

Uses T1027.003 Steganography: Leviathan has used steganography to hide stolen data inside other files stored on Github.

Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Leviathan has used WMI for execution.
Uses T1055.001 Dynamic-link Library Injection: Leviathan has utilized techniques like reflective DLL loading to write a DLL into memory and load a shell that provides backdoor access to the victim.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Leviathan has used PowerShell for execution.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: Leviathan has used VBScript.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: Leviathan has used C:\Windows\Debug and C:\Perflogs as staging directories.
Uses T1074.002 Remote Data Staging: Leviathan has staged data remotely prior to exfiltration.

text:

Uses T1546.003 Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription: Leviathan has used WMI for persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Leviathan has used JavaScript to create a shortcut file in the Startup folder that points to its main backdoor.

Uses T1583.001 Domains: Leviathan has established domains that impersonate legitimate entities to use for targeting efforts.

Uses T1584.008 Network Devices: Leviathan has used compromised networking devices, such as small office/home office (SOHO) devices, as operational command and control infrastructure.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: Leviathan has created new social media accounts for targeting efforts.
Uses T1585.002 Email Accounts: Leviathan has created new email accounts for targeting efforts.
Uses T1586.001 Social Media Accounts: Leviathan has compromised social media accounts to conduct social engineering attacks.
Uses T1586.002 Email Accounts: Leviathan has compromised email accounts to conduct social engineering attacks.
Uses T1587.004 Exploits: Leviathan has rapidly transformed and adapted public exploit proof-of-concept code for new vulnerabilities and utilized them against target networks.
Uses T1589.001 Credentials: Leviathan has collected compromised credentials to use for targeting efforts.

title: ATT&CK Group G0065: Leviathan
text:
ATT&CK Group G0065: Leviathan
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: Leviathan has conducted reconnaissance against target networks of interest looking for vulnerable, end-of-life, or no longer maintainted devices against which to rapidly deploy exploits.

title: ATT&CK Group G1046: Storm-1811
text:
ATT&CK Group G1046: Storm-1811
Storm-1811 is a financially-motivated entity linked to Black Basta ransomware deployment. Storm-1811 is notable for unique phishing and social engineering mechanisms for initial access, such as overloading victim email inboxes with non-malicious spam to prompt a fake "help desk" interaction leading to the deployment of adversary tools and capabilities.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Storm-1811 has attempted to move laterally in victim environments via SMB using Impacket.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Storm-1811 has used OpenSSH to establish an SSH tunnel to victims for persistent access.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Storm-1811 XOR encodes a Cobalt Strike installation payload in a DLL file that is decoded with a hardcoded key when called by a legitimate 7zip installation process.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: Storm-1811 has used `whoami.exe` to determine if the active user on a compromised system is an administrator.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: Storm-1811 has prompted users to download and execute batch scripts that masquerade as legitimate update files during initial access and social engineering operations.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Storm-1811 has disguised Cobalt Strike installers as a malicious DLL masquerading as part of a legitimate 7zip installation package.
Uses T1036.010 Masquerade Account Name: Storm-1811 has created Microsoft Teams accounts that spoof IT support and helpdesk members for use in application and voice phishing.
Uses T1048.002 Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol: Storm-1811 has exfiltrated captured user credentials via Secure Copy Protocol (SCP).
Uses T1056 Input Capture: Storm-1811 has used a PowerShell script to capture user credentials after prompting a user to authenticate to run a malicious script masquerading as a legitimate update item.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Storm-1811 has used PowerShell for multiple purposes, such as using PowerShell scripts executing in an infinite loop to create an SSH connection to a command and control server.

title: ATT&CK Group G1046: Storm-1811
text:
ATT&CK Group G1046: Storm-1811
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Storm-1811 has used multiple batch scripts during initial access and subsequent actions on victim machines.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: Storm-1811 has locally staged captured credentials for subsequent manual exfiltration.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: Storm-1811 has performed domain account enumeration during intrusions.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Storm-1811 has used scripted `cURL` commands, BITSAdmin, and other mechanisms to retrieve follow-on batch scripts and tools for execution on victim devices.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: Storm-1811 has distributed password-protected archives such as ZIP files during intrusions.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Storm-1811 has prompted users to execute downloaded software and payloads as the result of social engineering activity.
Uses T1219.002 Remote Desktop Software: Storm-1811 has abused multiple types of legitimate remote access software and tools, such as ScreenConnect, NetSupport Manager, and AnyDesk.
Uses T1222.001 Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification: Storm-1811 has used `cacls.exe` via batch script to modify file and directory permissions in victim environments.
Uses T1482 Domain Trust Discovery: Storm-1811 has enumerated domain accounts and access during intrusions.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: Storm-1811 is a financially-motivated entity linked to the deployment of Black Basta ransomware in victim environments.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Storm-1811 has created Windows Registry Run keys that execute various batch scripts to establish persistence on victim devices.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Storm-1811 has distributed malicious links to victims that redirect to EvilProxy-based phishing sites to harvest credentials.
Uses T1566.003 Spearphishing via Service: Storm-1811 has used Microsoft Teams to send messages and initiate voice calls to victims posing as IT support personnel.
Uses T1566.004 Spearphishing Voice: Storm-1811 has initiated voice calls with victims posing as IT support to prompt users to download and execute scripts and other tools for initial access.

title: ATT&CK Group G1046: Storm-1811
text:
ATT&CK Group G1046: Storm-1811
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: Storm-1811 has used the Impacket toolset to move and remotely execute payloads to other hosts in victim networks.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Storm-1811 has deployed a malicious DLL (7z.DLL) that is sideloaded by a modified, legitimate installer (7zG.exe) when that installer is executed with an additional command line parameter of `b` at runtime to load a Cobalt Strike beacon payload.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Storm-1811 has created domains for use with RMM tools.
Uses T1585.003 Cloud Accounts: Storm-1811 has created malicious accounts to enable activity via Microsoft Teams, typically spoofing various IT support and helpdesk themes.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Storm-1811 acquired various legitimate and malicious tools, such as RMM software and commodity malware packages, for operations.
Uses T1656 Impersonation: Storm-1811 impersonates help desk and IT support personnel for phishing and social engineering purposes during initial access to victim environments.
Uses T1667 Email Bombing: Storm-1811 has deployed large volumes of non-malicious email spam to victims in order to prompt follow-on interactions with the threat actor posing as IT support or helpdesk to resolve the problem.

title: ATT&CK Group G0130: Ajax Security Team
text:
ATT&CK Group G0130: Ajax Security Team
Associated names: Operation Woolen-Goldfish, AjaxTM, Rocket Kitten, Flying Kitten, Operation Saffron Rose.
Ajax Security Team is a group that has been active since at least 2010 and believed to be operating out of Iran.
