Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: Stealth Falcon malware gathers passwords from multiple sources, including Windows Credential Vault and Outlook.
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: Stealth Falcon malware gathers passwords from multiple sources, including Internet Explorer, Firefox, and Chrome.
Uses T1555.004 Windows Credential Manager: Stealth Falcon malware gathers passwords from the Windows Credential Vault.
Uses T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography: Stealth Falcon malware encrypts C2 traffic using RC4 with a hard-coded key.

title: ATT&CK Group G0105: DarkVishnya
text:
ATT&CK Group G0105: DarkVishnya
DarkVishnya is a financially motivated threat actor targeting financial institutions in Eastern Europe. In 2017-2018 the group attacked at least 8 banks in this region.
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: DarkVishnya used network sniffing to obtain login data.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: DarkVishnya performed port scanning to obtain the list of active services.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: DarkVishnya used PowerShell to create shellcode loaders.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: DarkVishnya used brute-force attack to obtain login data.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: DarkVishnya scanned the network for public shared folders.
Uses T1200 Hardware Additions: DarkVishnya physically connected Bash Bunny, Raspberry Pi, netbooks, and inexpensive laptops to the target organization's environment to access the company’s local network.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: DarkVishnya used DameWare Mini Remote Control for lateral movement.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: DarkVishnya created new services for shellcode loaders distribution.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: DarkVishnya used ports 5190 and 7900 for shellcode listeners, and 4444, 4445, 31337 for shellcode C2.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: DarkVishnya has obtained and used tools such as Impacket, Winexe, and PsExec.

title: ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
text:
ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
Associated names: InkySquid, ScarCruft, Reaper, Group123, TEMP.Reaper, Ricochet Chollima.
APT37 is a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. The group has targeted victims primarily in South Korea, but also in Japan, Vietnam, Russia, Nepal, China, India, Romania, Kuwait, and other parts of the Middle East. APT37 has also been linked to the following campaigns between 2016-2018: Operation Daybreak, Operation Erebus, Golden Time, Evil New Year, Are you Happy?, FreeMilk, North Korean Human Rights, and Evil New Year 2018.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT37 has collected data from victims' local systems.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT37 obfuscates strings and payloads.
Uses T1027.003 Steganography: APT37 uses steganography to send images to users that are embedded with shellcode.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT37 identifies the victim username.
Uses T1036.001 Invalid Code Signature: APT37 has signed its malware with an invalid digital certificates listed as “Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Company Limited.”
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT37 has created scheduled tasks to run malicious scripts on a compromised host.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT37 injects its malware variant, ROKRAT, into the cmd.exe process.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT37's Freenki malware lists running processes using the Microsoft Windows API.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: APT37 has used Ruby scripts to execute payloads.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: APT37 has used the command-line interface.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: APT37 executes shellcode and a VBA script to decode Base64 strings.
Uses T1059.006 Python: APT37 has used Python scripts to execute payloads.

title: ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
text:
ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT37 uses HTTPS to conceal C2 communications.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT37 collects the computer name, the BIOS model, and execution path.
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: APT37 leverages social networking sites and cloud platforms (AOL, Twitter, Yandex, Mediafire, pCloud, Dropbox, and Box) for C2.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT37 has downloaded second stage malware from compromised websites.
Uses T1106 Native API: APT37 leverages the Windows API calls: VirtualAlloc(), WriteProcessMemory(), and CreateRemoteThread() for process injection.
Uses T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: APT37 has a Bluetooth device harvester, which uses Windows Bluetooth APIs to find information on connected Bluetooth devices.
Uses T1123 Audio Capture: APT37 has used an audio capturing utility known as SOUNDWAVE that captures microphone input.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: APT37 has used strategic web compromises, particularly of South Korean websites, to distribute malware. The group has also used torrent file-sharing sites to more indiscriminately disseminate malware to victims. As part of their compromises, the group has used a Javascript …
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT37 has used exploits for Flash Player (CVE-2016-4117, CVE-2018-4878), Word (CVE-2017-0199), Internet Explorer (CVE-2020-1380 and CVE-2020-26411), and Microsoft Edge (CVE-2021-26411) for execution.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT37 has sent spearphishing attachments attempting to get a user to open them.
Uses T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot: APT37 has used malware that will issue the command shutdown /r /t 1 to reboot a system after wiping its MBR.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT37's has added persistence via the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\CurrentVersion\Run\.
Uses T1548.002 Bypass User Account Control: APT37 has a function in the initial dropper to bypass Windows UAC in order to execute the next payload with higher privileges.

title: ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
text:
ATT&CK Group G0067: APT37
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: APT37 has used a credential stealer known as ZUMKONG that can harvest usernames and passwords stored in browsers.
Uses T1559.002 Dynamic Data Exchange: APT37 has used Windows DDE for execution of commands and a malicious VBS.
Uses T1561.002 Disk Structure Wipe: APT37 has access to destructive malware that is capable of overwriting a machine's Master Boot Record (MBR).
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT37 delivers malware using spearphishing emails with malicious HWP attachments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0028: Threat Group-1314
text:
ATT&CK Group G0028: Threat Group-1314
Associated names: TG-1314.
Threat Group-1314 is an unattributed threat group that has used compromised credentials to log into a victim's remote access infrastructure.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Threat Group-1314 actors mapped network drives using net use.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Threat Group-1314 actors spawned shells on remote systems on a victim network to execute commands.
Uses T1072 Software Deployment Tools: Threat Group-1314 actors used a victim's endpoint management platform, Altiris, for lateral movement.
Uses T1078.002 Domain Accounts: Threat Group-1314 actors used compromised domain credentials for the victim's endpoint management platform, Altiris, to move laterally.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Associated names: Wicked Panda, Brass Typhoon, BARIUM.
APT41 is a threat group that researchers have assessed as Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially-motivated operations. Active since at least 2012, APT41 has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries. Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives. APT41 overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and Winnti Group.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT41 has used hashdump, Mimikatz, Procdump, and the Windows Credential Editor to dump password hashes from memory and authenticate to other user accounts.
Uses T1003.002 Security Account Manager: APT41 extracted user account data from the Security Account Managerr (SAM), making a copy of this database from the registry using the reg save command or by exploiting volume shadow copies.
Uses T1003.003 NTDS: APT41 used ntdsutil to obtain a copy of the victim environment ntds.dit file.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT41 has uploaded files and data from a compromised host.
Uses T1008 Fallback Channels: APT41 used the Steam community page as a fallback mechanism for C2.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: APT41 queried registry values to determine items such as configured RDP ports and network configurations.
Uses T1014 Rootkit: APT41 deployed rootkits on Linux systems.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: APT41 collected MAC addresses from victim machines.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: APT41 has used MiPing to discover active systems in the victim network.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT41 used RDP for lateral movement. APT41 used NATBypass to expose local RDP ports on compromised systems to the Internet.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: APT41 has transferred implant files using Windows Admin Shares and the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, then executes files through Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT41 used VMProtected binaries in multiple intrusions.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: APT41 uses packers such as Themida to obfuscate malicious files.
Uses T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits: APT41 transfers post-exploitation files dividing the payload into fixed-size chunks to evade detection.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: APT41 has executed whoami commands, including using the WMIEXEC utility to execute this on remote machines.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: APT41 has created services to appear as benign system tools.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: APT41 attempted to masquerade their files as popular anti-virus software.
Uses T1037 Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: APT41 used a hidden shell script in `/etc/rc.d/init.d` to leverage the `ADORE.XSEC`backdoor and `Adore-NG` rootkit.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: APT41 used a malware variant called WIDETONE to conduct port scans on specified subnets.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: APT41 used WMI in several ways, including for execution of commands via WMIEXEC as well as for persistence via PowerSploit. APT41 has executed files through Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT41 has enumerated IP addresses of network resources and used the netstat command as part of network reconnaissance. The group has also used a malware variant, HIGHNOON, to enumerate active RDP sessions.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT41 used a compromised account to create a scheduled task on a system.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: APT41 malware TIDYELF loaded the main WINTERLOVE component by injecting it into the iexplore.exe process.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: APT41 used a keylogger called GEARSHIFT on a target system.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT41 leveraged PowerShell to deploy malware families in victims’ environments.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: APT41 used cmd.exe /c to execute commands on remote machines. APT41 used a batch file to install persistence for the Cobalt Strike BEACON loader.
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: APT41 used Linux shell commands for system survey and information gathering prior to exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2019-19871.
Uses T1069 Permission Groups Discovery: APT41 used net group commands to enumerate various Windows user groups and permissions.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by clearing Windows security and system events.
Uses T1070.003 Clear Command History: APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by deleting Bash histories.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT41 deleted files from the system.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT41 used HTTP to download payloads for CVE-2019-19781 and CVE-2020-10189 exploits.
Uses T1071.002 File Transfer Protocols: APT41 used exploit payloads that initiate download via ftp.
Uses T1071.004 DNS: APT41 used DNS for C2 communications.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT41 used compromised credentials to log on to other systems.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT41 uses multiple built-in commands such as systeminfo and `net config Workstation` to enumerate victim system basic configuration information.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT41 has executed file /bin/pwd on exploited victims, perhaps to return architecture related information.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: APT41 used built-in net commands to enumerate local administrator groups.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: APT41 used built-in net commands to enumerate domain administrator users.
Uses T1090 Proxy: APT41 used a tool called CLASSFON to covertly proxy network communications.
Uses T1098.007 Additional Local or Domain Groups: APT41 has added user accounts to the User and Admin groups.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1102.001 Dead Drop Resolver: APT41 used legitimate websites for C2 through dead drop resolvers (DDR), including GitHub, Pastebin, and Microsoft TechNet.
Uses T1104 Multi-Stage Channels: APT41 used the storescyncsvc.dll BEACON backdoor to download a secondary backdoor.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT41 used certutil to download additional files. APT41 downloaded post-exploitation tools such as Cobalt Strike via command shell following initial access. APT41 has uploaded Procdump and NATBypass to a staging directory and has used these tools in follow-on activities.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: APT41 performed password brute-force attacks on the local admin account.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: APT41 used a malware variant called GOODLUCK to modify the registry in order to steal credentials.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: APT41 compromised an online billing/payment service using VPN access between a third-party service provider and the targeted payment service.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: APT41 used the net share command as part of network reconnaissance.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: APT41 has created user accounts.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: APT41 exploited CVE-2020-10189 against Zoho ManageEngine Desktop Central through unsafe deserialization, and CVE-2019-19781 to compromise Citrix Application Delivery Controllers (ADC) and gateway devices. APT41 leveraged vulnerabilities such as ProxyLogon exploitation or SQL injection for initial access. APT41 exploited CVE-2021-26855 against …
Uses T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain: APT41 gained access to production environments where they could inject malicious code into legitimate, signed files and widely distribute them to end users.
Uses T1197 BITS Jobs: APT41 used BITSAdmin to download and install payloads.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT41 leveraged the follow exploits in their operations: CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2015-1641, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882, and CVE-2019-3396.
Uses T1213.003 Code Repositories: APT41 cloned victim user Git repositories during intrusions.
Uses T1218.001 Compiled HTML File: APT41 used compiled HTML (.chm) files for targeting.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: APT41 has used rundll32.exe to execute a loader.
Uses T1480.001 Environmental Keying: APT41 has encrypted payloads using the Data Protection API (DPAPI), which relies on keys tied to specific user accounts on specific machines. APT41 has also environmentally keyed second stage malware with an RC5 key derived in part from the infected …
Uses T1484.001 Group Policy Modification: APT41 used scheduled tasks created via Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to deploy ransomware.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: APT41 used a ransomware called Encryptor RaaS to encrypt files on the targeted systems and provide a ransom note to the user. APT41 also used Microsoft Bitlocker to encrypt workstations and Jetico’s BestCrypt to encrypt servers.
Uses T1496.001 Compute Hijacking: APT41 deployed a Monero cryptocurrency mining tool in a victim’s environment.
Uses T1542.003 Bootkit: APT41 deployed Master Boot Record bootkits on Windows systems to hide their malware and maintain persistence on victim systems.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: APT41 modified legitimate Windows services to install malware backdoors. APT41 created the StorSyncSvc service to provide persistence for Cobalt Strike.
Uses T1546.008 Accessibility Features: APT41 leveraged sticky keys to establish persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT41 created and modified startup files for persistence. APT41 added a registry key in HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Svchost to establish persistence for Cobalt Strike.
Uses T1550.002 Pass the Hash: APT41 uses tools such as Mimikatz to enable lateral movement via captured password hashes.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: APT41 leveraged code-signing certificates to sign malware when targeting both gaming and non-gaming organizations.
Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: APT41 has obtained information about accounts, lists of employees, and plaintext and hashed passwords from databases.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: APT41 used BrowserGhost, a tool designed to obtain credentials from browsers, to retrieve information from password stores.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: APT41 created a RAR archive of targeted files for exfiltration. Additionally, APT41 used the makecab.exe utility to both download tools, such as NATBypass, to the victim network and to archive a file for exfiltration.
Uses T1562.006 Indicator Blocking: APT41 developed a custom injector that enables an Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, making malicious processes invisible to Windows logging.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT41 sent spearphishing emails with attachments such as compiled HTML (.chm) files to initially compromise their victims.
Uses T1568.002 Domain Generation Algorithms: APT41 has used DGAs to change their C2 servers monthly.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: APT41 used svchost.exe and Net to execute a system service installed to launch a Cobalt Strike BEACON loader.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: APT41 uses remote shares to move and remotely execute payloads during lateral movemement.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: APT41 has used search order hijacking to execute malicious payloads, such as Winnti for Windows. APT41 has also used legitimate executables to perform DLL side-loading of their malware.
Uses T1574.006 Dynamic Linker Hijacking: APT41 has configured payloads to load via LD_PRELOAD.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT41 has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz, pwdump, PowerSploit, and Windows Credential Editor.
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: APT41 used the Acunetix SQL injection vulnerability scanner in target reconnaissance operations, as well as the JexBoss tool to identify vulnerabilities in Java applications.
Uses T1595.003 Wordlist Scanning: APT41 leverages various tools and frameworks to brute-force directories on web servers.
Uses T1596.005 Scan Databases: APT41 uses the Chinese website fofa.su, similar to the Shodan scanning service, for passive scanning of victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
text:
ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41
Uses T1599 Network Boundary Bridging: APT41 used `NATBypass` to bypass firewall restrictions and to access compromised systems via RDP.
Uses T1656 Impersonation: APT41 impersonated an employee at a video game developer company to send phishing emails.

title: ATT&CK Group G1032: INC Ransom
text:
ATT&CK Group G1032: INC Ransom
Associated names: GOLD IONIC.
INC Ransom is a ransomware and data extortion threat group associated with the deployment of INC Ransomware that has been active since at least July 2023. INC Ransom has targeted organizations worldwide most commonly in the industrial, healthcare, and education sectors in the US and Europe.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: INC Ransom has used RDP to move laterally.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: INC Ransom has named a PsExec executable winupd to mimic a legitimate Windows update file.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: INC Ransom has used NETSCAN.EXE for internal reconnaissance.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: INC Ransom has used WMIC to deploy ransomware.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: INC Ransom has used RDP to test network connections.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: INC Ransom has used `cmd.exe` to launch malicious payloads.
Uses T1069.002 Domain Groups: INC Ransom has enumerated domain groups on targeted hosts.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: INC Ransom has uninstalled tools from compromised endpoints after use.
Uses T1071 Application Layer Protocol: INC Ransom has used valid accounts over RDP to connect to targeted systems.
Uses T1074 Data Staged: INC Ransom has staged data on compromised hosts prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: INC Ransom has used compromised valid accounts for access to victim environments.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: INC Ransom has scanned for domain admin accounts in compromised environments.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: INC Ransom has downloaded tools to compromised servers including Advanced IP Scanner.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: INC Ransom has used Internet Explorer to view folders on other systems.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: INC Ransom has exploited known vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-3519 in Citrix NetScaler for initial access.

title: ATT&CK Group G1032: INC Ransom
text:
ATT&CK Group G1032: INC Ransom
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: INC Ransom has used AnyDesk and PuTTY on compromised systems.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: INC Ransom has used INC Ransomware to encrypt victim's data.
Uses T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account: INC Ransom has used Megasync to exfiltrate data to the cloud.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: INC Ransom has used 7-Zip and WinRAR to archive collected data prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: INC Ransom can use SystemSettingsAdminFlows.exe, a native Windows utility, to disable Windows Defender.
Uses T1566 Phishing: INC Ransom has used phishing to gain initial access.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: INC Ransom has run a file encryption executable via `Service Control Manager/7045;winupd,%SystemRoot%\winupd.exe,user mode service,demand start,LocalSystem`.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: INC Ransom has used a rapid succession of copy commands to install a file encryption executable across multiple endpoints within compromised infrastructure.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: INC Ransom has acquired and used several tools including MegaSync, AnyDesk, esentutl and PsExec.
Uses T1657 Financial Theft: INC Ransom has stolen and encrypted victim's data in order to extort payment for keeping it private or decrypting it.

title: ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
text:
ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
Associated names: Elephant Beetle.
FIN13 is a financially motivated cyber threat group that has targeted the financial, retail, and hospitality industries in Mexico and Latin America, as early as 2016. FIN13 achieves its objectives by stealing intellectual property, financial data, mergers and acquisition information, or PII.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: FIN13 has obtained memory dumps with ProcDump to parse and extract credentials from a victim's LSASS process memory with Mimikatz.
Uses T1003.002 Security Account Manager: FIN13 has extracted the SAM and SYSTEM registry hives using the `reg.exe` binary for obtaining password hashes from a compromised machine.
Uses T1003.003 NTDS: FIN13 has harvested the NTDS.DIT file and leveraged the Impacket tool on the compromised domain controller to locally decrypt it.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: FIN13 has gathered stolen credentials, sensitive data such as point-of-sale (POS), and ATM data from a compromised network before exfiltration.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: FIN13 has used `nslookup` and `ipconfig` for network reconnaissance efforts. FIN13 has also utilized a compromised Symantec Altiris console and LanDesk account to retrieve network information.
Uses T1016.001 Internet Connection Discovery: FIN13 has used `Ping` and `tracert` for network reconnaissance efforts.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: FIN13 has remotely accessed compromised environments via Remote Desktop Services (RDS) for lateral movement.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: FIN13 has leveraged SMB to move laterally within a compromised network via application servers and SQL servers.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: FIN13 has remotely accessed compromised environments via secure shell (SSH) for lateral movement.
Uses T1021.006 Windows Remote Management: FIN13 has leveraged `WMI` to move laterally within a compromised network via application servers and SQL servers.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: FIN13 has masqueraded staged data by using the Windows certutil utility to generate fake Base64 encoded certificates with the input file.

title: ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
text:
ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: FIN13 has used scheduled tasks names such as `acrotyr` and `AppServicesr` to mimic the same names in a compromised network's `C:\Windows` directory.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: FIN13 has masqueraded WAR files to look like legitimate packages such as, wsexample.war, wsexamples.com, examples.war, and exampl3s.war.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: FIN13 has utilized `nmap` for reconnaissance efforts. FIN13 has also scanned for internal MS-SQL servers in a compromised network.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: FIN13 has utilized `WMI` to execute commands and move laterally on compromised Windows machines.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: FIN13 has used `netstat` and other net commands for network reconnaissance efforts.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: FIN13 has created scheduled tasks in the `C:\Windows` directory of the compromised network.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: FIN13 has logged the keystrokes of victims to escalate privileges.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: FIN13 has used PowerShell commands to obtain DNS data from a compromised network.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: FIN13 has leveraged `xp_cmdshell` and Windows Command Shell to execute commands on a compromised machine. FIN13 has also attempted to leverage the ‘xp_cmdshell’ SQL procedure to execute remote commands on internal MS-SQL servers.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: FIN13 has used VBS scripts for code execution on comrpomised machines.
Uses T1069 Permission Groups Discovery: FIN13 has enumerated all users and roles from a victim's main treasury system.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: FIN13 has used HTTP requests to chain multiple web shells and to contact actor-controlled C2 servers prior to exfiltrating stolen data.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: FIN13 has utilized the following temporary folders on compromised Windows and Linux systems for their operations prior to exfiltration: `C:\Windows\Temp` and `/tmp`.

title: ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
text:
ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
Uses T1078.001 Default Accounts: FIN13 has leveraged default credentials for authenticating myWebMethods (WMS) and QLogic web management interface to gain initial access.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: FIN13 has collected local host information by utilizing Windows commands `systeminfo`, `fsutil`, and `fsinfo`. FIN13 has also utilized a compromised Symantex Altiris console and LanDesk account to retrieve host information.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: FIN13 has used the Windows `dir` command to enumerate files and directories in a victim's network.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: FIN13 has enumerated all users and their roles from a victim's main treasury system.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: FIN13 can identify user accounts associated with a Service Principal Name and query Service Principal Names within the domain by utilizing the following scripts: `GetUserSPNs.vbs` and `querySpn.vbs`.
Uses T1090.001 Internal Proxy: FIN13 has utilized a proxy tool to communicate between compromised assets.
Uses T1098.007 Additional Local or Domain Groups: FIN13 has assigned newly created accounts the sysadmin role to maintain persistence.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: FIN13 has downloaded additional tools and malware to compromised systems.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: FIN13 has gained access to compromised environments via remote access services such as the corporate virtual private network (VPN).
Uses T1134.003 Make and Impersonate Token: FIN13 has utilized tools such as Incognito V2 for token manipulation and impersonation.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: FIN13 has executed net view commands for enumeration of open shares on compromised machines.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: FIN13 has created MS-SQL local accounts in a compromised network.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: FIN13 has utilized `certutil` to decode base64 encoded versions of custom malware.

title: ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
text:
ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: FIN13 has exploited known vulnerabilities such as CVE-2017-1000486 (Primefaces Application Expression Language Injection), CVE-2015-7450 (WebSphere Application Server SOAP Deserialization Exploit), CVE-2010-5326 (SAP NewWeaver Invoker Servlet Exploit), and EDB-ID-24963 (SAP NetWeaver ConfigServlet Remote Code Execution) to gain initial access.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: FIN13 has utilized obfuscated and open-source web shells such as JspSpy, reGeorg, MiniWebCmdShell, and Vonloesch Jsp File Browser 1.2 to enable remote code execution and to execute commands on compromised web server.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: FIN13 has used Windows Registry run keys such as, `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\hosts` to maintain persistence.
Uses T1550.002 Pass the Hash: FIN13 has used the PowerShell utility `Invoke-SMBExec` to execute the pass the hash method for lateral movement within an compromised environment.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: FIN13 has obtained administrative credentials by browsing through local files on a compromised machine.
Uses T1556 Modify Authentication Process: FIN13 has replaced legitimate KeePass binaries with trojanized versions to collect passwords from numerous applications.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: FIN13 has compressed the dump output of compromised credentials with a 7zip binary.
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: FIN13 has created hidden files and folders within a compromised Linux system `/tmp` directory. FIN13 also has used `attrib.exe` to hide gathered local host information.
Uses T1565 Data Manipulation: FIN13 has injected fraudulent transactions into compromised networks that mimic legitimate behavior to siphon off incremental amounts of money.
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: FIN13 has utilized web shells and Java tools for tunneling capabilities to and from compromised assets.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: FIN13 has used IISCrack.dll as a side-loading technique to load a malicious version of httpodbc.dll on old IIS Servers (CVE-2001-0507).
Uses T1587.001 Malware: FIN13 has utilized custom malware to maintain persistence in a compromised environment.

title: ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
text:
ATT&CK Group G1016: FIN13
Uses T1588.002 Tool: FIN13 has utilized publicly available tools such as Mimikatz, Impacket, PWdump7, ProcDump, Nmap, and Incognito V2 for targeting efforts.
Uses T1589 Gather Victim Identity Information: FIN13 has researched employees to target for social engineering attacks.
Uses T1590.004 Network Topology: FIN13 has searched for infrastructure that can provide remote access to an environment for targeting efforts.
Uses T1657 Financial Theft: FIN13 has observed the victim's software and infrastructure over several months to understand the technical process of legitimate financial transactions, prior to attempting to conduct fraudulent transactions.

title: ATT&CK Group G0043: Group5
text:
ATT&CK Group G0043: Group5
Group5 is a threat group with a suspected Iranian nexus, though this attribution is not definite. The group has targeted individuals connected to the Syrian opposition via spearphishing and watering holes, normally using Syrian and Iranian themes. Group5 has used two commonly available remote access tools (RATs), njRAT and NanoCore, as well as an Android RAT, DroidJack.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Group5 disguised its malicious binaries with several layers of obfuscation, including encrypting the files.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: Malware used by Group5 is capable of capturing keystrokes.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Malware used by Group5 is capable of remotely deleting files from victims.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: Malware used by Group5 is capable of watching the victim's screen.

title: ATT&CK Group G0068: PLATINUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0068: PLATINUM
PLATINUM is an activity group that has targeted victims since at least 2009. The group has focused on targets associated with governments and related organizations in South and Southeast Asia.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: PLATINUM has used keyloggers that are also capable of dumping credentials.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: PLATINUM has renamed rar.exe to avoid detection.
Uses T1055 Process Injection: PLATINUM has used various methods of process injection including hot patching.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: PLATINUM has used several different keyloggers.
Uses T1056.004 Credential API Hooking: PLATINUM is capable of using Windows hook interfaces for information gathering such as credential access.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: PLATINUM has leveraged a zero-day vulnerability to escalate privileges.
Uses T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol: PLATINUM has used the Intel® Active Management Technology (AMT) Serial-over-LAN (SOL) channel for command and control.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: PLATINUM has transferred files using the Intel® Active Management Technology (AMT) Serial-over-LAN (SOL) channel.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: PLATINUM has sometimes used drive-by attacks against vulnerable browser plugins.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: PLATINUM has attempted to get users to open malicious files by sending spearphishing emails with attachments to victims.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: PLATINUM has sent spearphishing emails with attachments to victims as its primary initial access vector.

title: ATT&CK Group G0093: GALLIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0093: GALLIUM
Associated names: Granite Typhoon.
GALLIUM is a cyberespionage group that has been active since at least 2012, primarily targeting telecommunications companies, financial institutions, and government entities in Afghanistan, Australia, Belgium, Cambodia, Malaysia, Mozambique, the Philippines, Russia, and Vietnam. This group is particularly known for launching Operation Soft Cell, a long-term campaign targeting telecommunications providers. Security researchers have identified GALLIUM as a likely Chinese state-sponsored group, based in part on tools used and TTPs commonly associated with Chinese threat actors.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: GALLIUM used a modified version of Mimikatz along with a PowerShell-based Mimikatz to dump credentials on the victim machines.
Uses T1003.002 Security Account Manager: GALLIUM used reg commands to dump specific hives from the Windows Registry, such as the SAM hive, and obtain password hashes.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: GALLIUM collected data from the victim's local system, including password hashes from the SAM hive in the Registry.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: GALLIUM used ipconfig /all to obtain information about the victim network configuration. The group also ran a modified version of NBTscan to identify available NetBIOS name servers.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: GALLIUM used a modified version of NBTscan to identify available NetBIOS name servers over the network as well as ping to identify remote systems.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: GALLIUM used a modified version of HTRAN in which they obfuscated strings such as debug messages in an apparent attempt to evade detection.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: GALLIUM packed some payloads using different types of packers, both known and custom.
Uses T1027.005 Indicator Removal from Tools: GALLIUM ensured each payload had a unique hash, including by using different types of packers.

title: ATT&CK Group G0093: GALLIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0093: GALLIUM
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: GALLIUM used whoami and query user to obtain information about the victim user.
Uses T1036.003 Rename Legitimate Utilities: GALLIUM used a renamed cmd.exe file to evade detection.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: GALLIUM used Web shells and HTRAN for C2 and to exfiltrate data.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: GALLIUM used WMI for execution to assist in lateral movement as well as for installing tools across multiple assets.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: GALLIUM used netstat -oan to obtain information about the victim network connections.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: GALLIUM established persistence for PoisonIvy by created a scheduled task.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: GALLIUM used PowerShell for execution to assist in lateral movement as well as for dumping credentials stored on compromised machines.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: GALLIUM used the Windows command shell to execute commands.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: GALLIUM compressed and staged files in multi-part archives in the Recycle Bin prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: GALLIUM leveraged valid accounts to maintain access to a victim network.
Uses T1090.002 External Proxy: GALLIUM used a modified version of HTRAN to redirect connections between networks.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: GALLIUM dropped additional tools to victims during their operation, including portqry.exe, a renamed cmd.exe file, winrar, and HTRAN.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: GALLIUM has used VPN services, including SoftEther VPN, to access and maintain persistence in victim environments.
Uses T1136.002 Domain Account: GALLIUM created high-privileged domain user accounts to maintain access to victim networks.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: GALLIUM exploited a publicly-facing servers including Wildfly/JBoss servers to gain access to the network.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: GALLIUM used Web shells to persist in victim environments and assist in execution and exfiltration.

title: ATT&CK Group G0093: GALLIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0093: GALLIUM
Uses T1550.002 Pass the Hash: GALLIUM used dumped hashes to authenticate to other machines via pass the hash.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: GALLIUM has used stolen certificates to sign its tools including those from Whizzimo LLC.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: GALLIUM used WinRAR to compress and encrypt stolen data prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: GALLIUM has used PsExec to move laterally between hosts in the target network.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: GALLIUM used DLL side-loading to covertly load PoisonIvy into memory on the victim machine.
Uses T1583.004 Server: GALLIUM has used Taiwan-based servers that appear to be exclusive to GALLIUM.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: GALLIUM has used a variety of widely-available tools, which in some cases they modified to add functionality and/or subvert antimalware solutions.

title: ATT&CK Group G0051: FIN10
text:
ATT&CK Group G0051: FIN10
FIN10 is a financially motivated threat group that has targeted organizations in North America since at least 2013 through 2016. The group uses stolen data exfiltrated from victims to extort organizations.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: FIN10 has used RDP to move laterally to systems in the victim environment.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: FIN10 has used Meterpreter to enumerate users on remote systems.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: FIN10 has established persistence by using S4U tasks as well as the Scheduled Task option in PowerShell Empire.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: FIN10 uses PowerShell for execution as well as PowerShell Empire to establish persistence.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: FIN10 has executed malicious.bat files containing PowerShell commands.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: FIN10 has used batch scripts and scheduled tasks to delete critical system files.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: FIN10 has used stolen credentials to connect remotely to victim networks using VPNs protected with only a single factor.
Uses T1078.003 Local Accounts: FIN10 has moved laterally using the Local Administrator account.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: FIN10 has established persistence by using the Registry option in PowerShell Empire to add a Run key.
Uses T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer: FIN10 has deployed Meterpreter stagers and SplinterRAT instances in the victim network after moving laterally.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: FIN10 has relied on publicly-available software to gain footholds and establish persistence in victim environments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0044: Winnti Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0044: Winnti Group
Associated names: Blackfly.
Winnti Group is a threat group with Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2010. The group has heavily targeted the gaming industry, but it has also expanded the scope of its targeting. Some reporting suggests a number of other groups, including Axiom, APT17, and Ke3chang, are closely linked to Winnti Group.
Uses T1014 Rootkit: Winnti Group used a rootkit to modify typical server functionality.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Winnti Group looked for a specific process running on infected servers.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Winnti Group has used a program named ff.exe to search for specific documents on compromised hosts.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Winnti Group has downloaded an auxiliary program named ff.exe to infected machines.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: Winnti Group used stolen certificates to sign its malware.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Winnti Group has registered domains for C2 that mimicked sites of their intended targets.

title: ATT&CK Group G0061: FIN8
text:
ATT&CK Group G0061: FIN8
Associated names: Syssphinx.
FIN8 is a financially motivated threat group that has been active since at least January 2016, and known for targeting organizations in the hospitality, retail, entertainment, insurance, technology, chemical, and financial sectors. In June 2021, security researchers detected FIN8 switching from targeting point-of-sale (POS) devices to distributing a number of ransomware variants.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: FIN8 harvests credentials using Invoke-Mimikatz or Windows Credentials Editor (WCE).
Uses T1016.001 Internet Connection Discovery: FIN8 has used the Ping command to check connectivity to actor-controlled C2 servers.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: FIN8 has used dsquery and other Active Directory utilities to enumerate hosts; they have also used nltest.exe /dclist to retrieve a list of domain controllers.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: FIN8 has used RDP for lateral movement.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: FIN8 has attempted to map to C$ on enumerated hosts to test the scope of their current credentials/context. FIN8 has also used smbexec from the Impacket suite for lateral movement.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: FIN8 has used environment variables and standard input (stdin) to obfuscate command-line arguments. FIN8 also obfuscates malicious macros delivered as payloads.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: FIN8 has executed the command `quser` to display the session details of a compromised machine.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: FIN8's malicious spearphishing payloads use WMI to launch malware and spawn `cmd.exe` execution. FIN8 has also used WMIC and the Impacket suite for lateral movement, as well as during and post compromise cleanup activities.
Uses T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol: FIN8 has used FTP to exfiltrate collected data.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: FIN8 has used scheduled tasks to maintain RDP backdoors.
Uses T1055.004 Asynchronous Procedure Call: FIN8 has injected malicious code into a new svchost.exe process.

title: ATT&CK Group G0061: FIN8
text:
ATT&CK Group G0061: FIN8
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: FIN8's malicious spearphishing payloads are executed as PowerShell. FIN8 has also used PowerShell for lateral movement and credential access.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: FIN8 has used a Batch file to automate frequently executed post compromise cleanup activities. FIN8 has also executed commands remotely via `cmd.exe`.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: FIN8 has exploited the CVE-2016-0167 local vulnerability.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: FIN8 has cleared logs during post compromise cleanup activities.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: FIN8 has deleted tmp and prefetch files during post compromise cleanup activities. FIN8 has also deleted PowerShell scripts to evade detection on compromised machines.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: FIN8 has used HTTPS for command and control.
Uses T1074.002 Remote Data Staging: FIN8 aggregates staged data from a network into a single location.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: FIN8 has used valid accounts for persistence and lateral movement.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: FIN8 has used PowerShell Scripts to check the architecture of a compromised machine before the selection of a 32-bit or 64-bit version of a malicious.NET loader.
Uses T1102 Web Service: FIN8 has used sslip.io, a free IP to domain mapping service that also makes SSL certificate generation easier for traffic encryption, as part of their command and control.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: FIN8 has used remote code execution to download subsequent payloads.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: FIN8 has deleted Registry keys during post compromise cleanup activities.
Uses T1134.001 Token Impersonation/Theft: FIN8 has used a malicious framework designed to impersonate the lsass.exe/vmtoolsd.exe token.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: FIN8 has used emails with malicious links to lure victims into installing malware.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: FIN8 has used malicious e-mail attachments to lure victims into executing malware.

title: ATT&CK Group G0061: FIN8
text:
ATT&CK Group G0061: FIN8
Uses T1482 Domain Trust Discovery: FIN8 has retrieved a list of trusted domains by using nltest.exe /domain_trusts.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: FIN8 has deployed ransomware such as Ragnar Locker, White Rabbit, and attempted to execute Noberus on compromised networks.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: FIN8 has used Registry keys to detect and avoid executing in potential sandboxes.
Uses T1546.003 Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription: FIN8 has used WMI event subscriptions for persistence.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: FIN8 has used RAR to compress collected data before exfiltration.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: FIN8 has distributed targeted emails containing Word documents with embedded malicious macros.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: FIN8 has distributed targeted emails containing links to malicious documents with embedded macros.
Uses T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography: FIN8 has used the Plink utility to tunnel RDP back to C2 infrastructure.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: FIN8 has used open-source tools such as Impacket for targeting efforts.
Uses T1588.003 Code Signing Certificates: FIN8 has used an expired open-source X.509 certificate for testing in the OpenSSL repository, to connect to actor-controlled C2 servers.

title: ATT&CK Group G0106: Rocke
text:
ATT&CK Group G0106: Rocke
Rocke is an alleged Chinese-speaking adversary whose primary objective appeared to be cryptojacking, or stealing victim system resources for the purposes of mining cryptocurrency. The name Rocke comes from the email address "rocke@live.cn" used to create the wallet which held collected cryptocurrency. Researchers have detected overlaps between Rocke and the Iron Cybercrime Group, though this attribution has not been confirmed.
Uses T1014 Rootkit: Rocke has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to hook libc functions in order to hide the installed dropper and mining software in process lists.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Rocke has looked for IP addresses in the known_hosts file on the infected system and attempted to SSH into them.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Rocke has spread its coinminer via SSH.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Rocke has modified UPX headers after packing files to break unpackers.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: Rocke's miner has created UPX-packed files in the Windows Start Menu Folder.
Uses T1027.004 Compile After Delivery: Rocke has compiled malware, delivered to victims as.c files, with the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC).
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Rocke has used shell scripts which download mining executables and saves them with the filename "java".
Uses T1037 Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Rocke has installed an "init.d" startup script to maintain persistence.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: Rocke conducted scanning for exposed TCP port 7001 as well as SSH and Redis servers.
Uses T1053.003 Cron: Rocke installed a cron job that downloaded and executed files from the C2.
Uses T1055.002 Portable Executable Injection: Rocke's miner, "TermsHost.exe", evaded defenses by injecting itself into Windows processes, including Notepad.exe.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Rocke can detect a running process's PID on the infected machine.

title: ATT&CK Group G0106: Rocke
text:
ATT&CK Group G0106: Rocke
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: Rocke used shell scripts to run commands which would obtain persistence and execute the cryptocurrency mining malware.
Uses T1059.006 Python: Rocke has used Python-based malware to install and spread their coinminer.
Uses T1070.002 Clear Linux or Mac System Logs: Rocke has cleared log files within the /var/log/ folder.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Rocke has deleted files on infected machines.
Uses T1070.006 Timestomp: Rocke has changed the time stamp of certain files.
Uses T1071 Application Layer Protocol: Rocke issued wget requests from infected systems to the C2.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Rocke has executed wget and curl commands to Pastebin over the HTTPS protocol.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Rocke has used uname -m to collect the name and information about the infected system's kernel.
Uses T1102 Web Service: Rocke has used Pastebin, Gitee, and GitLab for Command and Control.
Uses T1102.001 Dead Drop Resolver: Rocke has used Pastebin to check the version of beaconing malware and redirect to another Pastebin hosting updated malware.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Rocke used malware to download additional malicious files to the target system.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: Rocke has extracted tar.gz files after downloading them from a C2 server.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Rocke exploited Apache Struts, Oracle WebLogic (CVE-2017-10271), and Adobe ColdFusion (CVE-2017-3066) vulnerabilities to deliver malware.
Uses T1222.002 Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification: Rocke has changed file permissions of files so they could not be modified.
Uses T1496.001 Compute Hijacking: Rocke has distributed cryptomining malware.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: Rocke used scripts which detected and uninstalled antivirus software.
Uses T1543.002 Systemd Service: Rocke has installed a systemd service script to maintain persistence.

title: ATT&CK Group G0106: Rocke
text:
ATT&CK Group G0106: Rocke
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Rocke's miner has created UPX-packed files in the Windows Start Menu Folder.
Uses T1552.004 Private Keys: Rocke has used SSH private keys on the infected machine to spread its coinminer throughout a network.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Rocke used scripts which detected and uninstalled antivirus software.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: Rocke used scripts which killed processes and added firewall rules to block traffic related to other cryptominers.
Uses T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories: Rocke downloaded a file "libprocesshider", which could hide files on the target system.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: Rocke's miner connects to a C2 server using port 51640.
Uses T1574.006 Dynamic Linker Hijacking: Rocke has modified /etc/ld.so.preload to hook libc functions in order to hide the installed dropper and mining software in process lists.

title: ATT&CK Group G1042: RedEcho
text:
ATT&CK Group G1042: RedEcho
RedEcho is a People’s Republic of China-related threat actor associated with long-running intrusions in Indian critical infrastructure entities. RedEcho overlaps with various other PRC-linked threat groups, such as APT41, and is linked to ShadowPad malware use through shared infrastructure.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: RedEcho network activity is associated with SSL traffic via TCP 443 and proxied HTTP traffic over non-standard ports.
Uses T1568 Dynamic Resolution: RedEcho used dynamic DNS domains associated with malicious infrastructure.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: RedEcho has used non-standard ports such as TCP 8080 for HTTP communication.
Uses T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography: RedEcho uses SSL for network communication.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: RedEcho has registered domains spoofing Indian critical infrastructure entities.

title: ATT&CK Group G1031: Saint Bear
text:
ATT&CK Group G1031: Saint Bear
Associated names: Storm-0587, TA471, UAC-0056, Lorec53.
Saint Bear is a Russian-nexus threat actor active since early 2021, primarily targeting entities in Ukraine and Georgia. The group is notable for a specific remote access tool, Saint Bot, and information stealer, OutSteel in campaigns. Saint Bear typically relies on phishing or web staging of malicious documents and related file types for initial access, spoofing government or related entities. Saint Bear has previously been confused with Ember Bear operations, but analysis of behaviors, tools, and targeting indicates these are distinct clusters.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: Saint Bear clones.NET assemblies from other.NET binaries as well as cloning code signing certificates from other software to obfuscate the initial loader payload.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Saint Bear initial payloads included encoded follow-on payloads located in the resources file of the first-stage loader.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Saint Bear has used the Windows Script Host (wscript) to execute intermediate files written to victim machines.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Saint Bear relies extensively on PowerShell execution from malicious attachments and related content to retrieve and execute follow-on payloads.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Saint Bear initial loaders will also drop a malicious Windows batch file, available via open source GitHub repositories, that disables Microsoft Defender functionality.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: Saint Bear has delivered malicious Microsoft Office files containing an embedded JavaScript object that would, on execution, download and execute OutSteel and Saint Bot.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: Saint Bear will leverage malicious Windows batch scripts to modify registry values associated with Windows Defender functionality.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Saint Bear has leveraged vulnerabilities in client applications such as CVE-2017-11882 in Microsoft Office to enable code execution in victim environments.

title: ATT&CK Group G1031: Saint Bear
text:
ATT&CK Group G1031: Saint Bear
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Saint Bear has, in addition to email-based phishing attachments, used malicious websites masquerading as legitimate entities to host links to malicious files for user execution.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Saint Bear relies on user interaction and execution of malicious attachments and similar for initial execution on victim systems.
Uses T1497 Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: Saint Bear contains several anti-analysis and anti-virtualization checks.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: Saint Bear has used an initial loader malware featuring a legitimate code signing certificate associated with "Electrum Technologies GmbH."
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Saint Bear will modify registry entries and scheduled task objects associated with Windows Defender to disable its functionality.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Saint Bear uses a variety of file formats, such as Microsoft Office documents, ZIP archives, PDF documents, and other items as phishing attachments for initial access.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: Saint Bear has leveraged the Discord content delivery network to host malicious content for retrieval during initial access operations.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: Saint Bear gathered victim email information in advance of phishing operations for targeted attacks.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: Saint Bear has used the Discord content delivery network for hosting malicious content referenced in links and emails.
Uses T1656 Impersonation: Saint Bear has impersonated government and related entities in both phishing activity and developing web sites with malicious links that mimic legitimate resources.

title: ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
text:
ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
Associated names: Roasted 0ktapus, Octo Tempest, Storm-0875, UNC3944.
Scattered Spider is a native English-speaking cybercriminal group active since at least 2022. The group initially targeted customer relationship management (CRM) providers, business process outsourcing (BPO) firms, and telecommunications and technology companies before expanding in 2023 to gaming, hospitality, retail, managed service provider (MSP), manufacturing, and financial sectors. 
Scattered Spider relies heavily on social engineering, including impersonating IT and help-desk staff, to gain initial access, bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and compromise enterprise networks. The group has adapted its tooling to evade endpoint detection and response (EDR) defenses and used ransomware for financial gain. 
Scattered Spider had expanded into hybrid cloud and identity environments, using help-desk impersonation and MFA bypass to obtain administrator access in Okta, AWS, and Office 365.
Uses T1003.003 NTDS: Scattered Spider has extracted the `NTDS.dit` file by creating volume shadow copies of virtual domain controller disks.
Uses T1006 Direct Volume Access: Scattered Spider has created volume shadow copies of virtual domain controller disks to extract the `NTDS.dit` file.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Scattered Spider has used network reconnaissance commands for discovery including `ping` and `nltest`.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Scattered Spider can enumerate remote systems, such as VMware vCenter infrastructure.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Scattered Spider has used RDP to enable lateral movement.
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Scattered Spider has used SSH to move laterally in victim environments and to access the vSphere vCenter Server GUI.
Uses T1021.007 Cloud Services: Scattered Spider has also leveraged pre-existing AWS EC2 instances for lateral movement and data collection purposes.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: Scattered Spider has exfiltrated data from compromised VMware vCenter servers through an established C2 channel using the Teleport remote access tool.

title: ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
text:
ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Scattered Spider has used the PowerShell cmdlet Get-ADUser.
Uses T1059.004 Unix Shell: Scattered Spider has used the command shell to upload and install the Teleport remote access tool to a compromised vCenter Server Appliance.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: Scattered Spider has deployed a malicious kernel driver through exploitation of CVE-2015-2291 in the Intel Ethernet diagnostics driver for Windows (iqvw64.sys).
Uses T1069 Permission Groups Discovery: Scattered Spider has enumerated the vSphere Admins and ESX Admins groups in targeted environments.
Uses T1069.002 Domain Groups: Scattered Spider has enumerated Active Directory security groups including through the use of ADExplorer, ADRecon.ps1, and Get-ADUser.
Uses T1070.008 Clear Mailbox Data: Scattered Spider has manually deleted emails notifying users of suspicious account activity.
Uses T1074 Data Staged: Scattered Spider stages data in a centralized database prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Scattered Spider has used compromised credentials for initial access.
Uses T1078.004 Cloud Accounts: Scattered Spider has used compromised Microsoft Entra ID accounts to pivot in victim environments.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Scattered Spider has executed scripts to identify the underlying operating system to ensure it uses the correct installation package for malicious payloads.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Scattered Spider Spider enumerates a target organization for files and directories of interest, including source code, user provisioning, MFA device registration, network diagrams, and shared credentials in documents or spreadsheets.
Uses T1087 Account Discovery: Scattered Spider has identified vSphere administrator accounts.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: Scattered Spider has enumerated legitimate domain accounts which are used in the targeted environment.
Uses T1090 Proxy: Scattered Spider has used proxy networks to hamper detection and has installed legitimate proxy tools on VMware vCenter and adversary-controlled VMs.

title: ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
text:
ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
Uses T1098 Account Manipulation: Scattered Spider has added accounts to the ESX Admins group to grant them full admin rights in vSphere.
Uses T1098.003 Additional Cloud Roles: Scattered Spider has assigned user access admin roles in order to gain Tenant Root Group management permissions in Azure.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Scattered Spider has downloaded the Teleport remote access tool to compromised VMware vCenter Servers.
Uses T1114 Email Collection: Scattered Spider searched the victim’s Microsoft Exchange for emails about the intrusion and incident response.
Uses T1114.003 Email Forwarding Rule: Scattered Spider has redirected emails notifying users of suspicious account activity.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: Scattered Spider has leveraged legitimate remote management tools to maintain persistent access.
Uses T1136 Create Account: Scattered Spider creates new user identities within the compromised organization.
Uses T1204 User Execution: Scattered Spider has impersonated organization IT and helpdesk staff to instruct victims to execute commercial remote access tools to gain initial access.
Uses T1213.003 Code Repositories: Scattered Spider enumerates data stored within victim code repositories, such as internal GitHub repositories.
Uses T1213.005 Messaging Applications: Scattered Spider threat actors search the victim’s Slack and Microsoft Teams for conversations about the intrusion and incident response.
Uses T1217 Browser Information Discovery: Scattered Spider retrieves browser histories via infostealer malware such as Raccoon Stealer.
Uses T1219.002 Remote Desktop Software: In addition to directing victims to run remote software, Scattered Spider members themselves also deploy RMM software including TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn, ngrok, and ConnectWise to establish persistence on the compromised network.
Uses T1484.002 Trust Modification: Scattered Spider adds a federated identity provider to the victim’s SSO tenant and activates automatic account linking.
Uses T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact: Scattered Spider has used BlackCat and DragonForce ransomware to encrypt files including on VMWare ESXi servers.

title: ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
text:
ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
Uses T1490 Inhibit System Recovery: Scattered Spider has stopped the Volume Shadow Copy service on compromised hosts.
Uses T1530 Data from Cloud Storage: Scattered Spider enumerates data stored in cloud resources for collection and exfiltration purposes.
Uses T1538 Cloud Service Dashboard: Scattered Spider abused AWS Systems Manager Inventory to identify targets on the compromised network prior to lateral movement.
Uses T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie: Scattered Spider retrieves browser cookies via Raccoon Stealer.
Uses T1543.002 Systemd Service: Scattered Spider has run `SYSTEMD_UNIT_PATH="/lib/systemd/ system/teleport.service` to establish persistence for the Teleport remote access tool.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: Scattered Spider Spider searches for credential storage documentation on a compromised host.
Uses T1552.004 Private Keys: Scattered Spider enumerate and exfiltrate code-signing certificates from a compromised host.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: Scattered Spider has used self-signed and stolen certificates originally issued to NVIDIA and Global Software LLC.
Uses T1555.005 Password Managers: Scattered Spider has searched for credentials in password vaults and Privileged Access Management (PAM) solutions including HashiCorp Vault.
Uses T1556.006 Multi-Factor Authentication: After compromising user accounts, Scattered Spider registers their own MFA tokens.
Uses T1556.009 Conditional Access Policies: Scattered Spider has added additional trusted locations to Azure AD conditional access policies.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Scattered Spider has uninstalled and disabled security tools.
Uses T1564.008 Email Hiding Rules: Scattered Spider creates inbound rules on the compromised email accounts of security personnel to automatically delete emails from vendor security products.
Uses T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage: Scattered Spider has exfiltrated victim data to the MEGA file sharing site, SnowFlake, and AWS S3 buckets.
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: Scattered Spider has installed protocol-tunneling tools on VMware vCenter and adversary-controlled VMs, including Teleport.sh, Chisel (configured to communicate with trycloudflare[.]com subdomains), MobaXterm, ngrok, Pinggy, and Teleport.

title: ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
text:
ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
Uses T1578.002 Create Cloud Instance: Scattered Spider has created Amazon EC2 instances within the victim's environment.
Uses T1580 Cloud Infrastructure Discovery: Scattered Spider enumerates cloud environments including Amazon Web Services (AWS) S3 buckets to identify server and backup management infrastructure, resource access, databases and storage containers.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Scattered Spider has registered domains to spoof legitimate corporate login portals.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: Scattered Spider has created matching fake social media profiles to support new accounts created in victim environments.
Uses T1588.001 Malware: Scattered Spider has obtained malware to use at multiple stages of operations including information stealers, remote access tools, and ransomware.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Scattered Spider has obtained tools for use throughout the attack lifecycle to include remote access software, protocol tunneling and proxy tools, exploitation frameworks, and reconnaissance tools.
Uses T1589 Gather Victim Identity Information: Scattered Spider has used information from previous data breaches to identify employee names to be used in social engineering.
Uses T1598 Phishing for Information: Scattered Spider has used a combination of credential phishing and social engineering to capture one-time-password (OTP) codes.
Uses T1598.003 Spearphishing Link: Scattered Spider has used domains mirroring corporate login portals to socially engineer victims into providing credentials.
Uses T1598.004 Spearphishing Voice: Scattered Spider has used help desk voice-based phishing and also called employees at target organizations and compelled them to navigate to fake login portals using adversary-in-the-middle toolkits.
Uses T1621 Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation: Scattered Spider has used multifactor authentication (MFA) fatigue by sending repeated MFA authentication requests to targets.
Uses T1656 Impersonation: Scattered Spider utilized social engineering to compel IT help desk personnel to reset passwords and MFA tokens. Scattered Spider has also used Microsoft Teams to pose as internal IT support or help desk personnel.

title: ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
text:
ATT&CK Group G1015: Scattered Spider
Uses T1657 Financial Theft: Scattered Spider has deployed ransomware on compromised hosts and threatened to leak stolen data for financial gain.

title: ATT&CK Group G1012: CURIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G1012: CURIUM
Associated names: Crimson Sandstorm, TA456, Tortoise Shell, Yellow Liderc.
CURIUM is an Iranian threat group, first reported in September 2019 and active since at least July 2018, targeting IT service providers in the Middle East. CURIUM has since invested in building relationships with potential targets via social media over a period of months to establish trust and confidence before sending malware. Security researchers note CURIUM has demonstrated great patience and persistence by chatting with potential targets daily and sending benign files to help lower their security consciousness.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: CURIUM has exfiltrated data from a compromised machine.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: CURIUM has used IMAP and SMTPS for exfiltration via tools such as IMAPLoader.
Uses T1048.002 Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol: CURIUM has used SMTPS to exfiltrate collected data from victims.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: CURIUM has leveraged PowerShell scripts for initial process execution and data gathering in victim environments.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: CURIUM deploys information gathering tools focused on capturing IP configuration, running application, system information, and network connectivity information.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: CURIUM deployed mechanisms to check system time information following strategic website compromise attacks.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: CURIUM has used strategic website compromise to infect victims with malware such as IMAPLoader.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: CURIUM has lured users into opening malicious files delivered via social media.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: CURIUM has been linked to web shells following likely server compromise as an initial access vector into victim networks.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: CURIUM has used phishing with malicious attachments for initial access to victim environments.
Uses T1566.003 Spearphishing via Service: CURIUM has used social media to deliver malicious files to victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G1012: CURIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G1012: CURIUM
Uses T1583.001 Domains: CURIUM created domains to facilitate strategic website compromise and credential capture activities.
Uses T1583.003 Virtual Private Server: CURIUM created virtual private server instances to facilitate use of malicious domains and other items.
Uses T1583.004 Server: CURIUM has created dedicated servers for command and control and exfiltration purposes.
Uses T1584.006 Web Services: CURIUM has compromised legitimate websites to enable strategic website compromise attacks.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: CURIUM has established a network of fictitious social media accounts, including on Facebook and LinkedIn, to establish relationships with victims, often posing as an attractive woman.
Uses T1585.002 Email Accounts: CURIUM has created dedicated email accounts for use with tools such as IMAPLoader.
Uses T1598.003 Spearphishing Link: CURIUM used malicious links to adversary-controlled resources for credential harvesting.
Uses T1608.004 Drive-by Target: CURIUM used strategic website compromise to fingerprint then target victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0124: Windigo
text:
ATT&CK Group G0124: Windigo
The Windigo group has been operating since at least 2011, compromising thousands of Linux and Unix servers using the Ebury SSH backdoor to create a spam botnet. Despite law enforcement intervention against the creators, Windigo operators continued updating Ebury through 2019.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Windigo has used a script to gather credentials in files left on disk by OpenSSH backdoors.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windigo has used a Perl script for information gathering.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Windigo has used a script to detect which Linux distribution and version is currently installed on the system.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Windigo has used a script to check for the presence of files created by OpenSSH backdoors.
Uses T1090 Proxy: Windigo has delivered a generic Windows proxy Win32/Glubteta.M. Windigo has also used multiple reverse proxy chains as part of their C2 infrastructure.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Windigo has distributed Windows malware via drive-by downloads.
Uses T1518 Software Discovery: Windigo has used a script to detect installed software on targeted systems.

title: ATT&CK Group G0108: Blue Mockingbird
text:
ATT&CK Group G0108: Blue Mockingbird
Blue Mockingbird is a cluster of observed activity involving Monero cryptocurrency-mining payloads in dynamic-link library (DLL) form on Windows systems. The earliest observed Blue Mockingbird tools were created in December 2019.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: Blue Mockingbird has used Mimikatz to retrieve credentials from LSASS memory.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Blue Mockingbird has used Remote Desktop to log on to servers interactively and manually copy files to remote hosts.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Blue Mockingbird has used Windows Explorer to manually copy malicious files to remote hosts over SMB.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Blue Mockingbird has obfuscated the wallet address in the payload binary.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Blue Mockingbird has masqueraded their XMRIG payload name by naming it wercplsupporte.dll after the legitimate wercplsupport.dll file.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Blue Mockingbird has used wmic.exe to set environment variables.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Blue Mockingbird has used Windows Scheduled Tasks to establish persistence on local and remote hosts.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Blue Mockingbird has used PowerShell reverse TCP shells to issue interactive commands over a network connection.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Blue Mockingbird has used batch script files to automate execution and deployment of payloads.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Blue Mockingbird has collected hardware details for the victim's system, including CPU and memory information.
Uses T1090 Proxy: Blue Mockingbird has used FRP, ssf, and Venom to establish SOCKS proxy connections.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: Blue Mockingbird has used Windows Registry modifications to specify a DLL payload.
Uses T1134 Access Token Manipulation: Blue Mockingbird has used JuicyPotato to abuse the SeImpersonate token privilege to escalate from web application pool accounts to NT Authority\SYSTEM.

title: ATT&CK Group G0108: Blue Mockingbird
text:
ATT&CK Group G0108: Blue Mockingbird
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Blue Mockingbird has gained initial access by exploiting CVE-2019-18935, a vulnerability within Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX.
Uses T1218.010 Regsvr32: Blue Mockingbird has executed custom-compiled XMRIG miner DLLs using regsvr32.exe.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: Blue Mockingbird has executed custom-compiled XMRIG miner DLLs using rundll32.exe.
Uses T1496.001 Compute Hijacking: Blue Mockingbird has used XMRIG to mine cryptocurrency on victim systems.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: Blue Mockingbird has made their XMRIG payloads persistent as a Windows Service.
Uses T1546.003 Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription: Blue Mockingbird has used mofcomp.exe to establish WMI Event Subscription persistence mechanisms configured from a *.mof file.
Uses T1569.002 Service Execution: Blue Mockingbird has executed custom-compiled XMRIG miner DLLs by configuring them to execute via the "wercplsupport" service.
Uses T1574.012 COR_PROFILER: Blue Mockingbird has used wmic.exe and Windows Registry modifications to set the COR_PROFILER environment variable to execute a malicious DLL whenever a process loads the.NET CLR.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Blue Mockingbird has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz.

title: ATT&CK Group G1039: RedCurl
text:
ATT&CK Group G1039: RedCurl
RedCurl is a threat actor active since 2018 notable for corporate espionage targeting a variety of locations, including Ukraine, Canada and the United Kingdom, and a variety of industries, including but not limited to travel agencies, insurance companies, and banks. RedCurl is allegedly a Russian-speaking threat actor. The group’s operations typically start with spearphishing emails to gain initial access, then the group executes discovery and collection commands and scripts to find corporate data. The group concludes operations by exfiltrating files to the C2 servers.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: RedCurl used LaZagne to obtain passwords from memory.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: RedCurl has collected data from the local disk of compromised hosts.
Uses T1020 Automated Exfiltration: RedCurl has used batch scripts to exfiltrate data.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: RedCurl has used malware with string encryption. RedCurl has also encrypted data and has encoded PowerShell commands using Base64. RedCurl has used `PyArmor` to obfuscate code execution of LaZagne. Additionally, RedCurl has obfuscated downloaded files by renaming them as commonly …
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: RedCurl mimicked legitimate file names and scheduled tasks, e.g. ` MicrosoftCurrentupdatesCheck` and `MdMMaintenenceTask` to mask malicious files and scheduled tasks.
Uses T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive: RedCurl has collected data about network drives.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: RedCurl has used netstat to check if port 4119 is open.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: RedCurl has created scheduled tasks for persistence.
Uses T1056.002 GUI Input Capture: RedCurl prompts the user for credentials through a Microsoft Outlook pop-up.
