Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: TA551 has used obfuscated variable names in a JavaScript configuration file.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: TA551 has masked malware DLLs as dat and jpg files.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: TA551 has used cmd.exe to execute commands.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: TA551 has used HTTP for C2 communications.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: TA551 has retrieved DLLs and installer binaries for malware execution from C2.
Uses T1132.001 Standard Encoding: TA551 has used encoded ASCII text for initial C2 communications.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: TA551 has prompted users to enable macros within spearphishing attachments to install malware.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: TA551 has used mshta.exe to execute malicious payloads.
Uses T1218.010 Regsvr32: TA551 has used regsvr32.exe to load malicious DLLs.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: TA551 has used rundll32.exe to load malicious DLLs.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: TA551 has sent spearphishing attachments with password protected ZIP files.
Uses T1568.002 Domain Generation Algorithms: TA551 has used a DGA to generate URLs from executed macros.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: TA551 has used spoofed company emails that were acquired from email clients on previously infected hosts to target other individuals.

title: ATT&CK Group G1045: Salt Typhoon
text:
ATT&CK Group G1045: Salt Typhoon
Salt Typhoon is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-backed actor that has been active since at least 2019 and responsible for numerous compromises of network infrastructure at major U.S. telecommunication and internet service providers (ISP).
Uses T1021.004 SSH: Salt Typhoon has modified the loopback address on compromised switches and used them as the source of SSH connections to additional devices within the target environment, allowing them to bypass access control lists (ACLs).
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: Salt Typhoon has used a variety of tools and techniques to capture packet data between network interfaces.
Uses T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol: Salt Typhoon has exfiltrated configuration files from exploited network devices over FTP and TFTP.
Uses T1070.002 Clear Linux or Mac System Logs: Salt Typhoon has cleared logs including.bash_history, auth.log, lastlog, wtmp, and btmp.
Uses T1098.004 SSH Authorized Keys: Salt Typhoon has added SSH authorized_keys under root or other users at the Linux level on compromised network devices.
Uses T1110.002 Password Cracking: Salt Typhoon has cracked passwords for accounts with weak encryption obtained from the configuration files of compromised network devices.
Uses T1136 Create Account: Salt Typhoon has created Linux-level users on compromised network devices through modification of `/etc/shadow` and `/etc/passwd`.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Salt Typhoon has exploited CVE-2018-0171 in the Smart Install feature of Cisco IOS and Cisco IOS XE software for initial access.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: Salt Typhoon has made changes to the Access Control List (ACL) and loopback interface address on compromised devices.
Uses T1572 Protocol Tunneling: Salt Typhoon has modified device configurations to create and use Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) tunnels.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: Salt Typhoon has used custom tooling including JumbledPath.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Salt Typhoon has used publicly available tooling to exploit vulnerabilities.

title: ATT&CK Group G1045: Salt Typhoon
text:
ATT&CK Group G1045: Salt Typhoon
Uses T1590.004 Network Topology: Salt Typhoon has used configuration files from exploited network devices to help discover upstream and downstream network segments.
Uses T1602.002 Network Device Configuration Dump: Salt Typhoon has attempted to acquire credentials by dumping network device configurations.

title: ATT&CK Group G0001: Axiom
text:
ATT&CK Group G0001: Axiom
Associated names: Group 72.
Axiom is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group that has targeted the aerospace, defense, government, manufacturing, and media sectors since at least 2008. Some reporting suggests a degree of overlap between Axiom and Winnti Group but the two groups appear to be distinct based on differences in reporting on TTPs and targeting.
Uses T1001.002 Steganography: Axiom has used steganography to hide its C2 communications.
Uses T1003 OS Credential Dumping: Axiom has been known to dump credentials.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Axiom has collected data from a compromised network.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: Axiom has used RDP during operations.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Axiom has used previously compromised administrative accounts to escalate privileges.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Axiom has used watering hole attacks to gain access.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Axiom has been observed using SQL injection to gain access to systems.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: Axiom has used exploits for multiple vulnerabilities including CVE-2014-0322, CVE-2012-4792, CVE-2012-1889, and CVE-2013-3893.
Uses T1546.008 Accessibility Features: Axiom actors have been known to use the Sticky Keys replacement within RDP sessions to obtain persistence.
Uses T1553 Subvert Trust Controls: Axiom has used digital certificates to deliver malware.
Uses T1560 Archive Collected Data: Axiom has compressed and encrypted data prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1563.002 RDP Hijacking: Axiom has targeted victims with remote administration tools including RDP.
Uses T1566 Phishing: Axiom has used spear phishing to initially compromise victims.
Uses T1583.002 DNS Server: Axiom has acquired dynamic DNS services for use in the targeting of intended victims.
Uses T1583.003 Virtual Private Server: Axiom has used VPS hosting providers in targeting of intended victims.
Uses T1584.005 Botnet: Axiom has used large groups of compromised machines for use as proxy nodes.

title: ATT&CK Group G0070: Dark Caracal
text:
ATT&CK Group G0070: Dark Caracal
Dark Caracal is threat group that has been attributed to the Lebanese General Directorate of General Security (GDGS) and has operated since at least 2012.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: Dark Caracal collected complete contents of the 'Pictures' folder from compromised Windows systems.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: Dark Caracal has used UPX to pack Bandook.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Dark Caracal has obfuscated strings in Bandook by base64 encoding, and then encrypting them.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Dark Caracal has used macros in Word documents that would download a second stage if executed.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Dark Caracal's version of Bandook communicates with their server over a TCP port using HTTP payloads Base64 encoded and suffixed with the string “&&&”.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Dark Caracal collected file listings of all default Windows directories.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: Dark Caracal took screenshots using their Windows malware.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Dark Caracal leveraged a watering hole to serve up malicious code.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Dark Caracal makes their malware look like Flash Player, Office, or PDF documents in order to entice a user to click on it.
Uses T1218.001 Compiled HTML File: Dark Caracal leveraged a compiled HTML file that contained a command to download and run an executable.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Dark Caracal's version of Bandook adds a registry key to HKEY_USERS\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run for persistence.
Uses T1566.003 Spearphishing via Service: Dark Caracal spearphished victims via Facebook and Whatsapp.

title: ATT&CK Group G0133: Nomadic Octopus
text:
ATT&CK Group G0133: Nomadic Octopus
Associated names: DustSquad.
Nomadic Octopus is a Russian-speaking cyber espionage threat group that has primarily targeted Central Asia, including local governments, diplomatic missions, and individuals, since at least 2014. Nomadic Octopus has been observed conducting campaigns involving Android and Windows malware, mainly using the Delphi programming language, and building custom variants.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: Nomadic Octopus attempted to make Octopus appear as a Telegram Messenger with a Russian interface.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Nomadic Octopus has used PowerShell for execution.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Nomadic Octopus used cmd.exe /c within a malicious macro.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Nomadic Octopus has used malicious macros to download additional files to the victim's machine.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Nomadic Octopus as attempted to lure victims into clicking on malicious attachments within spearphishing emails.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: Nomadic Octopus executed PowerShell in a hidden window.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Nomadic Octopus has targeted victims with spearphishing emails containing malicious attachments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0005: APT12
text:
ATT&CK Group G0005: APT12
Associated names: IXESHE, DynCalc, Numbered Panda, DNSCALC.
APT12 is a threat group that has been attributed to China. The group has targeted a variety of victims including but not limited to media outlets, high-tech companies, and multiple governments.
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: APT12 has used blogs and WordPress for C2 infrastructure.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT12 has exploited multiple vulnerabilities for execution, including Microsoft Office vulnerabilities (CVE-2009-3129, CVE-2012-0158) and vulnerabilities in Adobe Reader and Flash (CVE-2009-4324, CVE-2009-0927, CVE-2011-0609, CVE-2011-0611).
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT12 has attempted to get victims to open malicious Microsoft Word and PDF attachment sent via spearphishing.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT12 has sent emails with malicious Microsoft Office documents and PDFs attached.
Uses T1568.003 DNS Calculation: APT12 has used multiple variants of DNS Calculation including multiplying the first two octets of an IP address and adding the third octet to that value in order to get a resulting command and control port.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Associated names: Gothic Panda, Pirpi, UPS Team, Buckeye, Threat Group-0110, TG-0110.
APT3 is a China-based threat group that researchers have attributed to China's Ministry of State Security. This group is responsible for the campaigns known as Operation Clandestine Fox, Operation Clandestine Wolf, and Operation Double Tap. As of June 2015, the group appears to have shifted from targeting primarily US victims to primarily political organizations in Hong Kong.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT3 has used a tool to dump credentials by injecting itself into lsass.exe and triggering with the argument "dig."
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT3 will identify Microsoft Office documents on the victim's computer.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: A keylogging tool used by APT3 gathers network information from the victim, including the MAC address, IP address, WINS, DHCP server, and gateway.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can detect the existence of remote systems.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: APT3 enables the Remote Desktop Protocol for persistence. APT3 has also interacted with compromised systems to browse and copy files through RDP sessions.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: APT3 will copy files over to Windows Admin Shares (like ADMIN$) as part of lateral movement.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT3 obfuscates files or information to help evade defensive measures.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: APT3 has been known to pack their tools.
Uses T1027.005 Indicator Removal from Tools: APT3 has been known to remove indicators of compromise from tools.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: An APT3 downloader uses the Windows command "cmd.exe" /C whoami to verify that it is running with the elevated privileges of “System.”
Uses T1036.010 Masquerade Account Name: APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, such as support_388945a0.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: APT3 has a tool that exfiltrates data over the C2 channel.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can enumerate current network connections.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: An APT3 downloader creates persistence by creating the following scheduled task: schtasks /create /tn "mysc" /tr C:\Users\Public\test.exe /sc ONLOGON /ru "System".
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: APT3 has used a keylogging tool that records keystrokes in encrypted files.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can list out currently running processes.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT3 has used PowerShell on victim systems to download and run payloads after exploitation.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: An APT3 downloader uses the Windows command "cmd.exe" /C whoami. The group also uses a tool to execute commands on remote computers.
Uses T1069 Permission Groups Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can enumerate the permissions associated with Windows groups.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT3 has a tool that can delete files.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: APT3 has been known to stage files for exfiltration in a single location.
Uses T1078.002 Domain Accounts: APT3 leverages valid accounts after gaining credentials for use within the victim domain.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT3 has a tool that can obtain information about the local system.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT3 has a tool that looks for files and directories on the local file system.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: APT3 has used a tool that can obtain info about local and global group users, power users, and administrators.
Uses T1090.002 External Proxy: An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections for its initial C2.
Uses T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol: An APT3 downloader establishes SOCKS5 connections for its initial C2.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Uses T1098.007 Additional Local or Domain Groups: APT3 has been known to add created accounts to local admin groups to maintain elevated access.
Uses T1104 Multi-Stage Channels: An APT3 downloader first establishes a SOCKS5 connection to 192.157.198[.]103 using TCP port 1913; once the server response is verified, it then requests a connection to 192.184.60[.]229 on TCP port 81.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT3 has a tool that can copy files to remote machines.
Uses T1110.002 Password Cracking: APT3 has been known to brute force password hashes to be able to leverage plain text credentials.
Uses T1136.001 Local Account: APT3 has been known to create or enable accounts, such as support_388945a0.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT3 has exploited the Adobe Flash Player vulnerability CVE-2015-3113 and Internet Explorer vulnerability CVE-2014-1776.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: APT3 has lured victims into clicking malicious links delivered through spearphishing.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: APT3 has a tool that can run DLLs.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: APT3 has a tool that creates a new service for persistence.
Uses T1546.008 Accessibility Features: APT3 replaces the Sticky Keys binary C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe for persistence.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT3 places scripts in the startup folder for persistence.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: APT3 has a tool that can locate credentials in files on the file system such as those from Firefox or Chrome.
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: APT3 has used tools to dump passwords from browsers.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: APT3 has used tools to compress data before exfilling it.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: APT3 has been known to use -WindowStyle Hidden to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: APT3 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious links.

title: ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
text:
ATT&CK Group G0022: APT3
Uses T1574.001 DLL: APT3 has been known to side load DLLs with a valid version of Chrome with one of their tools.

title: ATT&CK Group G0024: Putter Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0024: Putter Panda
Associated names: APT2, MSUpdater.
Putter Panda is a Chinese threat group that has been attributed to Unit 61486 of the 12th Bureau of the PLA’s 3rd General Staff Department (GSD).
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Droppers used by Putter Panda use RC4 or a 16-byte XOR key consisting of the bytes 0xA0 – 0xAF to obfuscate payloads.
Uses T1055.001 Dynamic-link Library Injection: An executable dropped onto victims by Putter Panda aims to inject the specified DLL into a process that would normally be accessing the network, including Outlook Express (msinm.exe), Outlook (outlook.exe), Internet Explorer (iexplore.exe), and Firefox (firefox.exe).
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: A dropper used by Putter Panda installs itself into the ASEP Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with a value named McUpdate.
Uses T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: Malware used by Putter Panda attempts to terminate processes corresponding to two components of Sophos Anti-Virus (SAVAdminService.exe and SavService.exe).

title: ATT&CK Group G1013: Metador
text:
ATT&CK Group G1013: Metador
Metador is a suspected cyber espionage group that was first reported in September 2022. Metador has targeted a limited number of telecommunication companies, internet service providers, and universities in the Middle East and Africa. Security researchers named the group Metador based on the "I am meta" string in one of the group's malware samples and the expectation of Spanish-language responses from C2 servers.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Metador has encrypted their payloads.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Metador has used the Windows command line to execute commands.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Metador has quickly deleted `cbd.exe` from a compromised host following the successful deployment of their malware.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Metador has used HTTP for C2.
Uses T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol: Metador has used TCP for C2.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Metador has downloaded tools and malware onto a compromised system.
Uses T1546.003 Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription: Metador has established persistence through the use of a WMI event subscription combined with unusual living-off-the-land binaries such as `cdb.exe`.
Uses T1588.001 Malware: Metador has used unique malware in their operations, including metaMain and Mafalda.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Metador has used Microsoft's Console Debugger in some of their operations.

title: ATT&CK Group G0062: TA459
text:
ATT&CK Group G0062: TA459
TA459 is a threat group believed to operate out of China that has targeted countries including Russia, Belarus, Mongolia, and others.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: TA459 has used PowerShell for execution of a payload.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: TA459 has a VBScript for execution.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: TA459 has exploited Microsoft Word vulnerability CVE-2017-0199 for execution.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: TA459 has attempted to get victims to open malicious Microsoft Word attachment sent via spearphishing.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: TA459 has targeted victims using spearphishing emails with malicious Microsoft Word attachments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0128: ZIRCONIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0128: ZIRCONIUM
Associated names: APT31, Violet Typhoon.
ZIRCONIUM is a threat group operating out of China, active since at least 2017, that has targeted individuals associated with the 2020 US presidential election and prominent leaders in the international affairs community.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to query the Registry for proxy settings.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to enumerate proxy settings in the target environment.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: ZIRCONIUM has used multi-stage packers for exploit code.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the username on a compromised host in order to register it with C2.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: ZIRCONIUM has spoofed legitimate applications in phishing lures and changed file extensions to conceal installation of malware.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: ZIRCONIUM has created a run key named Dropbox Update Setup to mask a persistence mechanism for a malicious binary.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: ZIRCONIUM has exfiltrated files via the Dropbox API C2.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to open a Windows Command Shell on a remote host.
Uses T1059.006 Python: ZIRCONIUM has used Python-based implants to interact with compromised hosts.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: ZIRCONIUM has exploited CVE-2017-0005 for local privilege escalation.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the processor architecture of a compromised host in order to register it with C2.
Uses T1090.003 Multi-hop Proxy: ZIRCONIUM has utilized an ORB (operational relay box) network – consisting compromised devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers, IoT devices, and leased virtual private servers (VPS) – to proxy traffic.

title: ATT&CK Group G0128: ZIRCONIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0128: ZIRCONIUM
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: ZIRCONIUM has used Dropbox for C2 allowing upload and download of files as well as execution of arbitrary commands.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: ZIRCONIUM has used tools to download malicious files to compromised hosts.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to capture the time on a compromised host in order to register it with C2.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: ZIRCONIUM has used the AES256 algorithm with a SHA1 derived key to decrypt exploit code.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: ZIRCONIUM has used malicious links in e-mails to lure victims into downloading malware.
Uses T1218.007 Msiexec: ZIRCONIUM has used the msiexec.exe command-line utility to download and execute malicious MSI files.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: ZIRCONIUM has created a Registry Run key named Dropbox Update Setup to establish persistence for a malicious Python binary.
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: ZIRCONIUM has used a tool to steal credentials from installed web browsers including Microsoft Internet Explorer and Google Chrome.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: ZIRCONIUM has used malicious links in e-mails to deliver malware.
Uses T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage: ZIRCONIUM has exfiltrated stolen data to Dropbox.
Uses T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography: ZIRCONIUM has used AES encrypted communications in C2.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: ZIRCONIUM has purchased domains for use in targeted campaigns.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: ZIRCONIUM has used GitHub to host malware linked in spearphishing e-mails.
Uses T1584.008 Network Devices: ZIRCONIUM has compromised network devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers and IoT devices for ORB (operational relay box) Proxy networks.
Uses T1598 Phishing for Information: ZIRCONIUM targeted presidential campaign staffers with credential phishing e-mails.
Uses T1598.003 Spearphishing Link: ZIRCONIUM has used web beacons in e-mails to track hits to attacker-controlled URL's.

title: ATT&CK Group G0128: ZIRCONIUM
text:
ATT&CK Group G0128: ZIRCONIUM
Uses T1665 Hide Infrastructure: ZIRCONIUM has utilized an ORB (operational relay box) network – consisting compromised devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers, IoT devices, and leased virtual private servers (VPS) – to obfuscate the origin of C2 traffic.

title: ATT&CK Group G0006: APT1
text:
ATT&CK Group G0006: APT1
Associated names: Comment Crew, Comment Group, Comment Panda.
APT1 is a Chinese threat group that has been attributed to the 2nd Bureau of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) General Staff Department’s (GSD) 3rd Department, commonly known by its Military Unit Cover Designator (MUCD) as Unit 61398.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT1 has been known to use credential dumping using Mimikatz.
Uses T1005 Data from Local System: APT1 has collected files from a local victim.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: APT1 used the commands net start and tasklist to get a listing of the services on the system.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: APT1 used the ipconfig /all command to gather network configuration information.
Uses T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol: The APT1 group is known to have used RDP during operations.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: The file name AcroRD32.exe, a legitimate process name for Adobe's Acrobat Reader, was used by APT1 as a name for malware.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: APT1 used the net use command to get a listing on network connections.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: APT1 gathered a list of running processes on the system using tasklist /v.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: APT1 has used the Windows command shell to execute commands, and batch scripting to automate execution.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: APT1 used the commands net localgroup,net user, and net group to find accounts on the system.
Uses T1114.001 Local Email Collection: APT1 uses two utilities, GETMAIL and MAPIGET, to steal email. GETMAIL extracts emails from archived Outlook.pst files.
Uses T1114.002 Remote Email Collection: APT1 uses two utilities, GETMAIL and MAPIGET, to steal email. MAPIGET steals email still on Exchange servers that has not yet been archived.

title: ATT&CK Group G0006: APT1
text:
ATT&CK Group G0006: APT1
Uses T1119 Automated Collection: APT1 used a batch script to perform a series of discovery techniques and saves it to a text file.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: APT1 listed connected network shares.
Uses T1550.002 Pass the Hash: The APT1 group is known to have used pass the hash.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: APT1 has used RAR to compress files before moving them outside of the victim network.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT1 has sent spearphishing emails containing malicious attachments.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: APT1 has sent spearphishing emails containing hyperlinks to malicious files.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: APT1 has registered hundreds of domains for use in operations.
Uses T1584.001 Domains: APT1 hijacked FQDNs associated with legitimate websites hosted by hop points.
Uses T1585.002 Email Accounts: APT1 has created email accounts for later use in social engineering, phishing, and when registering domains.
Uses T1588.001 Malware: APT1 used publicly available malware for privilege escalation.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT1 has used various open-source tools for privilege escalation purposes.

title: ATT&CK Group G0019: Naikon
text:
ATT&CK Group G0019: Naikon
Naikon is assessed to be a state-sponsored cyber espionage group attributed to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) Chengdu Military Region Second Technical Reconnaissance Bureau (Military Unit Cover Designator 78020). Active since at least 2010, Naikon has primarily conducted operations against government, military, and civil organizations in Southeast Asia, as well as against international bodies such as the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). 

While Naikon shares some characteristics with APT30, the two groups do not appear to be exact matches.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Naikon uses commands such as netsh interface show to discover network interface settings.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Naikon has used a netbios scanner for remote machine identification.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Naikon renamed a malicious service taskmgr to appear to be a legitimate version of Task Manager.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Naikon has disguised malicious programs as Google Chrome, Adobe, and VMware executables.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: Naikon has used the LadonGo scanner to scan target networks.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Naikon has used WMIC.exe for lateral movement.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Naikon has used schtasks.exe for lateral movement in compromised networks.
Uses T1078.002 Domain Accounts: Naikon has used administrator credentials for lateral movement in compromised networks.
Uses T1137.006 Add-ins: Naikon has used the RoyalRoad exploit builder to drop a second stage loader, intel.wll, into the Word Startup folder on the compromised host.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Naikon has convinced victims to open malicious attachments to execute malware.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: Naikon uses commands such as netsh advfirewall firewall to discover local firewall settings.

title: ATT&CK Group G0019: Naikon
text:
ATT&CK Group G0019: Naikon
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: Naikon has modified a victim's Windows Run registry to establish persistence.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Naikon has used malicious e-mail attachments to deliver malware.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Naikon has used DLL side-loading to load malicious DLL's into legitimate executables.

title: ATT&CK Group G0054: Sowbug
text:
ATT&CK Group G0054: Sowbug
Sowbug is a threat group that has conducted targeted attacks against organizations in South America and Southeast Asia, particularly government entities, since at least 2015.
Uses T1003 OS Credential Dumping: Sowbug has used credential dumping tools.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Sowbug named its tools to masquerade as Windows or Adobe Reader software, such as by using the file name adobecms.exe and the directory CSIDL_APPDATA\microsoft\security.
Uses T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive: Sowbug extracted Word documents from a file server on a victim network.
Uses T1056.001 Keylogging: Sowbug has used keylogging tools.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Sowbug has used command line during its intrusions.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Sowbug obtained OS version and hardware configuration from a victim.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Sowbug identified and extracted all Word documents on a server by using a command containing *.doc and *.docx. The actors also searched for documents based on a specific date range and attempted to identify all installed software on a victim.
Uses T1135 Network Share Discovery: Sowbug listed remote shared drives that were accessible from a victim.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: Sowbug extracted documents and bundled them into a RAR archive.

title: ATT&CK Group G0103: Mofang
text:
ATT&CK Group G0103: Mofang
Mofang is a likely China-based cyber espionage group, named for its frequent practice of imitating a victim's infrastructure. This adversary has been observed since at least May 2012 conducting focused attacks against government and critical infrastructure in Myanmar, as well as several other countries and sectors including military, automobile, and weapons industries.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Mofang has encrypted payloads before they are downloaded to victims.
Uses T1027.015 Compression: Mofang has compressed the ShimRat executable within malicious email attachments.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Mofang's spearphishing emails required a user to click the link to connect to a compromised website.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Mofang's malicious spearphishing attachments required a user to open the file after receiving.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Mofang delivered spearphishing emails with malicious documents, PDFs, or Excel files attached.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Mofang delivered spearphishing emails with malicious links included.

title: ATT&CK Group G0095: Machete
text:
ATT&CK Group G0095: Machete
Associated names: APT-C-43, El Machete.
Machete is a suspected Spanish-speaking cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2010. It has primarily focused its operations within Latin America, with a particular emphasis on Venezuela, but also in the US, Europe, Russia, and parts of Asia. Machete generally targets high-profile organizations such as government institutions, intelligence services, and military units, as well as telecommunications and power companies.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Machete's Machete MSI installer has masqueraded as a legitimate Adobe Acrobat Reader installer.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Machete has created scheduled tasks to maintain Machete's persistence.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Machete has used batch files to initiate additional downloads of malicious files.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: Machete has embedded malicious macros within spearphishing attachments to download additional files.
Uses T1059.006 Python: Machete used multiple compiled Python scripts on the victim’s system. Machete's main backdoor Machete is also written in Python.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Machete has distributed Machete through a fake blog website.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Machete has has relied on users opening malicious links delivered through spearphishing to execute malware.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Machete has relied on users opening malicious attachments delivered through spearphishing to execute malware.
Uses T1218.007 Msiexec: Machete has used msiexec to install the Machete malware.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Machete has delivered spearphishing emails that contain a zipped file with malicious contents.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Machete has sent phishing emails that contain a link to an external server with ZIP and RAR archives.

title: ATT&CK Group G0053: FIN5
text:
ATT&CK Group G0053: FIN5
FIN5 is a financially motivated threat group that has targeted personally identifiable information and payment card information. The group has been active since at least 2008 and has targeted the restaurant, gaming, and hotel industries. The group is made up of actors who likely speak Russian.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: FIN5 has used the open source tool Essential NetTools to map the network and build a list of targets.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: FIN5 scans processes on all victim systems in the environment and uses automated scripts to pull back the results.
Uses T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs: FIN5 has cleared event logs from victims.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: FIN5 uses SDelete to clean up the environment and attempt to prevent detection.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: FIN5 scripts save memory dump data into a specific directory on hosts in the victim environment.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: FIN5 has used legitimate VPN, RDP, Citrix, or VNC credentials to maintain access to a victim environment.
Uses T1090.002 External Proxy: FIN5 maintains access to victim environments by using FLIPSIDE to create a proxy for a backup RDP tunnel.
Uses T1110 Brute Force: FIN5 has has used the tool GET2 Penetrator to look for remote login and hard-coded credentials.
Uses T1119 Automated Collection: FIN5 scans processes on all victim systems in the environment and uses automated scripts to pull back the results.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: FIN5 has used legitimate VPN, Citrix, or VNC credentials to maintain access to a victim environment.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: FIN5 has obtained and used a customized version of PsExec, as well as use other tools such as pwdump, SDelete, and Windows Credential Editor.

title: ATT&CK Group G1035: Winter Vivern
text:
ATT&CK Group G1035: Winter Vivern
Associated names: TA473, UAC-0114.
Winter Vivern is a group linked to Russian and Belorussian interests active since at least 2020 targeting various European government and NGO entities, along with sporadic targeting of Indian and US victims. The group leverages a combination of document-based phishing activity and server-side exploitation for initial access, leveraging adversary-controlled and -created infrastructure for follow-on command and control.
Uses T1020 Automated Exfiltration: Winter Vivern delivered a PowerShell script capable of recursively scanning victim machines looking for various file types before exfiltrating identified files via HTTP.
Uses T1033 System Owner/User Discovery: Winter Vivern PowerShell scripts execute `whoami` to identify the executing user.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: Winter Vivern created specially-crafted documents mimicking legitimate government or similar documents during phishing campaigns.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Winter Vivern has distributed malicious scripts and executables mimicking virus scanners.
Uses T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel: Winter Vivern delivered a PowerShell script capable of recursively scanning victim machines looking for various file types before exfiltrating identified files via HTTP.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: Winter Vivern executed PowerShell scripts that would subsequently attempt to establish persistence by creating scheduled tasks objects to periodically retrieve and execute remotely-hosted payloads.
Uses T1056.003 Web Portal Capture: Winter Vivern registered and hosted domains to allow for creation of web pages mimicking legitimate government email logon sites to collect logon information.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Winter Vivern used XLM 4.0 macros for initial code execution for malicious document files.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Winter Vivern passed execution from document macros to PowerShell scripts during initial access operations. Winter Vivern used batch scripts that called PowerShell commands as part of initial access and installation operations.

title: ATT&CK Group G1035: Winter Vivern
text:
ATT&CK Group G1035: Winter Vivern
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: Winter Vivern distributed Windows batch scripts disguised as virus scanners to prompt download of malicious payloads using built-in system tools.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: Winter Vivern delivered malicious JavaScript to exploit targets when exploiting Roundcube Webmail servers.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Winter Vivern uses HTTP and HTTPS protocols for exfiltration and command and control activity.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: Winter Vivern script execution includes basic victim information gathering steps which are then transmitted to command and control servers.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Winter Vivern delivered malicious JavaScript payloads capable of listing folders and emails in exploited email servers.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Winter Vivern executed PowerShell scripts to create scheduled tasks to retrieve remotely-hosted payloads.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: Winter Vivern delivered PowerShell scripts capable of taking screenshots of victim machines.
Uses T1114.001 Local Email Collection: Winter Vivern delivered malicious JavaScript payloads capable of exfiltrating email messages from exploited email servers.
Uses T1119 Automated Collection: Winter Vivern delivered a PowerShell script capable of recursively scanning victim machines looking for various file types before exfiltrating identified files via HTTP.
Uses T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information: Winter Vivern delivered exploit payloads via base64-encoded payloads in malicious email messages.
Uses T1189 Drive-by Compromise: Winter Vivern created dedicated web pages mimicking legitimate government websites to deliver malicious fake anti-virus software.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Winter Vivern has exploited known and zero-day vulnerabilities in software usch as Roundcube Webmail servers and the "Follina" vulnerability.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Winter Vivern has mimicked legitimate government-related domains to deliver malicious webpages containing links to documents or other content for user execution.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Winter Vivern leverages malicious attachments delivered via email for initial access activity.

title: ATT&CK Group G1035: Winter Vivern
text:
ATT&CK Group G1035: Winter Vivern
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Winter Vivern registered domains mimicking other entities throughout various campaigns.
Uses T1583.003 Virtual Private Server: Winter Vivern used adversary-owned and -controlled servers to host web vulnerability scanning applications.
Uses T1584.006 Web Services: Winter Vivern has used compromised WordPress sites to host malicious payloads for download.
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: Winter Vivern has used remotely-hosted instances of the Acunetix vulnerability scanner.

title: ATT&CK Group G1008: SideCopy
text:
ATT&CK Group G1008: SideCopy
SideCopy is a Pakistani threat group that has primarily targeted South Asian countries, including Indian and Afghani government personnel, since at least 2019. SideCopy's name comes from its infection chain that tries to mimic that of Sidewinder, a suspected Indian threat group.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: SideCopy has identified the IP address of a compromised host.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: SideCopy has used a legitimate DLL file name, `Duser.dll` to disguise a malicious remote access tool.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: SideCopy has sent Microsoft Office Publisher documents to victims that have embedded malicious macros that execute an hta file via calling `mshta.exe`.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: SideCopy has identified the OS version of a compromised host.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: SideCopy has delivered trojanized executables via spearphishing emails that contacts actor-controlled servers to download malicious payloads.
Uses T1106 Native API: SideCopy has executed malware by calling the API function `CreateProcessW`.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: SideCopy has attempted to lure victims into clicking on malicious embedded archive files sent via spearphishing campaigns.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: SideCopy has utilized `mshta.exe` to execute a malicious hta file.
Uses T1518 Software Discovery: SideCopy has collected browser information from a compromised host.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: SideCopy uses a loader DLL file to collect AV product names from an infected host.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: SideCopy has sent spearphishing emails with malicious hta file attachments.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: SideCopy has used a malicious loader DLL file to execute the `credwiz.exe` process and side-load the malicious payload `Duser.dll`.
Uses T1584.001 Domains: SideCopy has compromised domains for some of their infrastructure, including for C2 and staging malware.

title: ATT&CK Group G1008: SideCopy
text:
ATT&CK Group G1008: SideCopy
Uses T1598.002 Spearphishing Attachment: SideCopy has crafted generic lures for spam campaigns to collect emails and credentials for targeting efforts.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: SideCopy has used compromised domains to host its malicious payloads.
Uses T1614 System Location Discovery: SideCopy has identified the country location of a compromised host.

title: ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
text:
ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
Associated names: HOLMIUM, Elfin, Peach Sandstorm.
APT33 is a suspected Iranian threat group that has carried out operations since at least 2013. The group has targeted organizations across multiple industries in the United States, Saudi Arabia, and South Korea, with a particular interest in the aviation and energy sectors.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne, Mimikatz, and ProcDump to dump credentials.
Uses T1003.004 LSA Secrets: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.
Uses T1003.005 Cached Domain Credentials: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: APT33 has used base64 to encode payloads.
Uses T1040 Network Sniffing: APT33 has used SniffPass to collect credentials by sniffing network traffic.
Uses T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol: APT33 has used FTP to exfiltrate files (separately from the C2 channel).
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT33 has created a scheduled task to execute a.vbe file multiple times a day.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: APT33 has utilized PowerShell to download files from the C2 server and run various scripts.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: APT33 has used VBScript to initiate the delivery of payloads.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: APT33 has used a publicly available exploit for CVE-2017-0213 to escalate privileges on a local system.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT33 has used HTTP for command and control.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT33 has used valid accounts for initial access and privilege escalation.
Uses T1078.004 Cloud Accounts: APT33 has used compromised Office 365 accounts in tandem with Ruler in an attempt to gain control of endpoints.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT33 has downloaded additional files and programs from its C2 server.

title: ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
text:
ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
Uses T1110.003 Password Spraying: APT33 has used password spraying to gain access to target systems.
Uses T1132.001 Standard Encoding: APT33 has used base64 to encode command and control traffic.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: APT33 has attempted to exploit a known vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2018-20250), and attempted to gain remote code execution via a security bypass vulnerability (CVE-2017-11774).
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: APT33 has lured users to click links to malicious HTML applications delivered via spearphishing emails.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT33 has used malicious e-mail attachments to lure victims into executing malware.
Uses T1546.003 Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription: APT33 has attempted to use WMI event subscriptions to establish persistence on compromised hosts.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT33 has deployed a tool known as DarkComet to the Startup folder of a victim, and used Registry run keys to gain persistence.
Uses T1552.001 Credentials In Files: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.
Uses T1552.006 Group Policy Preferences: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like Gpppassword to gather credentials.
Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.
Uses T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers: APT33 has used a variety of publicly available tools like LaZagne to gather credentials.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: APT33 has used WinRAR to compress data prior to exfil.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT33 has sent spearphishing e-mails with archive attachments.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: APT33 has sent spearphishing emails containing links to.hta files.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: APT33 has used HTTP over TCP ports 808 and 880 for command and control.

title: ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
text:
ATT&CK Group G0064: APT33
Uses T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography: APT33 has used AES for encryption of command and control traffic.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT33 has obtained and leveraged publicly-available tools for early intrusion activities.

title: ATT&CK Group G0030: Lotus Blossom
text:
ATT&CK Group G0030: Lotus Blossom
Associated names: DRAGONFISH, Spring Dragon, RADIUM, Raspberry Typhoon, Bilbug, Thrip.
Lotus Blossom is a long-standing threat group largely targeting various entities in Asia since at least 2009. In addition to government and related targets, Lotus Blossom has also targeted entities such as digital certificate issuers.
Uses T1012 Query Registry: Lotus Blossom has run commands such as `reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\[service name]\Parameters` to verify if installed implants are running as a service.
Uses T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery: Lotus Blossom has used commands such as `ipconfig` and `netstat` to gather network information on compromised hosts.
Uses T1016.001 Internet Connection Discovery: Lotus Blossom has performed checks to determine if a victim machine is able to access the Internet.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Lotus Blossom has used Ping to identify remote systems.
Uses T1046 Network Service Discovery: Lotus Blossom has used port scanners to enumerate services on remote hosts.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: Lotus Blossom has used WMI to enable lateral movement.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: Lotus Blossom has used commands such as `netstat` to identify system network connections.
Uses T1074.001 Local Data Staging: Lotus Blossom has locally staged compressed and archived data for follow-on exfiltration.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: Lotus Blossom has used commands such as `dir` to examine the local filesystem of victim machines.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: Lotus Blossom has used commands such as `net` to profile local system users.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: Lotus Blossom has used `net` commands and tools such as AdFind to profile domain accounts associated with victim machines and make Active Directory queries.
Uses T1090.001 Internal Proxy: Lotus Blossom has used publicly available tools such as the Venom proxy tool to proxy traffic out of victim environments.

title: ATT&CK Group G0030: Lotus Blossom
text:
ATT&CK Group G0030: Lotus Blossom
Uses T1090.003 Multi-hop Proxy: Lotus Blossom has used tools such as the publicly available HTran tool for proxying traffic in victim environments.
Uses T1112 Modify Registry: Lotus Blossom has installed tools such as Sagerunex by writing them to the Windows registry.
Uses T1134 Access Token Manipulation: Lotus Blossom has retrieved process tokens for processes to adjust the privileges of the launch process or other items.
Uses T1482 Domain Trust Discovery: Lotus Blossom has used tools such as AdFind to make Active Directory queries.
Uses T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie: Lotus Blossom has used publicly-available tools to steal cookies from browsers such as Chrome.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: Lotus Blossom has configured tools such as Sagerunex to run as Windows services.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: Lotus Blossom has used WinRAR for compressing data in RAR format.
Uses T1560.003 Archive via Custom Method: Lotus Blossom has used custom tools to compress and archive data on victim systems.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Lotus Blossom has used publicly-available tools such as a Python-based cookie stealer for Chrome browsers, Impacket, and the Venom proxy tool.

title: ATT&CK Group G0115: GOLD SOUTHFIELD
text:
ATT&CK Group G0115: GOLD SOUTHFIELD
Associated names: Pinchy Spider.
GOLD SOUTHFIELD is a financially motivated threat group active since at least 2018 that operates the REvil Ransomware-as-a Service (RaaS). GOLD SOUTHFIELD provides backend infrastructure for affiliates recruited on underground forums to perpetrate high value deployments. By early 2020, GOLD SOUTHFIELD started capitalizing on the new trend of stealing data and further extorting the victim to pay for their data to not get publicly leaked.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has executed base64 encoded PowerShell scripts on compromised hosts.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has staged and executed PowerShell scripts on compromised hosts.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has used the remote monitoring and management tool ConnectWise to obtain screen captures from victim's machines.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has used publicly-accessible RDP and remote management and monitoring (RMM) servers to gain access to victim machines.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has exploited Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities for initial compromise.
Uses T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has distributed ransomware by backdooring software installers via a strategic web compromise of the site hosting Italian WinRAR.
Uses T1199 Trusted Relationship: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has breached Managed Service Providers (MSP's) to deliver malware to MSP customers.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has used the cloud-based remote management and monitoring tool "ConnectWise Control" to deploy REvil.
Uses T1566 Phishing: GOLD SOUTHFIELD has conducted malicious spam (malspam) campaigns to gain access to victim's machines.

title: ATT&CK Group G0123: Volatile Cedar
text:
ATT&CK Group G0123: Volatile Cedar
Associated names: Lebanese Cedar.
Volatile Cedar is a Lebanese threat group that has targeted individuals, companies, and institutions worldwide. Volatile Cedar has been operating since 2012 and is motivated by political and ideological interests.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Volatile Cedar can deploy additional tools.
Uses T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application: Volatile Cedar has targeted publicly facing web servers, with both automatic and manual vulnerability discovery.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: Volatile Cedar can inject web shell code into a server.
Uses T1595.002 Vulnerability Scanning: Volatile Cedar has performed vulnerability scans of the target server.
Uses T1595.003 Wordlist Scanning: Volatile Cedar has used DirBuster and GoBuster to brute force web directories and DNS subdomains.

title: ATT&CK Group G0120: Evilnum
text:
ATT&CK Group G0120: Evilnum
Evilnum is a financially motivated threat group that has been active since at least 2018.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: Evilnum has used malicious JavaScript files on the victim's machine.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: Evilnum has deleted files used during infection.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Evilnum can deploy additional components or tools as needed.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: Evilnum has sent spearphishing emails designed to trick the recipient into opening malicious shortcut links which downloads a.LNK file.
Uses T1219.002 Remote Desktop Software: EVILNUM has used the malware variant, TerraTV, to run a legitimate TeamViewer application to connect to compromised machines.
Uses T1497.001 System Checks: Evilnum has used a component called TerraLoader to check certain hardware and file information to detect sandboxed environments.
Uses T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie: Evilnum can steal cookies and session information from browsers.
Uses T1548.002 Bypass User Account Control: Evilnum has used PowerShell to bypass UAC.
Uses T1555 Credentials from Password Stores: Evilnum can collect email credentials from victims.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Evilnum has sent spearphishing emails containing a link to a zip file hosted on Google Drive.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Evilnum has used the malware variant, TerraTV, to load a malicious DLL placed in the TeamViewer directory, instead of the original Windows DLL located in a system folder.

title: ATT&CK Group G0003: Cleaver
text:
ATT&CK Group G0003: Cleaver
Associated names: Threat Group 2889, TG-2889.
Cleaver is a threat group that has been attributed to Iranian actors and is responsible for activity tracked as Operation Cleaver. Strong circumstantial evidence suggests Cleaver is linked to Threat Group 2889 (TG-2889).
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: Cleaver has been known to dump credentials using Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor.
Uses T1557.002 ARP Cache Poisoning: Cleaver has used custom tools to facilitate ARP cache poisoning.
Uses T1585.001 Social Media Accounts: Cleaver has created fake LinkedIn profiles that included profile photos, details, and connections.
Uses T1587.001 Malware: Cleaver has created customized tools and payloads for functions including ARP poisoning, encryption, credential dumping, ASP.NET shells, web backdoors, process enumeration, WMI querying, HTTP and SMB communications, network interface sniffing, and keystroke logging.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Cleaver has obtained and used open-source tools such as PsExec, Windows Credential Editor, and Mimikatz.

title: ATT&CK Group G0088: TEMP.Veles
text:
ATT&CK Group G0088: TEMP.Veles
Associated names: XENOTIME.
TEMP.Veles is a Russia-based threat group that has targeted critical infrastructure. The group has been observed utilizing TRITON, a malware framework designed to manipulate industrial safety systems.

title: ATT&CK Group G0079: DarkHydrus
text:
ATT&CK Group G0079: DarkHydrus
DarkHydrus is a threat group that has targeted government agencies and educational institutions in the Middle East since at least 2016. The group heavily leverages open-source tools and custom payloads for carrying out attacks.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: DarkHydrus leveraged PowerShell to download and execute additional scripts for execution.
Uses T1187 Forced Authentication: DarkHydrus used Template Injection to launch an authentication window for users to enter their credentials.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: DarkHydrus has sent malware that required users to hit the enable button in Microsoft Excel to allow an.iqy file to be downloaded.
Uses T1221 Template Injection: DarkHydrus used an open-source tool, Phishery, to inject malicious remote template URLs into Microsoft Word documents and then sent them to victims to enable Forced Authentication.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: DarkHydrus has used -WindowStyle Hidden to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: DarkHydrus has sent spearphishing emails with password-protected RAR archives containing malicious Excel Web Query files (.iqy). The group has also sent spearphishing emails that contained malicious Microsoft Office documents that use the “attachedTemplate” technique to load a template from a …
Uses T1588.002 Tool: DarkHydrus has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz, Empire, and Cobalt Strike.

title: ATT&CK Group G0107: Whitefly
text:
ATT&CK Group G0107: Whitefly
Whitefly is a cyber espionage group that has been operating since at least 2017. The group has targeted organizations based mostly in Singapore across a wide variety of sectors, and is primarily interested in stealing large amounts of sensitive information. The group has been linked to an attack against Singapore’s largest public health organization, SingHealth.
Uses T1003.001 LSASS Memory: Whitefly has used Mimikatz to obtain credentials.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: Whitefly has encrypted the payload used for C2.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Whitefly has named the malicious DLL the same name as DLLs belonging to legitimate software from various security vendors.
Uses T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Whitefly has used a simple remote shell tool that will call back to the C2 server and wait for commands.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: Whitefly has used an open-source tool to exploit a known Windows privilege escalation vulnerability (CVE-2016-0051) on unpatched computers.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: Whitefly has the ability to download additional tools from the C2.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Whitefly has used malicious.exe or.dll files disguised as documents or images.
Uses T1574.001 DLL: Whitefly has used search order hijacking to run the loader Vcrodat.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Whitefly has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz.

title: ATT&CK Group G0122: Silent Librarian
text:
ATT&CK Group G0122: Silent Librarian
Associated names: TA407, COBALT DICKENS.
Silent Librarian is a group that has targeted research and proprietary data at universities, government agencies, and private sector companies worldwide since at least 2013. Members of Silent Librarian are known to have been affiliated with the Iran-based Mabna Institute which has conducted cyber intrusions at the behest of the government of Iran, specifically the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Silent Librarian has used compromised credentials to obtain unauthorized access to online accounts.
Uses T1110.003 Password Spraying: Silent Librarian has used collected lists of names and e-mail accounts to use in password spraying attacks against private sector targets.
Uses T1114 Email Collection: Silent Librarian has exfiltrated entire mailboxes from compromised accounts.
Uses T1114.003 Email Forwarding Rule: Silent Librarian has set up auto forwarding rules on compromised e-mail accounts.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: Silent Librarian has acquired domains to establish credential harvesting pages, often spoofing the target organization and using free top level domains.TK,.ML,.GA,.CF, and.GQ.
Uses T1585.002 Email Accounts: Silent Librarian has established e-mail accounts to receive e-mails forwarded from compromised accounts.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Silent Librarian has obtained free and publicly available tools including SingleFile and HTTrack to copy login pages of targeted organizations.
Uses T1588.004 Digital Certificates: Silent Librarian has obtained free Let's Encrypt SSL certificates for use on their phishing pages.
Uses T1589.002 Email Addresses: Silent Librarian has collected e-mail addresses from targeted organizations from open Internet searches.
Uses T1589.003 Employee Names: Silent Librarian has collected lists of names for individuals from targeted organizations.
Uses T1594 Search Victim-Owned Websites: Silent Librarian has searched victim's websites to identify the interests and academic areas of targeted individuals and to scrape source code, branding, and organizational contact information for phishing pages.

title: ATT&CK Group G0122: Silent Librarian
text:
ATT&CK Group G0122: Silent Librarian
Uses T1598.003 Spearphishing Link: Silent Librarian has used links in e-mails to direct victims to credential harvesting websites designed to appear like the targeted organization's login page.
Uses T1608.005 Link Target: Silent Librarian has cloned victim organization login pages and staged them for later use in credential harvesting campaigns. Silent Librarian has also made use of a variety of URL shorteners for these staged websites.

title: ATT&CK Group G0026: APT18
text:
ATT&CK Group G0026: APT18
Associated names: TG-0416, Dynamite Panda, Threat Group-0416.
APT18 is a threat group that has operated since at least 2009 and has targeted a range of industries, including technology, manufacturing, human rights groups, government, and medical.
Uses T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: APT18 obfuscates strings in the payload.
Uses T1053.002 At: APT18 actors used the native at Windows task scheduler tool to use scheduled tasks for execution on a victim network.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: APT18 uses cmd.exe to execute commands on the victim’s machine.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: APT18 actors deleted tools and batch files from victim systems.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: APT18 uses HTTP for C2 communications.
Uses T1071.004 DNS: APT18 uses DNS for C2 communications.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: APT18 actors leverage legitimate credentials to log into external remote services.
Uses T1082 System Information Discovery: APT18 can collect system information from the victim’s machine.
Uses T1083 File and Directory Discovery: APT18 can list files information for specific directories.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT18 can upload a file to the victim’s machine.
Uses T1133 External Remote Services: APT18 actors leverage legitimate credentials to log into external remote services.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: APT18 establishes persistence via the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key.

title: ATT&CK Group G0008: Carbanak
text:
ATT&CK Group G0008: Carbanak
Associated names: Anunak.
Carbanak is a cybercriminal group that has used Carbanak malware to target financial institutions since at least 2013. Carbanak may be linked to groups tracked separately as Cobalt Group and FIN7 that have also used Carbanak malware.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: Carbanak has copied legitimate service names to use for malicious services.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Carbanak has named malware "svchost.exe," which is the name of the Windows shared service host program.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Carbanak actors used legitimate credentials of banking employees to perform operations that sent them millions of dollars.
Uses T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication: Carbanak has used a VBScript named "ggldr" that uses Google Apps Script, Sheets, and Forms services for C2.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: Carbanak installs VNC server software that executes through rundll32.
Uses T1219 Remote Access Tools: Carbanak used legitimate programs such as AmmyyAdmin and Team Viewer for remote interactive C2 to target systems.
Uses T1543.003 Windows Service: Carbanak malware installs itself as a service to provide persistence and SYSTEM privileges.
Uses T1562.004 Disable or Modify System Firewall: Carbanak may use netsh to add local firewall rule exceptions.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: Carbanak has obtained and used open-source tools such as PsExec and Mimikatz.

title: ATT&CK Group G0071: Orangeworm
text:
ATT&CK Group G0071: Orangeworm
Orangeworm is a group that has targeted organizations in the healthcare sector in the United States, Europe, and Asia since at least 2015, likely for the purpose of corporate espionage. Reverse engineering of Kwampirs, directly associated with Orangeworm activity, indicates significant functional and development overlaps with Shamoon.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Orangeworm has copied its backdoor across open network shares, including ADMIN$, C$WINDOWS, D$WINDOWS, and E$WINDOWS.
Uses T1071.001 Web Protocols: Orangeworm has used HTTP for C2.

title: ATT&CK Group G0009: Deep Panda
text:
ATT&CK Group G0009: Deep Panda
Associated names: Shell Crew, WebMasters, KungFu Kittens, PinkPanther, Black Vine.
Deep Panda is a suspected Chinese threat group known to target many industries, including government, defense, financial, and telecommunications. The intrusion into healthcare company Anthem has been attributed to Deep Panda. This group is also known as Shell Crew, WebMasters, KungFu Kittens, and PinkPanther. Deep Panda also appears to be known as Black Vine based on the attribution of both group names to the Anthem intrusion. Some analysts track Deep Panda and APT19 as the same group, but it is unclear from open source information if the groups are the same.
Uses T1018 Remote System Discovery: Deep Panda has used ping to identify other machines of interest.
Uses T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares: Deep Panda uses net.exe to connect to network shares using net use commands with compromised credentials.
Uses T1027.005 Indicator Removal from Tools: Deep Panda has updated and modified its malware, resulting in different hash values that evade detection.
Uses T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation: The Deep Panda group is known to utilize WMI for lateral movement.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: Deep Panda uses the Microsoft Tasklist utility to list processes running on systems.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Deep Panda has used PowerShell scripts to download and execute programs in memory, without writing to disk.
Uses T1218.010 Regsvr32: Deep Panda has used regsvr32.exe to execute a server variant of Derusbi in victim networks.
Uses T1505.003 Web Shell: Deep Panda uses Web shells on publicly accessible Web servers to access victim networks.
Uses T1546.008 Accessibility Features: Deep Panda has used the sticky-keys technique to bypass the RDP login screen on remote systems during intrusions.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: Deep Panda has used -w hidden to conceal PowerShell windows by setting the WindowStyle parameter to hidden.

title: ATT&CK Group G0099: APT-C-36
text:
ATT&CK Group G0099: APT-C-36
Associated names: Blind Eagle.
APT-C-36 is a suspected South America espionage group that has been active since at least 2018. The group mainly targets Colombian government institutions as well as important corporations in the financial sector, petroleum industry, and professional manufacturing.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: APT-C-36 has used ConfuserEx to obfuscate its variant of Imminent Monitor, compressed payload and RAT packages, and password protected encrypted email attachments to avoid detection.
Uses T1036.004 Masquerade Task or Service: APT-C-36 has disguised its scheduled tasks as those used by Google.
Uses T1053.005 Scheduled Task: APT-C-36 has used a macro function to set scheduled tasks, disguised as those used by Google.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: APT-C-36 has embedded a VBScript within a malicious Word document which is executed upon the document opening.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: APT-C-36 has downloaded binary data from a specified domain after the malicious document is opened.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: APT-C-36 has prompted victims to accept macros in order to execute the subsequent payload.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: APT-C-36 has used spearphishing emails with password protected RAR attachment to avoid being detected by the email gateway.
Uses T1571 Non-Standard Port: APT-C-36 has used port 4050 for C2 communications.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: APT-C-36 obtained and used a modified variant of Imminent Monitor.

title: ATT&CK Group G0089: The White Company
text:
ATT&CK Group G0089: The White Company
The White Company is a likely state-sponsored threat actor with advanced capabilities. From 2017 through 2018, the group led an espionage campaign called Operation Shaheen targeting government and military organizations in Pakistan.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: The White Company has obfuscated their payloads through packing.
Uses T1070.004 File Deletion: The White Company has the ability to delete its malware entirely from the target system.
Uses T1124 System Time Discovery: The White Company has checked the current date on the victim system.
Uses T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution: The White Company has taken advantage of a known vulnerability in Microsoft Word (CVE 2012-0158) to execute code.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: The White Company has used phishing lure documents that trick users into opening them and infecting their computers.
Uses T1518.001 Security Software Discovery: The White Company has checked for specific antivirus products on the target’s computer, including Kaspersky, Quick Heal, AVG, BitDefender, Avira, Sophos, Avast!, and ESET.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: The White Company has sent phishing emails with malicious Microsoft Word attachments to victims.

title: ATT&CK Group G0033: Poseidon Group
text:
ATT&CK Group G0033: Poseidon Group
Poseidon Group is a Portuguese-speaking threat group that has been active since at least 2005. The group has a history of using information exfiltrated from victims to blackmail victim companies into contracting the Poseidon Group as a security firm.
Uses T1003 OS Credential Dumping: Poseidon Group conducts credential dumping on victims, with a focus on obtaining credentials belonging to domain and database servers.
Uses T1007 System Service Discovery: After compromising a victim, Poseidon Group discovers all running services.
Uses T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location: Poseidon Group tools attempt to spoof anti-virus processes as a means of self-defense.
Uses T1049 System Network Connections Discovery: Poseidon Group obtains and saves information about victim network interfaces and addresses.
Uses T1057 Process Discovery: After compromising a victim, Poseidon Group lists all running processes.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: The Poseidon Group's Information Gathering Tool (IGT) includes PowerShell components.
Uses T1087.001 Local Account: Poseidon Group searches for administrator accounts on both the local victim machine and the network.
Uses T1087.002 Domain Account: Poseidon Group searches for administrator accounts on both the local victim machine and the network.

title: ATT&CK Group G0140: LazyScripter
text:
ATT&CK Group G0140: LazyScripter
LazyScripter is threat group that has mainly targeted the airlines industry since at least 2018, primarily using open-source toolsets.
Uses T1027.010 Command Obfuscation: LazyScripter has leveraged the BatchEncryption tool to perform advanced batch script obfuscation and encoding techniques.
Uses T1036 Masquerading: LazyScripter has used several different security software icons to disguise executables.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: LazyScripter has used PowerShell scripts to execute malicious code.
Uses T1059.003 Windows Command Shell: LazyScripter has used batch files to deploy open-source and multi-stage RATs.
Uses T1059.005 Visual Basic: LazyScripter has used VBScript to execute malicious code.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: LazyScripter has used JavaScript in its attacks.
Uses T1071.004 DNS: LazyScripter has leveraged dynamic DNS providers for C2 communications.
Uses T1102 Web Service: LazyScripter has used GitHub to host its payloads to operate spam campaigns.
Uses T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer: LazyScripter had downloaded additional tools to a compromised host.
Uses T1204.001 Malicious Link: LazyScripter has relied upon users clicking on links to malicious files.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: LazyScripter has lured users to open malicious email attachments.
Uses T1218.005 Mshta: LazyScripter has used `mshta.exe` to execute Koadic stagers.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: LazyScripter has used `rundll32.exe` to execute Koadic stagers.
Uses T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder: LazyScripter has achieved persistence via writing a PowerShell script to the autorun registry key.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: LazyScripter has used spam emails weaponized with archive or document files as its initial infection vector.
Uses T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: LazyScripter has used spam emails that contain a link that redirects the victim to download a malicious document.
Uses T1583.001 Domains: LazyScripter has used dynamic DNS providers to create legitimate-looking subdomains for C2.
Uses T1583.006 Web Services: LazyScripter has established GitHub accounts to host its toolsets.

title: ATT&CK Group G0140: LazyScripter
text:
ATT&CK Group G0140: LazyScripter
Uses T1588.001 Malware: LazyScripter has used a variety of open-source remote access Trojans for its operations.
Uses T1608.001 Upload Malware: LazyScripter has hosted open-source remote access Trojans used in its operations in GitHub.

title: ATT&CK Group G0084: Gallmaker
text:
ATT&CK Group G0084: Gallmaker
Gallmaker is a cyberespionage group that has targeted victims in the Middle East and has been active since at least December 2017. The group has mainly targeted victims in the defense, military, and government sectors.
Uses T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information: Gallmaker obfuscated shellcode used during execution.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: Gallmaker used PowerShell to download additional payloads and for execution.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Gallmaker sent victims a lure document with a warning that asked victims to “enable content” for execution.
Uses T1559.002 Dynamic Data Exchange: Gallmaker attempted to exploit Microsoft’s DDE protocol in order to gain access to victim machines and for execution.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: Gallmaker has used WinZip, likely to archive data prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment: Gallmaker sent emails with malicious Microsoft Office documents attached.

title: ATT&CK Group G1019: MoustachedBouncer
text:
ATT&CK Group G1019: MoustachedBouncer
MoustachedBouncer is a cyberespionage group that has been active since at least 2014 targeting foreign embassies in Belarus.
Uses T1027.002 Software Packing: MoustachedBouncer has used malware plugins packed with Themida.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: MoustachedBouncer has used plugins to execute PowerShell scripts.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: MoustachedBouncer has used JavaScript to deliver malware hosted on HTML pages.
Uses T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation: MoustachedBouncer has exploited CVE-2021-1732 to execute malware components with elevated rights.
Uses T1074.002 Remote Data Staging: MoustachedBouncer has used plugins to save captured screenshots to `.\AActdata\` on an SMB share.
Uses T1090 Proxy: MoustachedBouncer has used a reverse proxy tool similar to the GitHub repository revsocks.
Uses T1113 Screen Capture: MoustachedBouncer has used plugins to take screenshots on targeted systems.
Uses T1659 Content Injection: MoustachedBouncer has injected content into DNS, HTTP, and SMB replies to redirect specifically-targeted victims to a fake Windows Update page to download malware.

title: ATT&CK Group G0052: CopyKittens
text:
ATT&CK Group G0052: CopyKittens
CopyKittens is an Iranian cyber espionage group that has been operating since at least 2013. It has targeted countries including Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the U.S., Jordan, and Germany. The group is responsible for the campaign known as Operation Wilted Tulip.
Uses T1059.001 PowerShell: CopyKittens has used PowerShell Empire.
Uses T1090 Proxy: CopyKittens has used the AirVPN service for operational activity.
Uses T1218.011 Rundll32: CopyKittens uses rundll32 to load various tools on victims, including a lateral movement tool named Vminst, Cobalt Strike, and shellcode.
Uses T1553.002 Code Signing: CopyKittens digitally signed an executable with a stolen certificate from legitimate company AI Squared.
Uses T1560.001 Archive via Utility: CopyKittens uses ZPP, a.NET console program, to compress files with ZIP.
Uses T1560.003 Archive via Custom Method: CopyKittens encrypts data with a substitute cipher prior to exfiltration.
Uses T1564.003 Hidden Window: CopyKittens has used -w hidden and -windowstyle hidden to conceal PowerShell windows.
Uses T1588.002 Tool: CopyKittens has used Metasploit, Empire, and AirVPN for post-exploitation activities.

title: ATT&CK Group G1033: Star Blizzard
text:
ATT&CK Group G1033: Star Blizzard
Associated names: SEABORGIUM, Callisto Group, TA446, COLDRIVER.
Star Blizzard is a cyber espionage and influence group originating in Russia that has been active since at least 2019. Star Blizzard campaigns align closely with Russian state interests and have included persistent phishing and credential theft against academic, defense, government, NGO, and think tank organizations in NATO countries, particularly the US and the UK.
Uses T1059.007 JavaScript: Star Blizzard has used JavaScript to redirect victim traffic from an adversary controlled server to a server hosting the Evilginx phishing framework.
Uses T1078 Valid Accounts: Star Blizzard has used stolen credentials to sign into victim email accounts.
Uses T1114.002 Remote Email Collection: Star Blizzard has remotely accessed victims' email accounts to steal messages and attachments.
Uses T1114.003 Email Forwarding Rule: Star Blizzard has abused email forwarding rules to monitor the activities of a victim, steal information, and maintain persistent access after compromised credentials are reset.
Uses T1204.002 Malicious File: Star Blizzard has lured targets into opening malicious.pdf files to deliver malware.
Uses T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie: Star Blizzard has used EvilGinx to steal the session cookies of victims directed to phishing domains.
